📝 Chapter 9 — CBA Practice Questions

Q1
What are the 4 required top-level fields in every catalog-info.yaml?
Show Answer
Answer

1. apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
2. kind — Component | API | System | Domain | Resource | User | Group
3. metadata — at minimum must contain name
4. spec — type-specific properties (varies by kind)

Explanation

If ANY of these 4 fields are missing, the entity WILL FAIL ingestion. The CBA exam tests this — you might be shown a YAML snippet and asked to identify what's missing.

# SKELETAL DIAGRAM — Minimum Valid catalog-info.yaml
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1   # ← REQUIRED
kind: Component                      # ← REQUIRED
metadata:
  name: my-service                   # ← REQUIRED (in metadata)
spec:
  type: service                      # ← REQUIRED
  owner: team-platform               # ← REQUIRED (in spec)
Q2
What is the difference between labels, tags, and annotations in metadata?
Show Answer
Answer

Labels: Key-value pairs for filtering entities (e.g., language: python). Use in catalog filters.
Tags: Simple strings for search (e.g., [django, backend]). Quick search in the search bar.
Annotations: Key-value pairs for integrations (e.g., github.com/project-slug). Connect to external tools.
The CBA will ask you which one to use for a given purpose.

Explanation

Labels=filter (key:value), Tags=search (strings), Annotations=integrations (key:value). Each serves a different purpose. CBA: know which to use — labels for filtering, tags for search, annotations for external tool connections.

# Labels vs Tags vs Annotations — Visual Distinction
metadata:
  labels:                        # ← FILTERING: key: value
    language: python
    tier: backend
  tags:                          # ← SEARCH: simple strings
    - django
    - postgresql
  annotations:                   # ← INTEGRATIONS: external tools
    github.com/project-slug: anihpj/jobpost
    backstage.io/kubernetes-id: jobpost
Q3
You have a catalog-info.yaml that fails ingestion with "YAML syntax error". What's the most common cause?
Show Answer
Answer

The most common causes are: (1) Trailing commas after the last item in a list (YAML doesn't use commas at all!), (2) Wrong indentation — YAML uses 2-space indentation, not tabs, (3) Mixed tabs and spaces, (4) Missing colon after a key. Always validate with yarn backstage-cli validate-entity before committing.

Explanation

4 common YAML errors: trailing commas, wrong indentation, tabs vs spaces, missing colon. Always run validate-entity before commit. CBA: know these 4 errors and the validation command.

# ❌ WRONG — trailing comma, tab indent, missed colon
kind Component
  metadata:
    name: my-service,
	tabs: evil

# ✅ CORRECT — no commas, 2-space indent, colon after key
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: my-service
  description: A clean entity
Q4
How do you define multiple entities in a single catalog-info.yaml file?
Show Answer
Answer

Use the --- separator between entity definitions. Each entity starts with --- on its own line, followed by the complete entity definition (apiVersion, kind, metadata, spec). This is standard YAML multi-document syntax. All entities in the file share the same location.

Explanation

Multi-entity files use --- (3 dashes) YAML separator. Each entity has its own apiVersion, kind, metadata, spec. All share the same catalog location. CBA: know --- syntax for multi-entity files.

# Multi-entity catalog-info.yaml — 3 dashes between entities
---
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: jobpost
spec:
  type: service
  owner: team-platform
---
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: API
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api
spec:
  type: openapi
  owner: team-platform
  definition: $text: ./openapi.yaml
Q5
Which annotation links a Component to its documentation in TechDocs?
Show Answer
Answer

backstage.io/techdocs-ref: dir:. — This tells TechDocs to look for an mkdocs.yml file and /docs folder in the same directory as the catalog-info.yaml. Alternatives: url:https://docs.example.com for external docs.

Explanation

TechDocs annotation = backstage.io/techdocs-ref. dir:. = docs in same directory. url: = external docs. CBA: know the annotation name and the dir:. vs url: options.

# TechDocs Annotation Options
# Option 1: Docs in same repo (MOST COMMON)
backstage.io/techdocs-ref: dir:.

# Option 2: External documentation URL
backstage.io/techdocs-ref: url:https://docs.mycompany.com
Q6
What annotation links a Component to its Kubernetes deployment?
Show Answer
Answer

backstage.io/kubernetes-id: jobpost — This matches the Component to a K8s Deployment with the same name. Alternatively, use backstage.io/kubernetes-namespace: anihpj-prod to scope to a specific namespace, or backstage.io/kubernetes-label-selector: app=jobpost for label-based matching.

Explanation

3 K8s annotation options: kubernetes-id (name match), kubernetes-namespace (scope), kubernetes-label-selector (label query). kubernetes-id is most common. CBA: know all 3 annotation formats.

# 3 Ways to Link a Component to K8s Resources
backstage.io/kubernetes-id: jobpost              # ← Exact name match
backstage.io/kubernetes-namespace: anihpj-prod   # ← Scope to namespace
backstage.io/kubernetes-label-selector: app=jobpost  # ← Label query
Q7
What is $text used for in an API entity's spec.definition?
Show Answer
Answer

$text is a placeholder that points to an external file containing the actual API spec. Example: definition: $text: https://github.com/anihpj/jobpost/blob/main/openapi.yaml. The catalog processor fetches the file at that URL and inlines it. Other placeholders include $json and $yaml.

Explanation

$text/$json/$yaml are placeholders for external content. Catalog processor fetches and inlines. Used for API specs, docs, etc. CBA: know the placeholder syntax and that the processor fetches external content.

Q8
What command validates a catalog-info.yaml file?
Show Answer
Answer

yarn backstage-cli validate-entity ./catalog-info.yaml — This checks the YAML syntax and validates that the entity has all required fields (apiVersion, kind, metadata.name, spec). Run this before committing catalog-info.yaml files to avoid ingestion failures.

Explanation

validate-entity = pre-commit YAML validation. Checks syntax + required fields. Prevents ingestion failures. CBA: know the exact command and that it should be run before commit.

Q9
You want to add a "View Dashboard" link to a Component's entity page. Where in the YAML do you add it?
Show Answer
Answer

In metadata.links. Example:
links:
- url: https://grafana.anihpj.com/d/jobpost
title: Dashboard
icon: dashboard
Links appear on the entity's Overview page. Each link can have a url, title, and optional icon.

Explanation

Links = metadata.links array. Each has url, title, icon. Appears on entity Overview page. CBA: know metadata.links is where external links are configured.

Q10
What happens if you omit the kind field from catalog-info.yaml?
Show Answer
Answer

The entity will fail catalog ingestion. The error message will say something like "kind is required" or "missing required field: kind". Without kind, Backstage doesn't know what type of entity this is (Component? API? Resource?) and cannot process it. The same applies to apiVersion, metadata.name, and spec — all 4 are mandatory.

Explanation

Missing kind = ingestion failure. All 4 required fields (apiVersion, kind, metadata.name, spec) are mandatory. Missing any = entity rejected. CBA: know the 4 mandatory fields and that missing any causes failure.

ity. Run before commit. Catches YAML errors.
📂$text PlaceholderPoints to external files. Catalog processor fetches & inlines. API specs, docs.
⚠️Common ErrorsTrailing commas, tab indentation, missing kind, missing owner, YAML syntax.

Chapter 10: Integrating Kubernetes with the Catalog

Backstage's Kubernetes plugin bridges the gap between your Catalog and your running infrastructure. It shows live K8s resource status (Deployments, Pods, Services) directly on entity pages. You'll learn how to configure it, link entities to K8s resources, and deploy anihpj to Kubernetes with full Backstage visibility.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours ☸️ K8s 🎯 CBA 22%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand what the Kubernetes plugin does and how it works
  • ✅ Configure the K8s plugin in app-config.yaml with cluster details
  • ✅ Link Catalog entities to K8s resources via annotations
  • ✅ View live K8s status on entity pages
  • ✅ Deploy anihpj/jobpost to Kubernetes with full Docker + K8s YAML
🎓 CBA Relevance
Backstage Catalog 22% Infrastructure 22%

10.1 The Kubernetes Plugin — What It Does

The K8s plugin connects to your Kubernetes clusters and displays live resource status on entity pages. When you view a Component in Backstage, the "Kubernetes" tab shows its Deployments, Pods, Services, and Ingresses — all in real time.

K8s Plugin Architecture
  ┌─────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │  ☸️ K8s Cluster      │───────▶│  Backstage               │
  │                     │        │  Kubernetes Plugin        │
  │  Deployment: jobpost│        │                          │
  │   ├── Pod 1 (Ready) │        │  jobpost Entity Page:    │
  │   ├── Pod 2 (Ready) │        │  ┌─────────────────────┐ │
  │   └── Pod 3 (Ready) │        │  │ ☸️ KUBERNETES       │ │
  │                     │        │  │ Deployment: jobpost │ │
  │  Service: jobpost   │        │  │ 3/3 Pods Running   │ │
  │  Ingress: jobpost   │        │  │ Service: :8000     │ │
  │                     │        │  │ Ingress: URL       │ │
  └─────────────────────┘        │  └─────────────────────┘ │
                                  └──────────────────────────┘

10.2 Kubernetes Plugin Configuration

Step 1: Install the Plugins

Install K8s Frontend + Backend Plugins

  # Install frontend plugin (adds the "Kubernetes" tab to entity pages)
  $ yarn add --cwd packages/app @backstage/plugin-kubernetes

  # Install backend plugin (connects to K8s API servers)
  $ yarn add --cwd packages/backend @backstage/plugin-kubernetes-backend

  # Register in packages/app/src/plugins.ts:
  export { kubernetesPlugin } from '@backstage/plugin-kubernetes';

  # Register in packages/backend/src/index.ts:
  backend.add(import('@backstage/plugin-kubernetes-backend'));

Step 2: Configure app-config.yaml

app-config.yaml — K8s Plugin Configuration

  # app-config.yaml
  kubernetes:
    serviceLocatorMethod:
      type: 'multiTenant'                # ← How services are found
    clusterLocatorMethods:
      - type: 'config'                   # ← Static cluster list
        clusters:
          - name: 'anihpj-prod'          # ← Cluster display name
            url: 'https://k8s-api.anihpj.com'  # ← API Server URL
            authProvider: 'serviceAccount'      # ← Auth method
            serviceAccountToken: ${K8S_SA_TOKEN}  # ← Token from env var
            skipTLSVerify: false         # ← TLS verification
            dashboardUrl: 'https://k8s-dash.anihpj.com'  # ← K8s dashboard link

Step 3: Create K8s ServiceAccount & RBAC

Backstage needs read-only access to your K8s cluster. Create a ServiceAccount with appropriate RBAC permissions:

K8s RBAC for Backstage Service Account

  # 1. Create ServiceAccount
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: ServiceAccount
  metadata:
    name: backstage-reader
    namespace: backstage
  ---
  # 2. Create ClusterRole (read-only)
  apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
  kind: ClusterRole
  metadata:
    name: backstage-reader
  rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods", "services", "configmaps"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  - apiGroups: ["apps"]
    resources: ["deployments", "replicasets"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  - apiGroups: ["networking.k8s.io"]
    resources: ["ingresses"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  ---
  # 3. Bind ClusterRole to ServiceAccount
  apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
  kind: ClusterRoleBinding
  metadata:
    name: backstage-reader
  subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: backstage-reader
    namespace: backstage
  roleRef:
    kind: ClusterRole
    name: backstage-reader
    apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  ---
  # 4. Get the ServiceAccount token
  $ kubectl create token backstage-reader -n backstage
  # → Copy this token to K8S_SA_TOKEN env var
⚠️ CBA Exam: Backstage K8s Permissions

Backstage needs get, list, watch on Pods, Services, Deployments, ReplicaSets, and Ingresses. It NEVER creates, updates, or deletes K8s resources — it's read-only. The CBA may ask what minimum RBAC permissions Backstage requires.

10.3 Linking K8s Resources to Catalog Entities

Backstage matches K8s resources to Catalog entities using annotations in catalog-info.yaml. There are 3 linking methods:

3 Methods to Link K8s to Entities

  # Method 1: By Name (simplest)
  metadata:
    annotations:
      backstage.io/kubernetes-id: jobpost
  # → Matches K8s Deployment named "jobpost"

  # Method 2: By Namespace
  metadata:
    annotations:
      backstage.io/kubernetes-namespace: anihpj-prod
  # → Shows ALL K8s resources in that namespace

  # Method 3: By Label Selector (most flexible)
  metadata:
    annotations:
      backstage.io/kubernetes-label-selector: app=jobpost
  # → Matches any K8s resource with label "app=jobpost"

10.4 Viewing K8s Resources in Backstage

When the K8s plugin is configured, every entity with a K8s annotation gets a "Kubernetes" tab. The data is live — it queries the K8s API directly each time you view the tab.

What You SeeDetails ShownWhere It Comes From
DeploymentsReplicas (ready/desired), strategy, selectorapps/v1 Deployment API
PodsStatus (Running/Pending/CrashLoopBackOff), restart count, agecore/v1 Pod API
Pod LogsStdout/stderr streams (last 100 lines)Pod logs sub-resource
Pod EventsSchedule, pull, start events with timestampscore/v1 Event API
ServicesType (ClusterIP/LoadBalancer), ports, selectorcore/v1 Service API
IngressesHost, path, TLS config, backend servicenetworking.k8s.io/v1 Ingress API
Resource UsageCPU/memory requests & limits (if metrics-server installed)metrics.k8s.io API

Chapter 10 CBA Quick Win: The K8s plugin connects clusters via kubernetes.clusterLocatorMethods in app-config.yaml. Entities link via backstage.io/kubernetes-id annotation. Authentication uses service account tokens (stored as env vars). The plugin shows live data — no caching by default. Backstage needs get/list/watch RBAC — it's read-only.

10.5 Deploying anihpj to Kubernetes — Complete Walkthrough

Dockerfile for anihpj/jobpost Django App

  FROM python:3.11-slim
  ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
  ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
  WORKDIR /app
  RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y gcc libpq-dev && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
  COPY requirements.txt .
  RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
  COPY . .
  RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
  EXPOSE 8000
  CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "3"]
Kubernetes Deployment for jobpost

  apiVersion: apps/v1
  kind: Deployment
  metadata:
    name: jobpost
    namespace: anihpj-prod
    labels:
      app: jobpost
  spec:
    replicas: 3
    selector:
      matchLabels:
        app: jobpost
    template:
      metadata:
        labels:
          app: jobpost
        annotations:
          backstage.io/kubernetes-id: jobpost  # ← Links to Backstage!
      spec:
        containers:
        - name: jobpost
          image: anihpj/jobpost:latest
          ports:
          - containerPort: 8000
          env:
          - name: DATABASE_URL
            valueFrom:
              secretKeyRef:
                name: jobpost-secrets
                key: database-url
          - name: DJANGO_SECRET_KEY
            valueFrom:
              secretKeyRef:
                name: jobpost-secrets
                key: django-secret-key
          - name: DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE
            valueFrom:
              configMapKeyRef:
                name: jobpost-config
                key: DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi
            limits:
              cpu: 500m
              memory: 512Mi
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health/
              port: 8000
            initialDelaySeconds: 30
            periodSeconds: 10
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready/
              port: 8000
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 5
  ---
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: ConfigMap
  metadata:
    name: jobpost-config
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  data:
    DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE: "anihpj.settings.production"
    ALLOWED_HOSTS: "jobpost.anihpj.com"
    LOG_LEVEL: "INFO"
  ---
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Secret
  metadata:
    name: jobpost-secrets
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  type: Opaque
  stringData:
    database-url: "postgresql://user:pass@postgres:5432/jobpost"
    django-secret-key: "super-secret-key-change-in-production"
  ---
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Service
  metadata:
    name: jobpost
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  spec:
    selector:
      app: jobpost
    ports:
    - port: 8000
      targetPort: 8000
    type: ClusterIP
⚡ SPEED TIP — K8s Annotations: The 3 essential K8s annotations for the CBA: backstage.io/kubernetes-id (matches Deployment name), backstage.io/kubernetes-namespace (overrides default namespace), and backstage.io/kubernetes-label-selector (finds resources by label). Without these annotations, the K8s tab shows nothing. This is tested on nearly every exam.

📝 Chapter 10 — CBA Practice Questions

Q1
What does the Kubernetes plugin in Backstage do?
Show Answer
Answer

The K8s plugin connects Backstage to your Kubernetes clusters and displays live resource status on entity pages. It shows Deployments (replicas, status), Pods (health, logs, events), Services (endpoints, ports), and Ingresses (URLs). Data is fetched live from the K8s API each time you view the tab.

Explanation

The K8s plugin is a full-stack plugin: frontend React component renders the K8s tab on entity pages, backend Node.js service communicates with the K8s API server. The data is always live — there's no caching by default. This means any pod crash or deployment rollback is visible instantly, but it also means Backstage needs a working network connection to the K8s API at all times.

Q2
Where do you configure K8s cluster connection details for Backstage?
Show Answer
Answer

In app-config.yaml under the kubernetes section. Configure clusterLocatorMethods with cluster name, API server URL, authentication method (serviceAccount), and token. All secrets should use ${ENV_VAR} syntax.

Explanation

The kubernetes config block has two main sections: serviceLocatorMethod (how to find resources — multiTenant or singleTenant) and clusterLocatorMethods (how to connect — config, gke, eks, aks). The config type requires explicit cluster listing; cloud types auto-discover. Always use ${ENV_VAR} for tokens and URLs — never hardcode K8s connection details.

Q3
What are the 3 ways to link a Catalog entity to K8s resources?
Show Answer
Answer

1. backstage.io/kubernetes-id: jobpost — Match by Deployment name
2. backstage.io/kubernetes-namespace: anihpj-prod — Show all resources in namespace
3. backstage.io/kubernetes-label-selector: app=jobpost — Match by K8s labels

Explanation

These 3 annotations are the bridge between Backstage Catalog entities and K8s resources. kubernetes-id is the most common — it must match the Deployment name EXACTLY (case-sensitive). kubernetes-namespace overrides the default namespace. kubernetes-label-selector uses K8s label query syntax. You can use any combination — Backstage OR's them together to find matching resources.

Q4
What authentication method does Backstage use to connect to K8s clusters?
Show Answer
Answer

Service Account tokens are the most common method. You create a ServiceAccount in the K8s cluster with appropriate RBAC permissions, get its token, and pass it to Backstage via serviceAccountToken: ${K8S_SA_TOKEN}. OIDC is also supported as an alternative.

Explanation

ServiceAccount tokens are the simplest auth method: create a SA, grant it RBAC, get the token, pass to Backstage via env var. OIDC is more complex but provides dynamic, short-lived tokens — better for production security. The CBA will test both: know that authProvider: serviceAccount is the most common, and authProvider: oidc is for cloud-managed clusters with identity providers.

Q5
Write the complete app-config.yaml kubernetes section to connect a cluster named "anihpj-prod".
Show Answer
Answer
kubernetes:
  serviceLocatorMethod:
    type: 'multiTenant'
  clusterLocatorMethods:
    - type: 'config'
      clusters:
        - name: 'anihpj-prod'
          url: 'https://k8s-api.anihpj.com'
          authProvider: 'serviceAccount'
          serviceAccountToken: ${K8S_SA_TOKEN}
Explanation

This is the complete minimum config for a single K8s cluster. serviceLocatorMethod: multiTenant enables namespace-per-team discovery. clusterLocatorMethods[0].type: config means you're manually listing clusters (vs. cloud auto-discovery). Each cluster needs: name (identifier), url (API server endpoint), authProvider (serviceAccount or oidc), and the token. Never hardcode the token — always use ${K8S_SA_TOKEN}.

Q6
You deployed jobpost to K8s but the entity page shows no K8s tab. What are 3 things to check?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Is the K8s plugin installed? (@backstage/plugin-kubernetes in frontend + backend)
2. Is the annotation present? (backstage.io/kubernetes-id: jobpost in catalog-info.yaml)
3. Is the cluster config correct? (URL, auth token, skipTLSVerify if self-signed cert)

Explanation

This is a classic CBA troubleshooting scenario. Debug order: (1) Plugin installed? Both frontend AND backend packages needed. (2) Annotation present? Without backstage.io/kubernetes-id, Backstage doesn't know what to look for. (3) Config correct? Check URL, auth, and TLS settings. 90% of "no K8s tab" issues are #2 — the annotation is missing or doesn't match the Deployment name exactly.

Q7
Where does Backstage get K8s resource data — from a cache or live?
Show Answer
Answer

Live — the K8s plugin calls the K8s API server directly each time you view the entity's K8s tab. There's no built-in caching by default. This means the data is always current but also means Backstage needs network connectivity to the K8s API server.

Explanation

Unlike the Catalog (which caches entity data), the K8s plugin is always live. Every page view triggers a fresh API call to the K8s cluster. Pros: data is always accurate — if a pod just crashed, you'll see it. Cons: adds latency to page loads, and if the K8s API is slow or unreachable, the K8s tab hangs. You can add caching via Redis if needed, but it's not built-in.

Q8
What K8s RBAC permissions does Backstage need to view resources?
Show Answer
Answer

At minimum: get, list, and watch on Deployments, Pods, Services, Ingresses, and ReplicaSets. Create a ClusterRole with these permissions and bind it to the ServiceAccount that Backstage uses. This is read-only — Backstage never modifies K8s resources.

Explanation

The CBA tests K8s RBAC understanding. Backstage only needs read-only verbs (get, list, watch) — it never creates or modifies K8s objects. The watch verb enables real-time streaming of resource changes. A common exam trap: suggesting Backstage needs create or update permissions. It doesn't. ClusterRole binds to a ServiceAccount, which Backstage uses to authenticate to the K8s API.

Q9
What does the multiTenant serviceLocatorMethod do?
Show Answer
Answer

multiTenant means Backstage looks for K8s resources in all namespaces that match the entity's annotations. The alternative is singleTenant which restricts to a single configured namespace. Multi-tenant is the most common configuration for organizations running multiple teams/services in different namespaces.

Explanation

The CBA expects you to know the difference between multiTenant and singleTenant. multiTenant is the default because it supports namespace-per-team architectures — each team's services live in their own K8s namespace, and Backstage discovers them all. singleTenant is simpler but only works when all services share one namespace. Choose multiTenant unless you have a specific reason for single.

Q10
You have 2 K8s clusters (prod and staging). How do you configure Backstage to show resources from both?
Show Answer
Answer

Add both clusters to the clusters array in kubernetes.clusterLocatorMethods[0].clusters. Each cluster gets its own name, URL, and auth token. Backstage queries ALL configured clusters and merges the results on the entity page. Example:
clusters:
- name: 'anihpj-prod'
url: 'https://k8s-prod.anihpj.com'
- name: 'anihpj-staging'
url: 'https://k8s-staging.anihpj.com'

Explanation

Multi-cluster configuration is a CBA favorite. Backstage queries ALL clusters in the clusters array and merges results on the entity page — if the same entity exists in both prod and staging, both appear labeled by cluster name. Each cluster can have different auth methods (serviceAccount for one, OIDC for another). Cloud locators (GKE/EKS/AKS) auto-discover clusters; config type requires manual listing.

🚀 Part 4: Software Templates — Scaffolding Made Easy 🟡 Intermediate

Chapter 11: Software Templates — Scaffolding New Projects

Software Templates are Backstage's "Create" button — they let developers scaffold new projects in minutes instead of hours. A template is a blueprint that combines user inputs, file skeletons, and automated actions to create production-ready repositories with CI/CD, K8s manifests, and Catalog registration — all from a single form.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2.5 hours 🚀 Templates 🎯 CBA 32%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand the problem templates solve — "2 hours → 2 minutes"
  • ✅ Master template anatomy: apiVersion, parameters, steps, actions
  • ✅ Define user input forms with parameters, validation, and UI pickers
  • ✅ Use built-in actions: fetch, publish, register
  • ✅ Integrate CI/CD pipelines into generated projects
  • ✅ Build a complete Docker build pipeline for anihpj
🎓 CBA Relevance
Customizing Backstage 32%
Templates Are the #1 CBA Topic (32% of Exam)

The CBA exam heavily tests Software Templates — knowing template YAML structure, parameter types, action sequences, and how templates integrate with the Catalog. You'll need to identify correct vs incorrect template YAML, understand the execution flow, and know how to register templates so they appear in the "Create" menu.

11.1 What are Software Templates? — The 2-Hour vs 2-Minute Problem

Templates — Before vs After Backstage
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ❌ WITHOUT TEMPLATES (Manual Scaffolding)                   │
  │  1. Find a similar repo to copy from... 20 min               │
  │  2. Clone it and delete what you don't need... 15 min        │
  │  3. Rename everything (files, packages, configs)... 30 min   │
  │  4. Update CI/CD configs... 20 min                            │
  │  5. Create repo in GitHub and push... 10 min                  │
  │  6. Set up Docker/K8s manifests... 25 min                     │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────────                 │
  │  TOTAL: ~2 HOURS of tedious manual work                       │
  │                                                               │
  │  ✅ WITH BACKSTAGE TEMPLATES (Automated Scaffolding)          │
  │  1. Click "Create" → Choose Template → Fill Form → Done      │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────────                 │
  │  TOTAL: ~2 MINUTES — everything automated!                   │
  │  • GitHub repo created automatically                         │
  │  • CI/CD pipeline pre-configured                             │
  │  • K8s manifests generated                                   │
  │  • Catalog entity registered automatically                   │
  │  • TechDocs skeleton ready to go                             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 Template = Blueprint + Parameters + Actions

A template has 3 parts: Blueprint (the skeleton files — Dockerfile, CI config, K8s YAML), Parameters (user input form — service name, owner, description), and Actions (what happens — fetch skeleton, publish to GitHub, register in Catalog). Together they automate the entire project creation process.

11.2 Template Anatomy — Complete template.yaml

Complete template.yaml for a Django Microservice

  apiVersion: scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3
  kind: Template
  metadata:
    name: django-service
    title: Django Microservice
    description: Scaffold a new Django service for the anihpj ecosystem
    tags: [django, python, microservice, recommended]
  spec:
    owner: team-platform
    type: service

    # ── USER INPUTS (the form developers fill in) ──
    parameters:
      - title: Service Details
        required: [name, owner]
        properties:
          name:
            title: Service Name
            type: string
            description: Unique name for your service
            pattern: '^[a-z0-9-]+$'
            ui:autofocus: true
          description:
            title: Description
            type: string
            description: What does this service do?
          owner:
            title: Owner
            type: string
            ui:field: OwnerPicker
            ui:options:
              allowedKinds: [Group]

    # ── ACTIONS TO EXECUTE ──
    steps:
      - id: fetch-base
        name: Fetch Template Skeleton
        action: fetch:template
        input:
          url: ./skeleton
          values:
            name: ${{ parameters.name }}
            description: ${{ parameters.description }}
            owner: ${{ parameters.owner }}

      - id: publish
        name: Publish to GitHub
        action: publish:github
        input:
          allowedHosts: ['github.com']
          description: ${{ parameters.description }}
          repoUrl: github.com?owner=${{ parameters.owner }}&repo=${{ parameters.name }}
          defaultBranch: main

      - id: register
        name: Register in Catalog
        action: catalog:register
        input:
          repoContentsUrl: ${{ steps.publish.output.repoContentsUrl }}
          catalogInfoPath: /catalog-info.yaml

11.3 Template Parameters — The User Input Form

Parameter TypeExampleUI Renders AsValidation
stringService nameText input fieldpattern, minLength, maxLength
numberPort numberNumber inputminimum, maximum
booleanEnable monitoringCheckbox toggle—
arrayTags listMulti-select / tag inputitems, minItems, uniqueItems
objectNested configGrouped fieldsproperties, required
💡 UI Fields — Beyond Basic Inputs

Backstage provides special UI fields for common inputs: OwnerPicker (select from Users/Groups), RepoUrlPicker (select GitHub org/repo), EntityPicker (select from Catalog entities). These provide auto-complete and validation out of the box.

11.4 Template Actions — What Happens When You Click "Create"

Template Execution Flow
  👤 User fills form
       │
       ▼
  📝 Parameters collected (name, owner, description)
       │
       ▼
  ⬇️ Step 1: fetch:template → Copy skeleton files, replace placeholders
       │
       ▼
  🔧 Step 2: (optional) Custom actions → Run cookiecutter, process templates
       │
       ▼
  🚀 Step 3: publish:github → Create GitHub repo, push code
       │
       ▼
  📦 Step 4: catalog:register → Register new entity in Catalog
       │
       ▼
  ✅ Done! New service visible in Backstage Catalog!

fetch:template / fetch:plain

fetch:template copies a local ./skeleton directory with placeholder replacement (${{ values.name }}). fetch:plain copies files from a URL without placeholder processing. Use fetch:template when you need customized files; use fetch:plain for static files like license templates.

publish:github / publish:gitlab

Creates a new repository on GitHub/GitLab, pushes the skeleton code, and sets the default branch. Requires the GitHub/GitLab integration token configured in app-config.yaml. The repoUrl parameter uses query string format: github.com?owner=ORG&repo=NAME.

catalog:register

Registers the newly created repository in the Backstage Catalog by reading its catalog-info.yaml. This makes the new service immediately discoverable. The action reads repoContentsUrl from the publish step's output.

Custom Actions

You can build custom actions for organization-specific needs — e.g., creating a Jira ticket, sending Slack notifications, provisioning cloud resources. Custom actions use createTemplateAction() from @backstage/plugin-scaffolder-backend.

End-to-End Flow: Template → Code → Docker → K8s

                           └──────────────────┘    └────────┬─────────┘
                                                            │
                                                            ▼

  ┌──────────────────┐                    ┌──────────────────┐

11.6 Docker Build Pipeline for anihpj/jobpost — Full End-to-End Flow

Real Project Structure — What Developers Create
  anihpj/
  ├── jobpost/              ← Django application code
  │   ├── models.py         ← Skills, User, JobPost, Location, Author
  │   ├── views.py          ← API endpoints (REST + GraphQL)
  │   └── urls.py           ← /api/jobs/, /api/skills/, /api/authors/

  │ $ curl -X POST :7007/api/catalog/entities        │

💡 7 Minutes from Git Push to Production

With a well-configured template + CI/CD pipeline, the flow is: 2 min (template execution) + 5 min (CI/CD pipeline) = 7 minutes from clicking "Create" to seeing your service live in Backstage with full K8s deployment status. This is the power of Backstage templates.

Real-Life: Creating a Template — Full 5-Step Workflow

Step-by-Step: From Zero to Template in Production

  # Step 1: Create the template directory structure
  $ mkdir -p templates/django-service/skeleton

  # Step 2: Write template.yaml and skeleton files
  $ vim templates/django-service/template.yaml
  $ vim templates/django-service/skeleton/catalog-info.yaml
  $ vim templates/django-service/skeleton/Dockerfile
  $ vim templates/django-service/skeleton/.github/workflows/ci.yml

  # Step 3: Register template in app-config.yaml
  scaffolder:
    templateLocations:
      - type: file
        target: ./templates/django-service/template.yaml

  # Step 4: Start Backstage and test the template
  $ yarn dev
  → Click CREATE → Choose "Django Microservice"
  → Fill form: Service Name, Owner, Description
  → Click CREATE again

  # Step 5: Verify the output
  Output:
  ✅ Fetch template skeleton... Done
  ✅ Publish to GitHub... Done (repo created: github.com/anihpj/my-service)
  ✅ Register in Catalog... Done (entity: Component:my-service)
  🎉 New service is live in the Catalog!
  🔗 GitHub: https://github.com/anihpj/my-service
  📋 Catalog: http://localhost:3000/catalog/default/component/my-service

11.8 Template Task List & Start Over — Managing Template Executions

Every template execution creates a unique task with its own ID. Backstage provides a Task List view and a "Start Over" feature for managing these executions.

📋
Template Task List

View all previously executed template tasks. Access from the "Create" page via the kebab menu (⋮) in the upper right corner. Each task shows its status (completed, failed, processing), template name, and execution time.

🔄
Start Over

Re-run a previously executed template with the same parameters pre-filled. Useful for: retrying failed templates, creating similar services, or re-running with minor parameter changes. Find it in the Task List context menu.

🔑 CBA Key Concept — Task Lifecycle

Each template execution is an async task: open → processing → completed/failed. The Task List shows history. "Start Over" pre-fills parameters but allows editing before re-execution. In case of failure, you can click each step to see its log output for debugging. You can also cancel a running task — the current step is cancelled if it supports the abort signal.

Disabling "Register Existing Component" Button

If you want to force all components to be created through templates (not manually registered), disable the button in app-config.yaml:

# app-config.yaml
app:
  routes:
    bindings:
      scaffolder.registerComponent: false  # ← Disables manual registration

📝 Chapter 11 — CBA Practice Questions

Q1
What problem do Software Templates solve? Describe the before/after.
Show Answer
Answer

Templates solve the manual project scaffolding problem. Before: developers spend ~2 hours copy-pasting from existing repos, renaming files, updating configs, creating repos, and setting up CI/CD. After: 2 minutes — click Create → fill form → everything is automated. Templates standardize project setup across the organization.

Explanation

The CBA tests the business value of templates: standardization (every new service follows the same patterns), speed (2 hours → 2 minutes), and self-service (no ops tickets). Templates are the #1 driver of Backstage ROI — every template execution is a manual process eliminated. The exam may ask: "What problem does Backstage's Scaffolder solve?" This is the answer.

Q2
What are the 3 essential parts of a template.yaml?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Parameters — User input form (name, owner, description, etc.)
2. Steps — Ordered list of actions to execute
3. Actions — What each step does (fetch:template, publish:github, catalog:register)

Explanation

These 3 parts are the skeleton of EVERY template. Parameters define what the user fills in. Steps define the execution order (sequential — step 2 runs only after step 1 completes). Actions are the actual work: fetch gets code, publish creates repos, register adds to catalog. The CBA will ask about the relationship between these 3 parts.

# TEMPLATE SKELETON — 3 Essential Parts
apiVersion: scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: django-service
spec:
  parameters:                    # ← PART 1: User input form
    - title: Service Details
      properties:
        name: { type: string }
        owner: { type: string }
  steps:                         # ← PART 2: Execution pipeline
    - id: fetch
      action: fetch:template     # ← PART 3: Action (copy skeleton)
    - id: publish
      action: publish:github     # ← PART 3: Action (create repo)
    - id: register
      action: catalog:register   # ← PART 3: Action (add to catalog)
Q3
What is the correct apiVersion for a Software Template?
Show Answer
Answer

apiVersion: scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3 — Note: it's scaffolder.backstage.io, NOT backstage.io. The kind is Template. This is different from catalog entities which use backstage.io/v1alpha1.

Explanation

This is a COMMON CBA trap. Catalog entities use backstage.io/v1alpha1 but templates use scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3. The exam will show template YAML with the wrong apiVersion and ask if it's valid. Remember: scaffolder for templates, backstage.io for catalog entities. Also: v1beta3 (current) not v1beta2 (deprecated).

# CBA TRAP — apiVersion Comparison
# ✅ Template entity (CORRECT)
apiVersion: scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3
kind: Template

# ✅ Catalog entity (CORRECT)
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component

# ❌ WRONG — mixing them up (exam trap!)
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Template           # ← WRONG apiVersion for Template!
Q4
What does the fetch:template action do?
Show Answer
Answer

fetch:template copies files from a local ./skeleton directory and replaces placeholders like ${{ values.name }} with actual parameter values. It's the first step in most templates — it creates the working directory with all boilerplate files customized for the new project.

Explanation

fetch:template does two things: (1) copies the skeleton directory, (2) performs cookiecutter-style placeholder replacement. Every ${{ values.X }} and ${{ parameters.X }} in ANY file in the skeleton gets replaced. This is how the template customizes code — package.json gets the project name, Dockerfile gets the port, catalog-info.yaml gets the owner. Without fetch:template, every new project would be identical.

Q5
How does publish:github create a repository?
Show Answer
Answer

publish:github uses the GitHub integration token (configured in app-config.yaml under integrations.github) to call the GitHub API and create a new repository. The repoUrl input uses query string format: github.com?owner=ORG&repo=NAME. It then pushes the scaffolded code to the new repo.

Explanation

The repoUrl format github.com?owner=X&repo=Y is unique to Backstage's Scaffolder — it's not a standard GitHub URL. The token comes from integrations.github[0].token in app-config.yaml. The action also sets up default branch protection if configured. Output: repoContentsUrl and repoUrl — these are used by subsequent steps like catalog:register.

Q6
What does catalog:register do in a template?
Show Answer
Answer

catalog:register reads the catalog-info.yaml from the newly created repository and registers it in the Backstage Catalog. This makes the new service immediately discoverable. It uses ${{ steps.publish.output.repoContentsUrl }} to reference the output from a previous publish step.

Explanation

The ${{ steps.STEP_ID.output.OUTPUT_NAME }} syntax is how steps pass data to each other. publish:github outputs repoContentsUrl (the URL to the repo's contents), and catalog:register reads it to know where to find catalog-info.yaml. This chaining is critical — without it, the register step doesn't know where the code was published. The CBA tests this inter-step data flow.

Q7
What is the OwnerPicker UI field and when would you use it?
Show Answer
Answer

OwnerPicker is a special UI field that provides an auto-complete dropdown for selecting Users or Groups from the Catalog. Use it for the owner parameter: ui:field: OwnerPicker with ui:options: allowedKinds: [Group]. It validates that the selected owner actually exists.

Explanation

OwnerPicker is a Backstage-specific UI component. It queries the Catalog API for Users/Groups and provides typeahead suggestions. The allowedKinds option restricts to Groups (teams) only — you typically want team ownership, not individual ownership. Without OwnerPicker, users would manually type owner names and risk typos. The CBA may ask which ui:field to use for entity reference selection.

Q8
How do you reference a parameter value inside a template skeleton file?
Show Answer
Answer

Use ${{ values.PARAM_NAME }} syntax. Example: in catalog-info.yaml inside the skeleton: name: ${{ values.name }}. The fetch:template action replaces these placeholders with actual values. You can also reference step outputs: ${{ steps.STEP_ID.output.OUTPUT_NAME }}.

Explanation

There are TWO placeholder syntaxes: ${{ values.X }} (parameter values passed to fetch:template) and ${{ steps.X.output.Y }} (outputs from previous steps). They look similar but serve different purposes. values are from user input; steps are from action execution. The CBA may show template YAML and ask which syntax to use in a specific context.

Q9
What are the 4 stages of the CI/CD pipeline for anihpj/jobpost?
Show Answer
Answer

1. TEST: pip install → pytest → linting
2. BUILD: docker build → tag → push to registry
3. DEPLOY: kubectl apply → rollout status
4. REGISTER: POST /api/catalog/entities to update Backstage

Explanation

This 4-stage CI/CD pipeline demonstrates Backstage's end-to-end integration. TEST ensures code quality, BUILD creates the Docker image, DEPLOY pushes to K8s, and REGISTER updates the catalog. Note that the REGISTER stage uses the Catalog API directly — this is how CI/CD pipelines auto-update entity metadata after each deployment (e.g., updating the deployed image tag in the catalog).

Q10
A developer uses your template but the new service doesn't appear in the Catalog. What 3 things could be wrong?
Show Answer
Answer

1. The catalog:register step might be missing or failed — check template execution logs
2. The catalog-info.yaml in the skeleton might have errors — validate with yarn backstage-cli validate-entity
3. The catalog location might not be configured — ensure the repo URL is registered in catalog.locations or the register step completed successfully

Explanation

This “not appearing in catalog” scenario is a CBA troubleshooting favorite. Debug order: (1) Check Scaffolder task logs — did catalog:register run? Did it fail? (2) Validate the catalog-info.yaml — missing apiVersion or kind = silent failure. (3) Check catalog locations — the register step creates a location, but if it fails, the entity won't appear. Also: give it 30 seconds — catalog ingestion is not instant.

11.7 Template Creation Walkthrough — Building the anihpj Django Template

Let's build a real Software Template from scratch — the same "Django Microservice" template used to scaffold the jobpost service. This end-to-end walkthrough covers every concept the CBA tests.

Part A: Create the Template Directory Structure

templates/
└── django-service/
    ├── template.yaml          # Template definition (metadata + parameters + steps)
    └── skeleton/               # Files copied to new project
        ├── catalog-info.yaml   # Auto-registers the new service
        ├── Dockerfile           # Container definition
        ├── mkdocs.yml           # TechDocs configuration
        └── docs/
            └── index.md         # Starter documentation

Part B: Write template.yaml — The Template Definition

apiVersion: scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3  # ← Note: scaffolder.backstage.io!
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: django-service
  title: Django Microservice
  description: Scaffolds a production-ready Django microservice
  tags: [recommended, python, django]
spec:
  owner: team-platform
  type: service

  # ── PARAMETERS: The form the user fills out ──
  parameters:
    - title: Service Details
      required: [name, owner]
      properties:
        name:
          title: Service Name
          type: string
          description: Unique name for the service
        owner:
          title: Owner
          type: string
          ui:field: OwnerPicker
          ui:options:
            allowedKinds: [Group]
        description:
          title: Description
          type: string
        port:
          title: Port
          type: number
          default: 8000

  # ── STEPS: The actions executed in order ──
  steps:
    - id: fetch
      name: Fetch Skeleton
      action: fetch:template
      input:
        url: ./skeleton
        values:
          name: ${{ parameters.name }}
          owner: ${{ parameters.owner }}
          description: ${{ parameters.description }}
          port: ${{ parameters.port }}

    - id: publish
      name: Publish to GitHub
      action: publish:github
      input:
        allowedHosts: [github.com]
        description: ${{ parameters.description }}
        repoUrl: github.com?owner=anihpj&repo=${{ parameters.name }}

    - id: register
      name: Register in Catalog
      action: catalog:register
      input:
        repoContentsUrl: ${{ steps.publish.output.repoContentsUrl }}
        catalogInfoPath: /catalog-info.yaml

Part C: Register the Template in Backstage

Add the template location to app-config.yaml:

scaffolder:
  templateLocations:
    - type: file
      target: ./templates/django-service/template.yaml
🔑 CBA Key Concept — The 3-Step Pipeline

Every template follows: fetch:template (get skeleton code) → publish:github (create repo) → catalog:register (add to catalog). The CBA WILL test this order. Steps are sequential — step 2 cannot start until step 1 completes. Each step's outputs are available to subsequent steps via ${{ steps.STEP_ID.output.OUTPUT_NAME }}.

⚡ SPEED TIP — Template 3-Step Pipeline: Every Software Template follows: fetch:template (get skeleton code) → publish:github (create repo) → catalog:register (add to catalog). The CBA will test this order. Additional actions like fs:delete or fetch:cookiecutter plug into this pipeline but never replace the core 3 steps.

Chapter 12: Template Actions & Customization

Actions are the engine behind every template — they do the actual work of creating repositories, registering entities, and transforming files. This chapter covers every built-in action, how to structure your template skeleton, and how to build custom actions for your organization's unique needs.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours ⚡ Actions 🎯 CBA 32%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Master all built-in template actions (fetch, publish, catalog, filesystem)
  • ✅ Understand action inputs/outputs and how they chain together
  • ✅ Structure template skeleton directories for maximum reusability
  • ✅ Build custom actions for organization-specific workflows

🎯 CBA Exam Relevance — Customizing Backstage 32%

Template actions are the heart of Backstage's self-service capability. The CBA tests your knowledge of which action to use for each scenario: fetch:template for skeleton code, publish:github for repo creation, and catalog:register for catalog integration. Expect questions about action inputs/outputs and the correct sequence of actions in a template.

🎯 CBA Exam Tip — Action Chain Order

The exam will test the CORRECT ORDER of actions: fetch → publish → register. You can't register before publishing, and you can't publish before fetching. Memorize: fetch:template (get code) → publish:github (create repo) → catalog:register (add to catalog). This 3-step pipeline is the heart of every template and a guaranteed exam topic.

12.1 Built-in Actions — Complete Reference

ActionWhat It DoesKey InputsKey Outputs

fetch:plainCopy files from URL (no placeholders)url, targetPath—

publish:gitlabCreate GitLab repo + push coderepoUrlrepoContentsUrl

12.2 The Template Skeleton — ./skeleton Directory

Skeleton Directory Structure for Django Template
  templates/django-service/
  ├── template.yaml              ← Template definition
  └── skeleton/                  ← Files copied to new project
      ├── catalog-info.yaml      ← Backstage entity (with ${{ values.xxx }})
      ├── Dockerfile             ← Container definition
      ├── requirements.txt       ← Python dependencies
      ├── manage.py              ← Django entry point
      ├── .github/
      │   └── workflows/
      │       └── ci.yml         ← CI/CD pipeline
      ├── k8s/
      │   ├── deployment.yaml    ← K8s deployment manifest

      └── docs/
          ├── index.md           ← TechDocs home page
          └── mkdocs.yml         ← MkDocs configuration

12.3 Custom Template Actions

When built-in actions aren't enough, you can create custom actions using createTemplateAction(). Common use cases: creating Jira tickets, sending Slack notifications, provisioning cloud resources, or running security scans.

Custom Action Example — Create Jira Ticket

  // packages/backend/src/plugins/scaffolder/actions/jira.ts
  import { createTemplateAction } from '@backstage/plugin-scaffolder-backend';

  export const createJiraTicketAction = () => {
    return createTemplateAction({
      id: 'anihpj:jira:create-ticket',
      description: 'Creates a Jira ticket for new service tracking',
      schema: {
        input: {
          type: 'object',
          required: ['project', 'summary'],
          properties: {
            project: { type: 'string', title: 'Jira Project Key' },
            summary: { type: 'string', title: 'Ticket Summary' },
          },
        },
      },
      async handler(ctx) {
        const { project, summary } = ctx.input;
        // Call Jira API...
        ctx.logger.info(`Created Jira ticket in ${project}`);
      },
    });
  };

12.4 Template Testing & Debugging

Debug Commands

  # 1. Validate template syntax
  $ yarn backstage-cli validate-template ./templates/django-service/template.yaml

  # 2. Run template in debug mode (shows detailed logs)
  $ yarn dev  # Then click Create → your template → check terminal output

  # 3. Test individual actions
  $ yarn backstage-cli test-action fetch:template

  # 4. Common errors:
  # ❌ "Step X failed: input validation error" → Check required parameters
  # ❌ "publish:github failed: 401" → Check GITHUB_TOKEN env var
  # ❌ "catalog:register: entity exists" → Entity already registered
  # ❌ "fetch:template: directory not found" → Check ./skeleton path

12.5 Template Actions — Visual Execution Map (CBA Essential)

How Template Actions Chain Together
  USER CLICKS "CREATE"

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STEP 1: fetch:template                                              │
  │  Input: url: ./skeleton, values: {name, owner}                       │
  │  Action: Copy + Replace ${{ values.X }} placeholders                 │
  │  Output: Working directory with customized files                     │
  └────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                                   │
                                   ▼

ActionPositionKey InputCan Fail If...

⚠️ CBA Exam Trap — Action Order Is Immutable

You CANNOT register before publishing, and you CANNOT publish before fetching. Order: fetch → publish → register. Each step depends on the previous. The CBA will show template YAML with reversed order and ask if it works — NO.

⚡ SPEED TIP — Action Chain Pattern: Every template follows the same 3-step flow: fetch:template (get skeleton code with placeholders replaced) → publish:github (create repo and push) → catalog:register (add to Backstage Catalog). Memorize this sequence — the CBA will test it. Additional actions like fs:delete or publish:gitlab plug into this pipeline but never replace the core 3.

📝 Chapter 12 — CBA Practice Questions

Q1
Name 5 built-in template actions and what each does.
Show Answer
Answer

1. fetch:template — Copy skeleton with placeholders
2. publish:github — Create GitHub repo + push code
3. catalog:register — Register in Catalog
4. fetch:plain — Copy files from URL
5. fs:delete — Delete files during template run

Explanation

The CBA expects you to know at least 5 actions by name and purpose. The core 3 (fetch:template, publish:github, catalog:register) appear in nearly every template. Additional ones like fetch:plain (static files), fetch:cookiecutter (legacy templates), publish:gitlab/bitbucket (alternative providers), and fs:delete (cleanup) round out the built-in set. The exam may ask "Which action would you use to..." scenarios.

Q2
What goes inside the ./skeleton directory?
Show Answer
Answer

All boilerplate files for the new project: catalog-info.yaml, Dockerfile, CI/CD workflow (.github/workflows/ci.yml), K8s manifests (k8s/deployment.yaml), TechDocs files (docs/index.md, mkdocs.yml), and source code stubs. Files use ${{ values.PARAM }} for customization.

Explanation

The skeleton is the blueprint for every new project. Key files every skeleton should include: (1) catalog-info.yaml — registers the service, (2) Dockerfile — containerizes it, (3) CI/CD workflow — automates testing/deployment, (4) K8s manifests — defines the deployment, (5) TechDocs — documentation scaffold. The ${{ values.X }} placeholders in these files ensure each generated project is unique.

Q3
How do you create a custom template action?
Show Answer
Answer

Use createTemplateAction() from @backstage/plugin-scaffolder-backend. Define: (1) a unique id, (2) input schema with JSON Schema, (3) an async handler function. Register the action in packages/backend/src/plugins/scaffolder.ts.

Explanation

Custom actions extend what templates can do. The id must be unique across all registered actions. The input schema (JSON Schema) defines what parameters the action accepts. The handler function receives ctx with input, logger, and workspace path. Common custom actions: create Jira ticket, send Slack notification, provision cloud resources, run security scans. Register in scaffolder.ts before the template using it.

Q4
How do you validate a template before using it?
Show Answer
Answer

Run yarn backstage-cli validate-template ./path/to/template.yaml. This checks YAML syntax, verifies required fields (apiVersion, kind, spec.parameters, spec.steps), and validates action definitions. Always validate before committing template changes.

Explanation

validate-template is like a linter for template.yaml. It catches: missing apiVersion, wrong kind (must be Template), missing parameters or steps, invalid action references, and YAML syntax errors. Run it in CI as a pre-commit check — a broken template affects everyone trying to create new services. The CBA may ask which command validates a template.

Q5
What's the difference between fetch:template and fetch:plain?
Show Answer
Answer

fetch:template copies local skeleton files AND replaces ${{ values.X }} placeholders with parameter values. fetch:plain copies files from a URL WITHOUT any placeholder processing. Use fetch:template for customizable boilerplate; use fetch:plain for static files.

Explanation

This is a classic CBA distinction. fetch:template does two things (copy + replace), fetch:plain does one (copy only). If your skeleton has no placeholders, both work the same. But if you need customization per project (different names, owners, ports), you MUST use fetch:template. The exam may show a template with fetch:plain and ask "Will the project name be customized?" Answer: No — fetch:plain ignores placeholders.

Q6
How do you pass data between template steps?
Show Answer
Answer

Using ${{ steps.STEP_ID.output.OUTPUT_NAME }}. For example, after a publish:github step with id "publish", you can reference its output: ${{ steps.publish.output.repoContentsUrl }}. This is how catalog:register knows which repo to register.

Explanation

Step output chaining is fundamental to multi-step templates. Each action declares what outputs it produces (e.g., publish:github outputs repoContentsUrl and repoUrl). Subsequent steps reference these using ${{ steps.ID.output.NAME }}. Without this mechanism, each step would be isolated — the register step wouldn't know where the code was published. The CBA tests this inter-step data flow pattern.

Q7
A template fails with "publish:github failed: 401". What's wrong?
Show Answer
Answer

The GitHub token is missing, expired, or lacks permissions. Check: (1) Is ${GITHUB_TOKEN} set as an environment variable? (2) Does the token have repo and workflow scopes? (3) Is the token configured in integrations.github in app-config.yaml?

Explanation

401 = Unauthorized. This is almost always a token issue. Debug order: (1) Is the env var set? echo $GITHUB_TOKEN — if empty, that's the problem. (2) Token scopes: classic PATs need repo (full control of private repos); fine-grained PATs need specific repo access. (3) app-config.yaml: check integrations.github[0].token: ${GITHUB_TOKEN} — the env var must match. Token expired? GitHub tokens can expire — rotate if needed.

Q8
Where should custom template actions be registered in the backend?
Show Answer
Answer

In packages/backend/src/plugins/scaffolder.ts. Import your custom action and add it to the scaffolder actions array. Example: scaffolderActions.push(createJiraTicketAction());. Actions must be registered before templates that use them.

Explanation

The scaffolder.ts file is the single registration point for all template actions. Every custom action must be imported and added to the actions array here. Order in the array doesn't matter — Backstage indexes by action ID. If a template references an unregistered action, it will fail at runtime with "action not found." Always restart Backstage after adding new actions.

Q9
What does publish:github output that catalog:register needs?
Show Answer
Answer

publish:github outputs repoContentsUrl (URL to fetch repo contents) and repoUrl (the clone URL). catalog:register uses repoContentsUrl to read the catalog-info.yaml from the newly created repository. The output is referenced as ${{ steps.publish.output.repoContentsUrl }}.

Explanation

The publish→register output chain is the most important data flow in templates. publish:github creates the repo and returns its location; catalog:register reads that location to find and ingest the entity YAML. Without repoContentsUrl, catalog:register has no idea where the code was published. This is why the publish step MUST complete before the register step — the output doesn't exist yet.

Q10
Your template works locally but fails on a colleague's machine. What are 3 possible causes?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Missing env vars — GITHUB_TOKEN or other secrets not set on their machine
2. Different Backstage version — template uses actions/features from a newer version
3. Skeleton path issue — relative paths in template.yaml may resolve differently depending on working directory. Always use paths relative to template.yaml location.

Explanation

\"Works on my machine\" problems in Backstage are usually environment-specific. (1) Env vars: GITHUB_TOKEN is per-developer — each dev needs their own token. (2) Version mismatch: if template uses a feature from Backstage v1.20 but colleague runs v1.18, it fails. (3) Path resolution: skeleton paths are relative to template.yaml — if the colleague cloned the repo in a different location, relative paths break. Use path.join(__dirname, './skeleton') for reliability.

Now let's build real templates for the anihpj ecosystem — a Django microservice, a React frontend, a database migration job, and an infrastructure-as-code template. Each template is production-ready with CI/CD, K8s manifests, and Catalog registration built in.

  • ✅ Build a React frontend template

13.1 Template: New Django Microservice

Django Service Template — Key Parameters & Skeleton
  Parameters: name, description, owner, pythonVersion, includeDocker
  Skeleton includes:
    ├── catalog-info.yaml     ← Pre-configured for jobpost-style projects
    ├── Dockerfile            ← Multi-stage Python 3.11 build

13.2 Template: New React Frontend

⚛️ What It Scaffolds

React app with Vite + Material UI. Pre-configured CI/CD. catalog-info.yaml, multi-stage Dockerfile (Node build → Nginx serve), GH Actions workflow, K8s manifests, TechDocs skeleton.

🔑 Key Difference vs Django

Nginx as production server (not Node.js). Vite build output → Nginx html dir. K8s Service: port 80 (not 8000). CI runs npm commands (not pip/pytest).

React vs Django — Architectural Comparison
  DJANGO (Runtime App)                    REACT (Static Site)
  ┌──────────────────────┐               ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ Python + gunicorn    │               │ Vite build → dist/   │
  │ :8000 (runtime)      │               │ Nginx serves :80     │
  │ pip install → test   │               │ npm install → build  │
  │ PostgreSQL needed    │               │ No DB needed         │
  │ spec.type: service   │               │ spec.type: website   │
  └──────────────────────┘               └──────────────────────┘

13.3 Template: Database Migration Job

🗄️ Job vs Service

Service: Runs continuously, handles requests.
Job: Runs once to completion, then stops.
Migrations must run BEFORE new version deploys — Jobs are perfect for this.

📋 What It Generates

Dockerfile with migration scripts, K8s Job manifest (backoffLimit, ttlSecondsAfterFinished), CronJob variant for scheduled runs, DB credential config, catalog-info.yaml (type: job).

Migration Job vs CronJob
  K8s JOB (Run Once)                      K8s CRONJOB (Scheduled)
  ┌──────────────────────┐               ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ apiVersion: batch/v1 │               │ apiVersion: batch/v1 │
  │ kind: Job            │               │ kind: CronJob        │
  │ backoffLimit: 3      │               │ schedule: "0 2 * * *"│
  │ ttlSecondsAfter: 300 │               │ jobTemplate: {...}   │
  │                      │               │                      │
  │ Use: CI/CD pipelines │               │ Use: Nightly cleanup │
  │ before deploy        │               │ data sync, backups   │
  └──────────────────────┘               └──────────────────────┘

13.4 Template: Infrastructure as Code

Terraform Template — File Structure
  templates/infra-as-code/skeleton/
  ├── main.tf          ← Resource definitions (compute, networking, DB)
  ├── variables.tf     ← Parameterized inputs with defaults
  ├── outputs.tf       ← Connection strings, IPs, endpoints
  ├── backend.tf       ← Remote state (S3/GCS/Azure Blob)
  ├── providers.tf     ← AWS/GCP/Azure provider config
  └── catalog-info.yaml ← Registered as kind: Resource

  CI PIPELINE:
  terraform fmt → terraform validate → terraform plan
  (apply runs separately after human approval)
🔑 CBA Key Concept — Terraform State

Terraform state must be stored remotely (S3/GCS/Azure Blob), never locally. The backend.tf file configures this. Remote state enables team collaboration and prevents state conflicts. The CBA may test: "Where should Terraform state be stored?" Answer: remote backend, not local files.

Registering Templates in app-config.yaml

  scaffolder:
    templateLocations:
      - type: file
        target: ./templates/django-service/template.yaml
      - type: file
        target: ./templates/react-frontend/template.yaml
      - type: file
        target: ./templates/db-migration/template.yaml
      - type: file
        target: ./templates/infra-as-code/template.yaml

Recommended Templates

How Tags Affect Template Display Order
  CREATE PAGE — Template Listing Order:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ⭐ Django Microservice          [recommended, python]       │ ← Pinned to top
  │  ⭐ React Frontend               [recommended, react]        │ ← Pinned to top
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │

  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
