📝 Chapter 13 — CBA Practice Questions

Q1
What files should a Django microservice template skeleton include?
Show Answer
Answer

catalog-info.yaml, Dockerfile, requirements.txt, manage.py, .github/workflows/ci.yml, k8s/deployment.yaml, k8s/service.yaml, docs/index.md. Each file uses ${{ values.XXX }} for customization.

Explanation

A production-ready Django template skeleton should produce a deployable service from day one. The catalog-info.yaml auto-registers it, Dockerfile containerizes it, CI/CD pipeline automates testing/deployment, K8s manifests define the runtime, and docs/index.md seeds the TechDocs. The ${{ values.X }} placeholders ensure each generated project is unique (different name, owner, description).

Q2
How do templates appear in the Backstage UI?
Show Answer
Answer

Templates appear on the Create page (the + button in the sidebar). They're listed as cards with title, description, and tags. Templates tagged recommended appear first. Users click a template, fill the form, and click Create to execute.

Explanation

The Create page is Backstage's self-service storefront. Template cards show metadata (title, description, tags) so developers can browse and choose. The recommended tag pins templates to the top — use it for your most-used, golden-path templates. The UI is generated automatically from template.yaml — no frontend code needed. This is a CBA concept: templates are self-documenting based on their YAML definition.

Q3
Where do you configure template locations?
Show Answer
Answer

In app-config.yaml under scaffolder.templateLocations. Each location has a type (file or url) and target (path to template.yaml). Templates can also be registered as Catalog entities of kind Template.

Explanation

There are TWO ways to register templates: (1) scaffolder.templateLocations in app-config.yaml (simpler, static), (2) Catalog entity of kind Template (more flexible, supports URL-based discovery). For local development, use type: file with relative paths. For production, use type: url pointing to template.yaml in Git — this enables GitOps-style template management.

Q4
How does the React frontend template differ from the Django template?
Show Answer
Answer

The React template uses Vite for building and Nginx for serving (not gunicorn). The Dockerfile copies the Vite build output to Nginx's html directory. K8s Service exposes port 80 instead of 8000. The CI pipeline runs npm commands (lint, test, build) instead of pip/pytest.

Explanation

The key architectural difference: Django is a runtime application (needs Python + gunicorn), React is a static site (needs nginx to serve built files). The CBA tests this distinction: know that spec.type: website vs spec.type: service maps to different build and deployment patterns in the template skeleton.

Q5
What's the purpose of a database migration job template?
Show Answer
Answer

It scaffolds a Kubernetes Job that runs Django database migrations. Unlike a service (which runs continuously), a Job runs once to completion. The template includes a CronJob variant for scheduled migrations. This ensures migrations run reliably in CI/CD pipelines before new versions deploy.

Explanation

Database migration jobs are a common pattern: they need to run BEFORE the new service version deploys (to update the DB schema), and they must run exactly once (not continuously). K8s Jobs are perfect for this — they run to completion and record success/failure. CronJob variants handle scheduled tasks like data cleanup. The CBA may test this distinction: Job (run once) vs CronJob (run on schedule).

Q6
What Terraform files does the infrastructure-as-code template generate?
Show Answer
Answer

main.tf (resources), variables.tf (inputs with defaults), outputs.tf (connection strings, IPs), backend.tf (remote state config), providers.tf (AWS/GCP/Azure provider). The CI pipeline runs terraform fmt, terraform validate, and terraform plan.

Explanation

Terraform templates follow a standard module structure: main.tf defines what to create, variables.tf makes it configurable, outputs.tf exposes results to other systems, backend.tf stores state remotely (never local!), providers.tf sets up cloud credentials. The CI pipeline validates (fmt+validate) and plans (plan shows what will change) — apply runs separately after human approval.

Q7
What does the recommended tag do for templates?
Show Answer
Answer

Templates tagged recommended are pinned to the top of the Create page. They appear first before other templates. Use this tag for your most-used, battle-tested templates that every developer should see first. It's an organizational best practice.

Explanation

The recommended tag is UX optimization — it guides developers toward the golden-path templates. Without it, all templates appear alphabetically or by registration order, which may bury your best templates. Tags also enable filtering — developers can filter by language, framework, or team. The CBA expects you to know how tags affect template visibility.

Q8
How do you manage template lifecycle (experimental → production → deprecated)?
Show Answer
Answer

Add lifecycle: experimental to template metadata for new/testing templates. Change to lifecycle: production when stable. Use lifecycle: deprecated when retiring. Deprecated templates still appear but with a warning — they should be removed after all users have migrated.

Explanation

Template lifecycle mirrors entity lifecycle: experimental (testing, subject to change) → production (stable, recommended) → deprecated (retiring, use alternative). This prevents developers from accidentally using outdated templates. The CBA tests lifecycle management concepts — know that deprecated templates show a warning banner in the UI, encouraging migration to the replacement.

Q9
You want to add a template that creates a new microservice AND provisions its database. How would you combine actions?
Show Answer
Answer

Use multiple steps in sequence: (1) fetch:template to copy the service skeleton, (2) a custom action to call your cloud API and provision a database, (3) publish:github to create the repo, (4) another custom action to create the database connection string as a K8s Secret, (5) catalog:register. Pass the database connection details between steps via ${{ steps.X.output.Y }}.

Explanation

This multi-step pattern demonstrates template extensibility. The key insight: custom actions can sit BETWEEN the standard fetch→publish→register pipeline. The database provisioning action (step 2) runs before publishing, and the secret creation action (step 4) runs after. Step outputs chain the data: step 2 outputs the DB connection string, step 4 reads it to create the K8s Secret. This is real-world template engineering.

Q10
How would you test a new template before making it available to all developers?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Validate with yarn backstage-cli validate-template
2. Tag it experimental (not recommended) initially
3. Run it manually in dev mode and check the terminal logs
4. Verify the output: GitHub repo created, files correct, Catalog entity registered
5. Have a colleague test it on their machine
6. After successful testing, change to lifecycle: production and add recommended tag

Explanation

6-step template testing: validate → experimental tag → manual run → verify output → peer test → promote. The validate-template CLI command catches YAML errors early. Experimental tag prevents accidental use. CBA: know the full testing workflow and that validate-template is the first step.

📖 Part 5: TechDocs — Documentation-as-Code 🟡 Intermediate

Chapter 14: TechDocs — Documentation That Lives With Your Code

TechDocs is Backstage's documentation-as-code engine. Your docs live in the same repo as your code, written in Markdown, and are auto-published to Backstage whenever you push. No more stale wikis, scattered Confluence pages, or out-of-date READMEs — TechDocs makes documentation a first-class citizen of your engineering workflow.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 📖 Docs 🎯 CBA 32%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand the TechDocs pipeline — write → build → publish → display
  • ✅ Configure mkdocs.yml for navigation and extensions
  • ✅ Master TechDocs configuration in app-config.yaml (builder, generator, publisher)
  • ✅ Write effective docs with admonitions, code blocks, and Mermaid diagrams
  • ✅ Choose the right storage strategy for production
  • ✅ Follow documentation best practices that keep docs useful and current
🎓 CBA Relevance
Customizing Backstage 32%
TechDocs Is a Core Customizing Topic (CBA 32%)

The CBA exam tests your understanding of the TechDocs pipeline — builder, generator, publisher. You'll need to know: (1) Which annotation links an entity to its docs (backstage.io/techdocs-ref), (2) The difference between local and cloud storage for production, (3) How mkdocs.yml controls navigation and appearance. TechDocs is one of Backstage's 4 pillars — expect multiple exam questions.

14.1 What are TechDocs? — Documentation-as-Code

TechDocs follows the docs-as-code philosophy: documentation lives in the same Git repository as your source code, written in Markdown (.md) or MDX (.mdx), and is automatically built and published every time you push. Under the hood, TechDocs uses MkDocs — a Python-based static site generator that converts Markdown files into beautiful, searchable HTML documentation. MDX support allows embedding React components directly in your docs for interactive examples.

The TechDocs Pipeline — From Markdown to Beautiful Docs
  📝 Developer writes docs in Markdown
       │
       ▼
  📦 Docs live in same repo as code (/docs/)
       │  index.md, architecture.md, api-reference.md
       ▼
  🚀 Git push triggers TechDocs build
       │
       ▼
  ⚙️ TechDocs Generator (MkDocs)
       │  • Converts Markdown → Static HTML
       │  • Applies MkDocs theme & navigation
       │  • Creates search index
       │  • Renders Mermaid diagrams
       ▼
  📤 TechDocs Publisher
       │  • Publishes to storage (local/GCS/S3/Azure)
       │
       ▼
  🖥️ Backstage TechDocs Reader
          • Displays docs on entity page's "Docs" tab
          • Full-text search across all docs
          • Navigation sidebar from mkdocs.yml

14.2 Setting Up TechDocs

Complete mkdocs.yml for jobpost Documentation

  # mkdocs.yml — Place at repo root, next to /docs/ folder
  site_name: 'jobpost Documentation'
  site_description: 'Job posting and recruitment application — Developer Docs'
  repo_url: https://github.com/anihpj/jobpost

  nav:                                  # ← Controls the sidebar navigation
    - Home: index.md
    - Architecture: architecture.md
    - 'API Reference': api-reference.md
    - 'Getting Started': getting-started.md
    - Deployment: deployment.md
    - Contributing: contributing.md

  plugins:
    - techdocs-core                     # ← Required TechDocs plugin

  markdown_extensions:
    - admonition                        # ← !!! note, !!! warning, !!! tip
    - codehilite                        # ← Syntax highlighting
    - pymdownx.superfences:             # ← Mermaid diagram support
        custom_fences:
          - name: mermaid
            class: mermaid
            format: !!python/name:pymdownx.superfences.fence_div_format
    - toc:                              # ← Auto-generate table of contents
        permalink: true

14.3 TechDocs Configuration in app-config.yaml

app-config.yaml — TechDocs Section

  techdocs:
    builder: 'local'              # ← 'local' for dev, 'external' for CI/CD
    generator:
      runIn: 'local'              # ← 'local' (needs Python+MkDocs) or 'docker'
      dockerImage: 'spotify/techdocs'  # ← Docker image for MkDocs
    publisher:
      type: 'local'               # ← 'local' | 'googleGcs' | 'awsS3' | 'azureBlobStorage'
      # For GCS:
      # type: 'googleGcs'
      # googleGcs:
      #   bucketName: 'anihpj-techdocs'
      #   credentials: ${GCS_CREDENTIALS}

Builder (local | external)

local: Backstage builds docs on-demand when viewing. Best for development. external: Docs are pre-built by CI/CD pipeline. Best for production — build in CI, publish to cloud storage, Backstage just serves.

Generator (local | docker)

local: Runs MkDocs directly on the Backstage server (requires Python + MkDocs installed). docker: Runs MkDocs in a Docker container using the spotify/techdocs image — isolated, no Python needed on host, consistent builds across environments. Docker is recommended for production because you don't want to manage Python/MkDocs dependencies on your Backstage server. Configure with generator.runIn: 'docker'.

Publisher (local | GCS | S3 | Azure)

local: Stores generated HTML in ./techdocs-output/. Only works for single-instance dev. googleGcs/awsS3/azureBlobStorage: Cloud storage — required for multi-replica production deployments so all pods can access the same docs.

14.4 Writing Effective TechDocs

✅ DO❌ DON'T
Keep docs next to code (/docs/ in each repo)Put docs in a separate wiki/Confluence
Use Mermaid for diagrams (text-based, versionable)Use screenshots that go stale quickly
Structure with clear nav (mkdocs.yml nav section)One giant README with everything
Use admonitions for notes/warnings/tipsBury important warnings in paragraphs
Include code snippets with syntax highlightingDescribe code without showing it
Write for NEW developers (explain acronyms, context)Assume everyone knows the context
Update docs WITH code (same PR as code change)"I'll update docs later" (never happens)

14.5 TechDocs Storage Strategies — Dev vs Production

PublisherDevProductionNotes
local✅ Default❌ Not scalableStores in ./techdocs-output/. Single pod only.
Local (dev)✅ Simple❌No config needed. Best for local development.
googleGcs🟡 Config needed✅ RecommendedAuto-scales, cheap, CDN-ready. Set bucketName.
awsS3🟡 Config needed✅ RecommendedAuto-scales, CDN via CloudFront. Set bucketName + region.
azureBlobStorage🟡 Config needed✅ RecommendedAuto-scales, CDN-ready. Set containerName.
openStackSwift🟡 Config needed✅ For OpenStackOpenStack Swift object storage. For OpenStack-based deployments.

14.6 TechDocs Writing Best Practices

Example: Well-Written TechDocs Page

  # Job Posting API Reference

  !!! note "Prerequisites"
      You need an API key to access these endpoints.
      Contact the platform team to get one.

  ## List Jobs
  Returns a paginated list of job postings.

  **Endpoint:** `GET /api/jobs/`
  **Auth:** API Key required

  ```python
  # Example request
  import requests
  response = requests.get(
      'https://jobpost.anihpj.com/api/jobs/',
      headers={'Authorization': 'Bearer YOUR_API_KEY'}
  )
  ```

  ## System Architecture
  ```mermaid
  graph TD
      A[Browser] --> B[Nginx Ingress]
      B --> C[jobpost Service]
      C --> D[(PostgreSQL)]
      C --> E[(Redis Cache)]
  ```

  !!! warning "Rate Limiting"
      The API is rate-limited to 1000 requests per hour per API key.

14.7 TechDocs Addon Framework — Extending the Reading Experience

The TechDocs Addon Framework (introduced in Backstage 1.2) lets you augment TechDocs pages at read-time. Addons are React components that render alongside documentation — think report-issue buttons, feedback widgets, or custom headers.

🛠️ Built-in: ReportIssue Addon

Adds a feedback button to every TechDocs page. Readers can report issues (broken links, outdated content) directly from the docs. Fosters a documentation culture.

🎨 Custom Addons

Build your own addons: add company headers, "Last updated" timestamps, reading time estimates, or "Was this helpful?" widgets. Any React component can be an addon.

📦 TechDocs Tech Stack (Official)

Frontend: @backstage/plugin-techdocs + @backstage/plugin-techdocs-react
Backend: @backstage/plugin-techdocs-backend
CLI (local dev): @techdocs/cli
Docker (generation): techdocs-container

⚡ SPEED TIP — TechDocs Pipeline: Memorize the 3-stage pipeline: Build (mkdocs converts Markdown to HTML) → Generate (TechDocs CLI creates static site) → Publish (upload to cloud storage). For CBA: builder: external means CI/CD handles build, not Backstage. publisher: awsS3/googleGcs/azureBlob determines storage. Know which stage fails when docs aren't appearing.

📝 Chapter 14 — CBA Practice Questions

Q1
What does the TechDocs pipeline do? Describe the flow.
Show Answer
Answer

Developer writes Markdown → Git push triggers build → MkDocs converts to static HTML → Publisher stores HTML → Backstage displays on entity page's Docs tab. The pipeline has 3 configurable stages: builder (local/external), generator (local/docker), publisher (local/GCS/S3/Azure).

Explanation

The 3 stages are the CBA's core TechDocs concept: builder (who builds docs? Backstage or CI/CD), generator (how? locally or in Docker), publisher (where? local disk or cloud). In production: use builder:external (CI/CD builds), generator:docker (isolated build env), publisher:awsS3/googleGcs/azureBlob (shared cloud storage). Dev mode: builder:local, generator:local, publisher:local.

Q2
What annotation links an entity to its TechDocs?
Show Answer
Answer

backstage.io/techdocs-ref: dir:. — This tells TechDocs to look for mkdocs.yml and /docs/ in the same directory. Alternative: url:https://docs.example.com for externally hosted docs.

Explanation

This is the #1 TechDocs annotation — without it, no Docs tab appears. dir:. = docs in repo root alongside code (most common). dir:./docs = docs in subdirectory. url: = external docs location. The CBA will almost certainly test which annotation enables TechDocs for an entity.

Q3
What is mkdocs.yml used for?
Show Answer
Answer

mkdocs.yml configures MkDocs — the static site generator behind TechDocs. It defines: site name, navigation structure (nav section), enabled plugins (must include techdocs-core), and Markdown extensions (admonition, code highlighting, Mermaid diagrams).

Explanation

mkdocs.yml is the TechDocs configuration file. The nav section defines the sidebar navigation — this is what users see on the left. The plugins list MUST include techdocs-core — without it, TechDocs won't render. Extensions like admonition (callout boxes), pymdownx.superfences (Mermaid diagrams), and pymdownx.highlight (code syntax) enhance documentation quality.

Q4
What's the difference between builder: local and builder: external?
Show Answer
Answer

local: Backstage builds docs on-demand when a user views them. Best for dev. external: Docs are pre-built by CI/CD and Backstage only serves them. Best for production — faster page loads and no MkDocs dependency on Backstage server.

Explanation

This is THE most important TechDocs production decision. builder: local means every user request triggers a build — slow and resource-intensive. builder: external means CI/CD builds once and publishes — fast and scalable. For multi-pod K8s deployments, external is essentially required. The CBA will ask: "Which builder setting for production?" Answer: external.

Q5
Why use cloud storage (GCS/S3/Azure) instead of local for production TechDocs?
Show Answer
Answer

With multiple Backstage replicas on K8s, local storage only works on one pod — other pods can't access the files. Cloud storage provides shared access for ALL pods, auto-scales, and can use CDN for faster global delivery.

Explanation

This is the same reasoning as PostgreSQL over SQLite: multi-pod deployments need SHARED state. Local storage means each pod has different files — Pod A might have docs that Pod B doesn't. Cloud storage (S3/GCS/Azure) is the single source of truth all pods read from. Plus CDN integration (CloudFront/Cloud CDN) makes docs fast worldwide. The CBA connects this to stateless architecture principles.

Q6
What Markdown extension enables Mermaid diagrams in TechDocs?
Show Answer
Answer

pymdownx.superfences with custom fences configured for Mermaid. This allows rendering Mermaid diagrams directly from Markdown code blocks marked with ```mermaid. Diagrams are text-based and versionable — they stay in sync with code.

Explanation

Mermaid diagrams are a CBA differentiator — they enable architecture diagrams directly in Markdown without external tools. The pymdownx.superfences extension allows custom code fences like ```mermaid. When TechDocs builds, these are converted to SVG diagrams. Since they're text-based (not images), they're versionable in Git and can be reviewed in PRs just like code.

Q7
What are admonitions in TechDocs and how do you use them?
Show Answer
Answer

Admonitions are styled callout boxes: !!! note, !!! warning, !!! tip, !!! danger. They require the admonition Markdown extension in mkdocs.yml. Use them to highlight important information, warnings, or tips that should stand out from regular text.

Explanation

Admonitions are the CBA's key TechDocs formatting concept. They're like Backstage's info boxes rendered in documentation: note (blue), warning (yellow), tip (green), danger (red). They require TWO things: the admonition extension in mkdocs.yml AND the techdocs-core plugin. Without both, admonitions render as plain text. The CBA may ask which extension enables callout boxes.

Q8
Where in app-config.yaml do you configure TechDocs?
Show Answer
Answer

Under the techdocs top-level section with 3 subsections: builder (local|external), generator (runIn: local|docker), and publisher (type: local|googleGcs|awsS3|azureBlobStorage). Each publisher type has its own config (bucketName, credentials, etc).

Explanation

The CBA expects you to know the 3 subsections and their values. Builder: local for dev, external for prod. Generator: runIn: local (needs Python on server) or runIn: docker (isolated container, recommended). Publisher: local for single-pod dev, cloud (awsS3/googleGcs/azureBlobStorage) for multi-pod prod. Each cloud publisher needs bucket name and credentials configured.

Q9
Your TechDocs aren't appearing on the entity page. What 3 things do you check?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Annotation: Is backstage.io/techdocs-ref: dir:. in catalog-info.yaml?
2. mkdocs.yml: Does it exist at the repo root with techdocs-core plugin?
3. TechDocs config: Is the techdocs section properly configured in app-config.yaml? Check backend logs for build errors.

Explanation

This troubleshooting flow is a CBA favorite. Debug order: (1) Annotation — most common issue, without it no Docs tab appears. (2) mkdocs.yml — must have techdocs-core plugin, valid YAML syntax. (3) Config — check builder/generator/publisher settings, verify cloud credentials if using cloud storage. Also check: does the repo have a /docs directory with .md files? Empty docs = empty page.

Q10
What's the #1 best practice for keeping TechDocs current?
Show Answer
Answer

Update docs in the same PR as code changes. When you change an API endpoint, update the docs in the same Git commit. This ensures docs never fall behind code. Make doc updates part of your definition of done — "code change isn't complete until docs are updated."

Explanation

This is the core "docs-as-code" philosophy. The key insight: documentation that lives separately from code (Confluence, Google Docs) inevitably becomes outdated. By putting docs in the same repo and same PR as code changes, documentation becomes a first-class deliverable — reviewed, tested, and deployed just like code. The CBA may ask: "What's the main benefit of TechDocs over a wiki?" Answer: docs stay with code and are updated in the same PR.

Chapter 15: TechDocs for anihpj — Complete Setup

Let's build a complete documentation system for the anihpj/jobpost project. You'll plan the doc structure, write architecture docs with Mermaid diagrams, document the REST API, write deployment guides, and publish everything to Backstage.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 📖 Practical 🎯 CBA 32%

15.1 Planning TechDocs for anihpj

  Returns paginated list of job postings.

15.4 Writing Deployment Documentation

Document the complete K8s deployment process so any developer can deploy the service. Cover environment variables, K8s manifests, scaling, rollback, and CI/CD integration.

deployment.md — Key Sections to Include

  # Deploying jobpost to Kubernetes

  ## Prerequisites
  - kubectl configured for anihpj-prod cluster
  - Docker image pushed to registry.anihpj.com

  ## Environment Variables
  | Variable | Required | Description | Example |
  |----------|----------|-------------|---------|
  | DATABASE_URL | ✅ | PostgreSQL connection | postgresql://user:pass@host:5432/db |
  | DJANGO_SECRET_KEY | ✅ | Django secret | (use: openssl rand -hex 32) |
  | ALLOWED_HOSTS | ✅ | Comma-separated hosts | jobpost.anihpj.com |

  ## Deploy
  ```bash
  kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
  kubectl apply -f k8s/service.yaml
  kubectl apply -f k8s/ingress.yaml
  ```

  ## Scale
  ```bash
  kubectl scale deployment jobpost --replicas=5
  ```

  ## Rollback
  ```bash
  kubectl rollout undo deployment/jobpost
  ```

📝 Chapter 15 — CBA Practice Questions

Q1
What documents should you plan for a production service like jobpost?
Show Answer
Answer

Architecture (system design, data flow diagrams), API Reference (endpoints, auth, examples), Deployment Guide (K8s, env vars, scaling), Contributing Guide (local setup, code style, PR process), and an index.md as the entry point with quick links.

Explanation

5 essential doc types: Architecture, API Ref, Deploy Guide, Contributing, index.md. These cover the full service lifecycle from understanding to contributing. CBA: know the minimum doc set for a production service.

Q2
Why use Mermaid diagrams instead of screenshots in TechDocs?
Show Answer
Answer

Mermaid diagrams are text-based — they're version-controlled in Git, reviewable in PRs, and auto-update when the code changes. Screenshots go stale quickly, can't be diff'd in PRs, and require manual re-creation when the UI changes. Mermaid diagrams stay in sync with your code.

Explanation

Mermaid = text-based (Git-friendly). Screenshots = binary (stale, can't diff). Mermaid renders in TechDocs via superfences plugin. CBA: Mermaid preferred over screenshots for version-controlled docs.

Q3
How do you verify TechDocs are working after setup?
Show Answer
Answer

Visit the entity page in Backstage (e.g., /catalog/default/component/jobpost), click the "Docs" tab. You should see your documentation with navigation sidebar, search bar, and properly rendered Markdown, code blocks, and diagrams. Check backend logs if docs don't appear.

Explanation

Verify TechDocs: entity page → Docs tab → check rendering + nav + search. Backend logs if missing. CBA: know the verification flow and that Docs tab is on entity pages.

Q4
Where should the mkdocs.yml file be placed relative to the repository?
Show Answer
Answer

At the repository root, next to the /docs/ folder. Backstage looks for mkdocs.yml in the same directory referenced by the backstage.io/techdocs-ref annotation. If the annotation is dir:., mkdocs.yml must be at the repo root.

Explanation

mkdocs.yml = repo root, next to /docs/. Must match techdocs-ref annotation directory. CBA: know the file location and its relationship to the annotation.

Q5
What plugin must be included in mkdocs.yml for TechDocs to work?
Show Answer
Answer

techdocs-core — this is the requiredBackstage plugin for MkDocs. Without it, TechDocs won't render properly. Add it under the plugins section: plugins: [techdocs-core]. This plugin handles Backstage-specific features like the TechDocs theme and search integration.

Explanation

techdocs-core is mandatory — without it, MkDocs builds but Backstage can't display the output. It provides the Backstage theme, search backend integration, and entity page embedding. Always the first plugin in your mkdocs.yml plugins list. The CBA may ask "which plugin is required for TechDocs to work?" — answer is always techdocs-core.

Q6
How do you update TechDocs after making changes to your documentation?
Show Answer
Answer

Push to Git — TechDocs rebuilds automatically. If using builder: local, docs rebuild on the next page view. If using builder: external, your CI/CD pipeline rebuilds and publishes to cloud storage. No manual steps needed — it's fully automated.

Explanation

Auto-rebuild on git push. Local builder = rebuild on page view. External builder = CI/CD rebuilds. CBA: know both builder modes and that push triggers rebuild.

Q7
What's the difference between the nav section and the actual /docs/ folder structure?
Show Answer
Answer

The nav section in mkdocs.yml defines the display order and hierarchy of pages in the sidebar. The /docs/ folder is where the actual Markdown files live. You can organize nav differently from folder structure — e.g., put deployment.md before api-reference.md in nav even if they're alphabetically reversed.

Explanation

nav = display order (sidebar). /docs/ = file storage. Can differ — nav is independent of folder structure. CBA: know that nav controls sidebar, not folder structure.

Q8
Your TechDocs show a blank page. The annotation is correct and mkdocs.yml exists. What else could be wrong?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Generator issue: Is Python + MkDocs installed (if runIn: local) or Docker available (if runIn: docker)?
2. Publisher issue: For cloud storage, are credentials correct and accessible?
3. Build error: Check the backend logs — MkDocs may have failed to build due to Markdown syntax errors or missing files referenced in nav.

Explanation

Blank page = build succeeded but output is empty or unreachable. Generator issues mean MkDocs never ran. Publisher issues mean it built but can't store/retrieve. Build errors mean MkDocs ran but produced empty output (syntax error, missing files). Check Backstage logs first — they'll tell you which stage failed. For cloud publisher, verify the bucket exists and credentials have read/write access.

Q9
What is the repo_url setting in mkdocs.yml used for?
Show Answer
Answer

repo_url adds an "Edit on GitHub" (or GitLab/Bitbucket) link to every TechDocs page. Set it to your repository URL: repo_url: https://github.com/anihpj/jobpost. This lets readers quickly navigate to the source code or suggest edits to the documentation.

Explanation

repo_url = "Edit on GitHub" link on every page. Links docs back to source. CBA: know repo_url adds the edit link in TechDocs pages.

Q10
You're deploying Backstage on K8s with 3 replicas. Which TechDocs publisher should you use and why?
Show Answer
Answer

Use cloud storage (googleGcs, awsS3, or azureBlobStorage). The local publisher stores files on the pod's filesystem — with 3 replicas, each pod has its own copy and they won't be in sync. Cloud storage provides a single shared location accessible by all replicas. Configure the publisher in app-config.yaml with the appropriate bucket/container and credentials.

Explanation

This is the #1 TechDocs production question on the CBA. Multi-pod = cloud storage, always. Local publisher works for single-pod dev but fails silently in production — some users see docs, others don't, depending on which pod serves their request. Cloud storage is the single source of truth. Also: cloud storage enables CDN (CloudFront/Cloud CDN) for global doc delivery.

# TechDocs Publisher — Production vs Development
# Development (single pod only — filesystem storage)
techdocs:
  builder: local
  publisher:
    type: local           # ← Files on pod disk (NOT for multi-replica!)

# Production (multi-replica — cloud storage)
techdocs:
  builder: external       # ← CI/CD builds docs
  publisher:
    type: googleGcs       # ← GCS/S3/Azure (all replicas share)
    googleGcs:
      bucketName: anihpj-techdocs
      credentials: ${GCS_CREDENTIALS}

16.1 What are Backstage Plugins?

Plugin Architecture — How Plugins Extend Backstage
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    BACKSTAGE APP                             │
  │  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐       │
  │  │ Catalog  │ │Scaffolder│ │ TechDocs │ │  Search  │  ...  │
  │  │ Plugin   │ │ Plugin   │ │ Plugin   │ │ Plugin   │       │
  │  └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘       │
  │       │            │            │            │              │
  │  ┌────┴────────────┴────────────┴────────────┴────┐        │
  │  │              PLUGIN FRAMEWORK                   │        │
  │  │  • Plugin Registry (register/load plugins)     │        │
  │  │  • Route Management (URL routing)              │        │
  │  │  • API Client Proxy (frontend→backend calls)   │        │
  │  │  • Component Mounting (render in UI)           │        │
  │  │  • Event Bus (cross-plugin communication)      │        │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

16.2 Frontend Plugins

Frontend plugins render UI components. They use createPlugin() to define the plugin, createRoutableExtension() for page routing (lazy-loaded), and createComponentExtension() for embedding cards on entity pages. They access backend data via the API client proxy — never directly calling databases or external services.

Frontend Plugin Skeleton

  // plugins/my-plugin/src/plugin.ts
  import { createPlugin, createRoutableExtension } from '@backstage/core-plugin-api';

  export const myPlugin = createPlugin({ id: 'my-plugin' });

  export const MyPage = myPlugin.provide(
    createRoutableExtension({
      name: 'MyPage',
      component: () => import('./components/MyPage').then(m => m.MyPage),
      mountPoint: rootRouteRef,
    }),
  );

16.3 Backend Plugins

Backend plugins provide API endpoints and data processing. They use createRouter() for HTTP routes, access databases via PluginDatabaseManager, read URLs via UrlReader, and communicate with other plugins through the event system. Backend plugins can also schedule recurring tasks (cron-like jobs).

Backend Plugin Skeleton

  // plugins/my-plugin-backend/src/index.ts
  import { createRouter } from '@backstage/backend-defaults';
  import { Router } from 'express';

  export async function createPlugin(env) {
    const router = Router();
    router.get('/health', (_, res) => res.json({ status: 'ok' }));
    router.get('/data', async (_, res) => {
      const db = await env.database.getClient();
      const data = await db('my_table').select('*');
      res.json(data);
    });
    return router;
  }

16.7 Plugin Communication — Visual Architecture (CBA Core)

How Plugins Connect Frontend to Backend
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    FULL-STACK PLUGIN ARCHITECTURE                     │
  │                                                                     │
  │  FRONTEND (Browser)               BACKEND (Node.js)                  │
  │  ┌────────────────────┐           ┌────────────────────┐            │
  │  │ createPlugin()      │           │ createRouter()      │            │
  │  │  → createRoutable.. │──REST──▶  │  → GET /api/data   │            │
  │  │  → createApiRef()   │           │  → POST /api/action │            │
  │  │  → createComponent..│           │  → DB access (knex) │            │
  │  └────────────────────┘           │  → External APIs    │            │
  │                                    └────────────────────┘            │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  COMMON PACKAGE: TypeScript interfaces, API client, permissions │ │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  EVENT BUS: Plugins communicate via publish/subscribe — never directly!
  Catalog publishes "entity.created" → Search plugin subscribes → indexes it
🖥️ Frontend-Only

React components. No backend. Example: Home page, theme plugin. Fastest to build.

⚙️ Backend-Only

Express routes. No UI. Example: Auth providers, catalog processors. Extends server.

🔗 Full-Stack

Both frontend + backend. Example: Catalog, Scaffolder, K8s. Most common type.

⚡ SPEED TIP — Plugin Types: The CBA distinguishes: Frontend plugins (React components rendered in browser, use createPlugin() and createRoutableExtension()), Backend plugins (Node.js/Express routers, use createRouter()), and Entity page cards (widgets on entity pages, use createComponentExtension()). Scenario: "Display data on entity page" → Entity card. "Full page with routes" → Frontend plugin.

📝 Chapter 16 — CBA Practice Questions

Q1
What are the 3 types of Backstage plugins? Give an example of each.
Show Answer
Answer

1. Frontend-only: Renders UI only, calls external APIs from browser. Example: GitHub README card.
2. Backend-only: Provides API endpoints, no UI. Example: Auth providers, catalog processors.
3. Full-stack: Both frontend UI + backend logic. Example: Kubernetes plugin, Scaffolder.

Explanation

The 3 plugin types are the CBA's core plugin concept. Frontend-only plugins run in the browser (React), backend-only run on the server (Node.js/Express), full-stack span both. Most production plugins are full-stack — they need a frontend to display data AND a backend to fetch/process it. The CBA will ask: "You need to display CI/CD status on entity pages — which plugin type?" Answer: Full-stack (frontend card + backend API client).

Q2
What does createPlugin() do?
Show Answer
Answer

createPlugin() is the entry point for any Backstage frontend plugin. It creates a plugin instance with a unique ID, registers API factories, and provides the plugin's React components. Every frontend plugin starts with createPlugin({ id: 'my-plugin', ... }).

Explanation

createPlugin() is the first function called in every plugin's plugin.ts file. The id must be unique across all plugins in your Backstage instance. This function returns a BackstagePlugin instance that you use to register routes, API factories, and components. The CBA tests this as the fundamental plugin creation pattern.

Q3
How many community plugins are available for Backstage?
Show Answer
Answer

200+ community plugins are available at backstage.io/plugins. They cover CI/CD (Jenkins, GitHub Actions, ArgoCD), monitoring (Grafana, Prometheus, Datadog), incident management (PagerDuty, OpsGenie), project management (Jira), and communication (Slack, Teams).

Explanation

The plugin marketplace (backstage.io/plugins) is the CBA's reference for extensibility. Know the major categories: CI/CD, monitoring, incident management, project management, communication, security. The exam may ask: "Which plugin would you use for X?" Always check the marketplace first before building custom — the CBA expects you to know that 200+ plugins exist.

Q4
How does a frontend plugin access data from a backend plugin?
Show Answer
Answer

Through the API Client Proxy. The frontend defines an API ref with createApiRef() and uses useApi() to call it. The proxy routes requests from the browser through Backstage's backend, which then calls the actual backend plugin. This avoids CORS issues and centralizes authentication.

Explanation

The API proxy pattern is fundamental to Backstage security. Instead of frontend plugins calling external APIs directly (exposing tokens in the browser), all calls go through Backstage's backend. The frontend calls /api/proxy/..., the backend adds auth headers, forwards to the external API, and returns results. This means API tokens NEVER reach the browser. The CBA tests this security pattern.

Q5
What is the Backstage event bus and how do plugins use it?
Show Answer
Answer

The event bus allows plugins to communicate asynchronously. One plugin publishes events, others subscribe. Example: when the Catalog ingests a new entity, it publishes an event — other plugins (like the Scaffolder or Search) react to it. This keeps plugins loosely coupled.

Explanation

The event bus is Backstage's publish-subscribe system. Plugins don't call each other directly — they publish events and subscribe to events they care about. This loose coupling means plugins can be added/removed independently. Example flow: Catalog ingests new entity → publishes catalog.entity.created → Search plugin subscribes and indexes it → Scaffolder subscribes and validates templates. The CBA tests this decoupling pattern.

Q6
What does createRoutableExtension() do?
Show Answer
Answer

createRoutableExtension() creates a lazy-loaded page component for a plugin. It defines the route's mount point and component. The component is only loaded when the user navigates to that route — improving initial page load performance.

Explanation

Lazy loading is critical for Backstage performance with many plugins. Without it, ALL plugin code loads at startup — slow initial load. With createRoutableExtension(), each plugin's code loads only when the user navigates to its route. This is analogous to React.lazy() — code splitting at the route level. The CBA tests this as a plugin performance concept.

Q7
What is the difference between a core plugin and a community plugin?
Show Answer
Answer

Core plugins are built and maintained by the Backstage team and ship with every Backstage installation (Catalog, Scaffolder, TechDocs, Search, Kubernetes, Auth). Community plugins are contributed by external developers/companies (Jenkins, PagerDuty, Grafana, Sentry). Core plugins follow strict quality standards; community plugins vary in maintenance.

Explanation

The core vs community distinction is important for the CBA. Core plugins (Catalog, Scaffolder, TechDocs, Search, K8s, Auth) are guaranteed to work and are always available. Community plugins (Jenkins, PagerDuty, Grafana, Sentry, Jira) may vary in quality and maintenance. The CBA may ask: "Is the Jenkins plugin a core or community plugin?" Answer: Community. Know the 6 core plugins by name.

Q8
Where are frontend plugins registered to appear in Backstage?
Show Answer
Answer

In packages/app/src/App.tsx (for route registration) and packages/app/src/components/Root.tsx (for sidebar navigation). The App.tsx file imports the plugin and defines its route; Root.tsx adds a SidebarItem with an icon and link.

Explanation

Two files, two purposes: App.tsx registers the ROUTE (what URL loads the plugin), Root.tsx registers the SIDEBAR LINK (what users click to navigate). A plugin can have a route without a sidebar link (internal pages), but most user-facing plugins need both. The CBA may ask: "Where do you add a new plugin to the sidebar?" Answer: Root.tsx, using <SidebarItem icon={...} to="/plugin-route" />.

Q9
What is createComponentExtension() used for?
Show Answer
Answer

createComponentExtension() creates a card component that can be embedded on entity pages. Unlike createRoutableExtension (which creates full pages), this creates smaller UI pieces like the "About" card, "CI/CD" card, or "K8s" card that appear on entity overview pages.

Explanation

Entity page cards are the most common plugin type. They're small, focused widgets that show specific data: CI/CD status, K8s health, Sentry errors, etc. createComponentExtension() creates a card; createRoutableExtension() creates a full page. The CBA distinguishes: "Display Jenkins build status on entity page" → use createComponentExtension. "Create a full Jenkins dashboard" → use createRoutableExtension.

Q10
You install a community plugin but it doesn't appear. What are 3 things to check?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Installation: Did you run yarn add in both packages/app AND packages/backend?
2. Registration: Did you import and register the plugin in App.tsx (route) and/or Root.tsx (sidebar)?
3. Configuration: Does the plugin need config in app-config.yaml (e.g., API tokens, URLs)? Check the plugin's documentation for required config.

Explanation

This is the standard plugin troubleshooting flow for the CBA. Most "plugin not appearing" issues are #2 (not registered). Remember: frontend plugins need registration in App.tsx AND Root.tsx. Backend plugins need registration in packages/backend/src/index.ts. Always check the plugin's README for specific setup steps — some need additional config in app-config.yaml.

17.2 CI/CD Plugins — Build & Deploy Visibility

PluginAnnotationWhat It ShowsProxy Required?
Jenkinsjenkins.io/job-full-nameBuild history, trigger jobs, test results✅ Yes
GitHub Actionsgithub.com/project-slugWorkflow runs, status, logs, duration❌ (uses integration)
ArgoCDargocd/app-nameGitOps sync status, health, history✅ Yes
GitLab CIgitlab.com/project-idPipeline status, MR overview, job logs✅ Yes
💡 CBA Tip — Proxy Pattern for CI/CD

ALL CI/CD plugins except GitHub Actions use the Backstage proxy. Configure proxy.endpoints in app-config.yaml with the CI/CD tool's URL and auth token. The frontend calls /api/proxy/..., Backstage injects the token server-side, and forwards the request. Token NEVER reaches the browser.

17.3 Monitoring Plugins — Unified Observability

📊 Grafana

Embeds dashboards via iframes. Configure dashboard URLs per service. Each entity gets its own metrics view.

🚨 Prometheus

Shows alert status and firing alerts. Links entities to Prometheus alert rules via annotation.

🔍 Datadog

Service health, APM data, dashboards. Full observability from Datadog into Backstage.

📋 Monitoring Plugin Pattern

Monitoring plugins work differently from CI/CD plugins — they don't always use annotations. Grafana uses iframe embeds (configured per entity in app-config.yaml), Prometheus reads alert rules by label matching, and Datadog uses the Datadog API via proxy. Each has its own integration pattern.

17.4 Incident Management — On-Call Visibility

🔔 OpsGenie

Alert management and on-call rotations. Integrates with Slack for notifications. Annotation: opsgenie.com/team.

17.5 Error Tracking — Catch Bugs Before Users Do

ToolAnnotationWhat It ShowsSetup Complexity

🔗 Error Tracking + CI/CD = Complete Picture

Combine Sentry with Jenkins/GitHub Actions: when a deploy triggers a spike in errors, both the deploy card AND the error card update on the same entity page. This correlation is what makes Backstage's "single pane of glass" so powerful for debugging.

17.6 Communication — Stay Notified

💬 Slack

Send notifications when builds fail, deployments complete, or incidents occur. Configure webhook URLs per team. Keep everyone informed without leaving their workflow.

🟣 Microsoft Teams

Channel integration for enterprise organizations on Office 365. Post build status, incident alerts, and deployment notifications directly to team channels.

💡 CBA Tip — Communication Plugins

Communication plugins are different from other plugins — they PUSH notifications out rather than PULL data in. They use webhooks (Slack) or connectors (Teams) to send messages. Configure them in app-config.yaml under their respective sections, not via entity annotations.

⚡ SPEED TIP — Plugin-Annotation Mapping: For the CBA, memorize the plugin→annotation pairs: GitHub → github.com/project-slug, Jenkins → jenkins.io/job-full-name, PagerDuty → pagerduty.com/service-id, Sentry → sentry.io/project-slug, K8s → backstage.io/kubernetes-id, TechDocs → backstage.io/techdocs-ref. These 6 annotations appear in almost every plugin-related exam question.

📝 Chapter 17 — CBA Practice Questions

Q1
What annotation links an entity to its GitHub repository?
Show Answer
Answer

github.com/project-slug: owner/repo. Example: github.com/project-slug: anihpj/jobpost. This annotation tells the GitHub plugin which repository to display information from.

Explanation

This is the most-used annotation in Backstage. Format is always owner/repo (not a full URL). The GitHub plugin reads this to show README, contributors, languages, and Actions CI/CD. Without it, the GitHub card shows nothing. The CBA will almost certainly test this annotation.

Q2
What annotation links an entity to its Jenkins job?
Show Answer
Answer

jenkins.io/job-full-name: folder/job-name. Example: jenkins.io/job-full-name: anihpj/jobpost-build.

Explanation

Jenkins annotation format: folder/job-name. The Jenkins plugin also needs a proxy endpoint configured in app-config.yaml to route requests through Backstage securely. The token (${JENKINS_TOKEN}) is injected server-side — never exposed to the browser.

Q3
What annotation links an entity to PagerDuty?
Show Answer
Answer

pagerduty.com/service-id: SERVICE_ID. Links the entity to its PagerDuty service for on-call and incident information.

Explanation

The PagerDuty plugin shows on-call schedules and active incidents. The service ID is found in the PagerDuty service URL. This annotation is one of the 6 key plugin annotations tested on the CBA.

Q4
What does the Grafana plugin show on entity pages?
Show Answer
Answer

The Grafana plugin embeds Grafana dashboards directly in Backstage via iframes. It shows service-level metrics, graphs, and panels configured in Grafana. Configure dashboard URLs and they render on entity pages — giving teams instant access to monitoring data without leaving Backstage.

Explanation

Grafana integration uses iframes to embed dashboards — this means the Grafana server must be accessible from the browser. Configure dashboard URLs per service so each entity shows its own metrics. The plugin doesn't need a specific annotation — you configure which dashboards map to which entities in app-config.yaml.

Q5
How does the ArgoCD plugin integrate with Backstage?
Show Answer
Answer

The ArgoCD plugin shows GitOps deployment status on entity pages — sync state, application health, and deployment history. It connects to the ArgoCD API server and displays: which version is deployed, whether the app is synced with Git, and the health status of K8s resources.

Explanation

ArgoCD integration is critical for GitOps workflows. The annotation is argocd/app-name. It shows whether the live cluster state matches the desired Git state — synced = good, out-of-sync = drift detected. The plugin also enables one-click rollback directly from Backstage. CBA: know that ArgoCD = GitOps visibility.

Q6
What annotation links an entity to Sentry error tracking?
Show Answer
Answer

sentry.io/project-slug: org/project. Example: sentry.io/project-slug: anihpj/jobpost. This links the entity to its Sentry project, showing recent errors, crash rates, and issue lists on the entity page.

Explanation

Sentry annotation follows the org/project format (same as GitHub). The Sentry plugin shows error frequency, recent issues, and stack traces on the entity page. Combined with CI/CD and K8s plugins, it provides complete visibility: build → deploy → errors — all on one page.

Q7
How do you configure the Jenkins plugin for Backstage?
Show Answer
Answer

Add the Jenkins proxy endpoint in app-config.yaml under proxy.endpoints, install both frontend and backend packages, and add the jenkins.io/job-full-name annotation to entity YAML. The plugin then fetches build history and status from Jenkins and displays it on the entity's CI/CD card.

Explanation

Jenkins setup requires 3 steps: (1) proxy config in app-config.yaml (routes requests securely), (2) package installation (frontend + backend), (3) annotation on entities. The proxy is the security layer — browser calls /api/proxy/jenkins/..., Backstage adds auth, forwards to Jenkins. Token never reaches browser.

Q8
What's the difference between the GitHub integration plugin and the GitHub Actions plugin?
Show Answer
Answer

The GitHub integration plugin shows repository metadata (README, contributors, languages, about) and is configured in integrations.github. GitHub Actions is part of the same plugin and shows CI/CD workflow runs and status. They work together — the integration provides repo info; Actions provides build/deploy status.

Explanation

GitHub integration (repo metadata) and GitHub Actions (CI/CD) are often conflated on the CBA. Integration shows static info (README, contributors); Actions shows dynamic CI/CD status. Both use the same github.com/project-slug annotation. Integration config goes in integrations.github; Actions is part of the GitHub plugin package.

Q9
You install the PagerDuty plugin but see no data. What 3 things do you check?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Annotation: Is pagerduty.com/service-id in the entity's catalog-info.yaml?
2. API Token: Is the PagerDuty API token configured in app-config.yaml?
3. Service ID: Is the service ID correct? Find it in PagerDuty → Service Directory → your service → URL contains the ID.

Explanation

Standard plugin troubleshooting: annotation → config → data. The PagerDuty service ID is NOT the service name — it's a unique alphanumeric ID found in the URL. API token needs read access to services and incidents. The CBA tests this troubleshooting pattern for multiple plugins.

Q10
How would you add monitoring visibility for the jobpost service using Backstage plugins?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Install the Grafana plugin and configure a dashboard URL showing jobpost metrics
2. Install the Prometheus plugin and link jobpost's alert rules
3. Add Sentry plugin for error tracking with sentry.io/project-slug: anihpj/jobpost
4. Add Kubernetes plugin for pod health and deployment status
All four give complete observability on the jobpost entity page.

Explanation

This is the "single pane of glass" concept applied to monitoring. Four plugins combine to give complete visibility: Grafana (metrics), Prometheus (alerts), Sentry (errors), K8s (infrastructure). Each shows different data but all appear on the same entity page. The CBA tests this multi-plugin integration pattern.

Chapter 18: Building Custom Plugins

When existing plugins don't cover your needs, you build custom plugins. This chapter walks through creating a custom dashboard plugin for anihpj — from scaffolding to testing. You'll learn the complete plugin development workflow.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~2 hours🛠️ Hands-On🎯 CBA 32%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Know when to build a custom plugin vs using an existing one
  • ✅ Scaffold a frontend plugin using yarn backstage-cli create-plugin
  • ✅ Understand the plugin directory structure and key files
  • ✅ Register the plugin in App.tsx and add routes
  • ✅ Build a real custom dashboard plugin for the anihpj ecosystem

🎯 CBA Exam Relevance — Customizing Backstage 32%

Custom plugin development is tested at a conceptual level. The CBA will ask about: (1) frontend vs backend plugin differences, (2) the createPlugin() function, (3) how plugins register routes and components, and (4) when to create a custom plugin. You don't need to write full plugin code on the exam, but you must understand the architecture.

🎯 CBA Exam Tip — Frontend vs Backend Plugins

The CBA frequently tests this distinction: Frontend plugins (UI components, pages, cards) run in the browser and use React. Backend plugins (API endpoints, data processing) run on the server and use Node.js/Express. Scenario: "You need to fetch data from an internal API and display it as a card — which type of plugin?" Answer: Both — a backend plugin to fetch the data + a frontend plugin to render it.

18.1 When to Build a Custom Plugin

✅ Build Custom When...

• No existing plugin for your tool
• Custom internal workflows needed
• Organization-specific dashboards
• Aggregating data from multiple sources
• Unique compliance/security requirements

❌ Use Existing When...

• Plugin exists on backstage.io/plugins
• Standard CI/CD tool (Jenkins, GH Actions)
• Standard monitoring (Grafana, Datadog)
• Standard incidents (PagerDuty, Sentry)
• 200+ plugins already available!

Build vs Buy Decision Flow
  Need new Backstage feature?
       │
       ▼
  Check backstage.io/plugins ──▶ Found? ──▶ ✅ Use existing plugin
       │
       ▼
  Similar plugin exists? ──▶ Yes ──▶ 🔧 Extend with custom module
       │
       ▼
  Unique to your org? ──▶ Yes ──▶ 🛠️ Build custom plugin

18.2 Creating a Frontend Plugin — Step by Step

Custom Plugin Directory Structure

  plugins/anihpj-dashboard/
  ├── src/
  │   ├── index.ts              ← Plugin entry, exports
  │   ├── plugin.ts             ← createPlugin() definition
  │   ├── api.ts                ← API client (if backend needed)
  │   ├── routes.ts             ← Route definitions
  │   └── components/
  │       ├── AnihpjPage.tsx    ← Main plugin page
  │       ├── JobStatsCard.tsx  ← Dashboard card
  │       └── ServiceHealth.tsx ← Health status component
  ├── package.json
  └── README.md
Scaffold & Register Steps

  # 1. Scaffold the plugin
  $ yarn backstage-cli create-plugin
  ? Plugin ID: anihpj-dashboard

  # 2. Register in packages/app/src/App.tsx
  import { AnihpjDashboardPage } from '@internal/plugin-anihpj-dashboard';
  <Route path="/anihpj-dashboard" element={<AnihpjDashboardPage />} />

  # 3. Add to sidebar in packages/app/src/components/Root.tsx
  <SidebarItem icon={DashboardIcon} to="anihpj-dashboard" text="anihpj" />

18.3 Creating a Backend Plugin

Backend plugins use createRouter() from Express to define API endpoints. They access the database, read URLs, and communicate with other plugins via the event bus. Scaffold with yarn backstage-cli create-plugin --backend.

Backend Plugin Architecture
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    BACKEND PLUGIN ANATOMY                      │
  │                                                              │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  yarn backstage-cli create-plugin --backend           │   │
  │  │       │                                               │   │
  │  │       ▼                                               │   │
  │  │  packages/backend/src/plugins/my-plugin/              │   │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │   │
  │  │  │  index.ts    ← createRouter() entry point    │    │   │
  │  │  │  router.ts   ← Express Router + endpoints   │    │   │
  │  │  │  run.ts      ← Standalone runner (optional) │    │   │
  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │   │
  │  │                                                      │   │
  │  │  Exports: createRouter() → Express Router             │   │
  │  │  Registers in: packages/backend/src/index.ts          │   │
  │  │       backend.add(myPlugin)                           │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                              │
  │  🔑 Capabilities:                                            │
  │  • Database access (PluginDatabaseManager)                   │
  │  • URL reading (UrlReader)                                   │
  │  • Event publishing/subscribing (EventBroker)                │
  │  • HTTP endpoints (Express Router)                           │
  │  • Plugin-to-plugin communication                            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

// packages/backend/src/plugins/anihpj-metrics/src/index.ts
import { createRouter } from './router';
import { PluginEnvironment } from '../types';

export default async function createPlugin(env: PluginEnvironment) {
  // 🔑 env provides: logger, database, config, scheduler, permissions, etc.
  return await createRouter({
    logger: env.logger,
    database: env.database,       // PluginDatabaseManager → knex.js
    config: env.config,
    discovery: env.discovery,     // Service discovery for other plugins
    tokenManager: env.tokenManager,
  });
}

// router.ts — Define API endpoints
import express from 'express';
import Router from 'express-promise-router';

export async function createRouter(options: RouterOptions) {
  const router = Router();
  router.use(express.json());

  // GET /api/anihpj-metrics/health
  router.get('/health', async (_, res) => {
    res.json({ status: 'ok' });
  });

  // GET /api/anihpj-metrics/job-stats
  router.get('/job-stats', async (req, res) => {
    const db = await options.database.getClient();
    const stats = await db('jobpost_jobs')
      .select('status')
      .count('* as total')
      .groupBy('status');
    res.json(stats);
  });

  return router;
}
🗄️
Database Access

Via PluginDatabaseManager. Provides knex.js client. All DB queries run server-side — NEVER exposed to browser.

📡
Event Bus

Publish/subscribe to events. Example: Catalog entity changes → your plugin re-indexes. Loose coupling between plugins.

🔗
Express Router

Standard Express.js patterns. router.get(), router.post(). Frontend calls via /api/plugin-name/....

18.4 Building the anihpj Dashboard Plugin

Purpose: Custom dashboard showing jobpost metrics — active job listings, applications per day, deployment status, and recent errors. Frontend: React components with Material UI cards and charts. Backend: API endpoints aggregating data from the jobpost database, Kubernetes API, and Sentry.

anihpj Dashboard Plugin — Full-Stack Architecture

  │  │  ┌──────────────────┐  │        │    job-stats           │──▶ jobpost DB
  │  │  │  JobStatsCard     │──┼───────▶│                        │  │
  │  │  │  📊 Active: 12   │  │        │  GET /api/anihpj/       │  │
  │  │  │  📈 Today:  45   │  │        │    k8s-status           │──▶ K8s API
  │  │  │  ✅ Deploy: ok   │  │        │                        │  │
  │  │  └──────────────────┘  │        │  GET /api/anihpj/       │  │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────┐  │        │    errors               │──▶ Sentry
  │  │  │  ErrorWidget      │──┼───────▶│                        │  │
  │  │  │  ⚠️ 3 errors/24h │  │        └────────────────────────┘  │
  │  │  │  🔴 1 critical   │  │                                    │
  │  │  └──────────────────┘  │        ┌────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────┐  │        │  BACKEND Data Sources  │  │
  │  │  │  DeployStatusCard│──┼───────▶│                        │  │
  │  │  │  🟢 v2.4.1       │  │        │  jobpost DB (PostgreSQL)│  │
  │  │  │  🏥 Healthy      │  │        │  K8s API (pod status)  │  │
  │  │  └──────────────────┘  │        │  Sentry API (errors)   │  │
  │  └────────────────────────┘        └────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                  │
  │  📂 FILE STRUCTURE:                                               │
  │  packages/app/src/plugins/anihpj/                                 │
  │    ├── plugin.ts          ← createPlugin('anihpj-dashboard')     │
  │    ├── routes.ts          ← DashboardPage route                  │
  │    ├── api.ts             ← API client (useApi)                  │
  │    └── components/                                                │
  │        ├── DashboardPage.tsx                                      │
  │        ├── JobStatsCard.tsx                                       │
  │        ├── ErrorWidget.tsx                                        │
  │        └── DeployStatusCard.tsx                                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

// plugin.ts — Frontend plugin entry point
import { createPlugin, createRoutableExtension } from '@backstage/core-plugin-api';

export const anihpjDashboardPlugin = createPlugin({
  id: 'anihpj-dashboard',
  routes: {
    root: '/anihpj-dashboard',
  },
});

// routes.ts — Lazy-loaded route
export const AnihpjDashboardPage = anihpjDashboardPlugin.provide(
  createRoutableExtension({
    name: 'AnihpjDashboardPage',
    component: () => import('./components/DashboardPage').then(m => m.DashboardPage),
    mountPoint: '/anihpj-dashboard',
  }),
);
📊
3 Data Sources

jobpost DB (active listings, applications), K8s API (pod health, restarts), Sentry API (error counts, critical issues). Backend aggregates; frontend displays.

🎨
MUI Components

Cards with elevation, LinearProgress bars for metrics, Typography for text, Grid for layout, and Backstage's own <InfoCard> for consistent styling.

18.5 Testing Custom Plugins

Test plugins with: (1) Jest unit tests for components and API logic, (2) Integration tests for full plugin workflows, (3) Manual testing with yarn dev — the plugin appears in the sidebar and can be tested interactively.

Test LayerToolWhat It TestsCommand
UnitJest + React Testing LibraryIndividual components, API functions, utility logicyarn test
IntegrationJest + SupertestFull plugin workflow: API call → DB query → responseyarn test --integration
Manualyarn dev + BrowserReal UI rendering, sidebar visibility, route navigation, API callsyarn dev
E2EPlaywright / CypressFull user journey: click sidebar → load page → interact with cardsyarn test:e2e
// __tests__/DashboardPage.test.tsx — Jest Unit Test Example
import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import { DashboardPage } from '../components/DashboardPage';
import { TestApiProvider } from '@backstage/test-utils';

jest.mock('../api', () => ({
  anihpjDashboardApiRef: {},
  useDashboardApi: () => ({
    getJobStats: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue({
      active: 12, today: 45, deploy: 'ok', errors: 3,
    }),
  }),
}));

describe('DashboardPage', () => {
  it('renders job stats card with active count', async () => {
    render();
    // Wait for async data to load
    expect(await screen.findByText('Active: 12')).toBeInTheDocument();
    expect(screen.getByText('Today: 45')).toBeInTheDocument();
    expect(screen.getByText('Deploy: ok')).toBeInTheDocument();
  });

  it('shows error count when > 0', async () => {
    render();
    expect(await screen.findByText('⚠️ 3 errors/24h')).toBeInTheDocument();
  });
});
🧪
Jest Unit Tests

Mock API calls with jest.fn(). Test component rendering, state changes, and edge cases. Fast feedback (<1 second).

🔗
Integration Tests

Test the full stack: frontend → API proxy → backend → database. Use Supertest for HTTP assertions against backend routes.

👁️
Manual Testing

Run yarn dev, navigate to localhost:3000/anihpj-dashboard, verify cards render with real data from a running database.

💡 CBA Testing Tip

The CBA expects you to know the 3 testing layers (unit, integration, manual) and which tool each uses. Jest is the standard for unit/integration. yarn dev is for manual testing. Backstage plugins use standard React testing patterns — no proprietary testing framework.

⚡ SPEED TIP — Plugin Development Workflow: The CBA tests the plugin creation flow: (1) yarn backstage-cli create-plugin → (2) implement createPlugin() with routes → (3) add to packages/app/src/App.tsx → (4) build with yarn backstage-cli build. Frontend plugins export React components; backend plugins export Express routers. Know this distinction for the exam.

📝 Chapter 18 — CBA Practice Questions

Q1
What command scaffolds a new Backstage plugin?
Show Answer
Answer

yarn backstage-cli create-plugin. This scaffolds the plugin with the required structure: plugin.ts, route definitions, and component files. Add --backend for a backend-only plugin.

Explanation

create-plugin generates a frontend plugin by default. --backend flag creates a backend-only plugin with Express routes. For full-stack plugins, create both separately. The scaffolded structure includes plugin.ts (entry), routes.ts (URLs), and components/ (UI). CBA tests this as the standard plugin creation workflow.

Q2
After creating a plugin, what 3 files must you update to make it visible?
Show Answer
Answer

1. packages/app/src/App.tsx — Import the plugin and add a route
2. packages/app/src/components/Root.tsx — Add a SidebarItem
3. (If backend) packages/backend/src/index.ts — Register the backend plugin

Explanation

Three files, three purposes: App.tsx for routing, Root.tsx for navigation visibility, backend/index.ts for server-side logic. Missing any one = plugin won't work properly. App.tsx makes it accessible; Root.tsx makes it discoverable; backend makes it functional. CBA: know which file does what.

Q3
When should you build a custom plugin vs using an existing one?
Show Answer
Answer

Build custom when: no existing plugin exists, you need custom internal workflows, or you need organization-specific data aggregation. Always check the marketplace (200+ plugins) first — it may already exist.

Explanation

The CBA expects you to know the make-vs-buy decision: check backstage.io/plugins first, then build custom only if nothing exists. Custom plugins have maintenance cost — they need updates when Backstage APIs change. Community plugins are maintained by others. Always prefer existing over custom.

Q4
What are the 3 files you must update after creating a frontend plugin to make it visible?
Show Answer
Answer

1. packages/app/src/App.tsx — Import and add a <Route> for the plugin page
2. packages/app/src/components/Root.tsx — Add a <SidebarItem> with icon and link
3. (Optional but common) packages/backend/src/index.ts — Register backend plugin if it has one

Explanation

This is the plugin registration trifecta. App.tsx uses React Router's <Route> component. Root.tsx uses Backstage's <SidebarItem>. The backend registration adds the plugin's Express router to the backend server. CBA: App.tsx = routing, Root.tsx = sidebar, backend/index.ts = server logic.

Q5
What files would an anihpj dashboard plugin contain?
Show Answer
Answer

plugin.ts (createPlugin definition), routes.ts (URL routing), api.ts (API client for backend data), and components/ with AnihpjPage.tsx (main page), JobStatsCard.tsx (job metrics), ServiceHealth.tsx (K8s health). Standard pattern: plugin → routes → api → components.

Explanation

Standard plugin file structure: plugin.ts (entry), routes.ts (URLs), api.ts (data access), components/ (UI). This pattern applies to all custom plugins. The names change (anihpj-specific) but the structure doesn't. CBA: know the 4 file types and what each does.

Q6
How do you test a custom plugin before deploying?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Jest unit tests: Test individual components and API logic
2. Integration tests: Test the plugin as a whole with mock data
3. Manual testing: Run yarn dev — the plugin appears in the sidebar and can be tested interactively in the browser

Explanation

Three testing layers: Jest for isolated component tests, integration tests for plugin-wide behavior, manual testing in yarn dev for real-world validation. Backstage plugins use standard React testing patterns. The CBA may ask about testing methodology — know the 3 layers.

Q7
What's the difference between yarn backstage-cli create-plugin and create-plugin --backend?
Show Answer
Answer

create-plugin scaffolds a frontend-only plugin with React components and routing. create-plugin --backend scaffolds a backend-only plugin with Express routes and database access. For a full-stack plugin, you typically create both a frontend and backend plugin separately.

Explanation

Frontend plugins = UI (React), backend plugins = API (Express). Frontend-only is simplest (no backend needed). Backend-only has no UI — useful for data processing. Full-stack = both, created separately. The CBA tests this distinction: know when to use which type based on the scenario.

Q8
How does a custom plugin access the Backstage database?
Show Answer
Answer

Through PluginDatabaseManager in the backend plugin. The plugin requests a database client, which provides access to the PostgreSQL database. Plugins should NEVER access the database directly from the frontend — all database access must go through backend API endpoints for security.

Explanation

Security rule: frontend NEVER touches the database. All DB access goes through backend plugins, which use PluginDatabaseManager to get a Knex connection. This keeps database credentials server-side and prevents SQL injection from the browser. CBA: this is a critical security pattern.

Q9
Your custom plugin builds successfully but doesn't appear in the sidebar. What did you miss?
Show Answer
Answer

You likely missed the Root.tsx registration. Creating the plugin and adding a route in App.tsx makes the page accessible, but to show it in the sidebar, you must add a <SidebarItem icon={...} to="plugin-route" text="Plugin Name" /> in packages/app/src/components/Root.tsx.

Explanation

Most common plugin mistake: forgetting Root.tsx. App.tsx makes the page load at a URL; Root.tsx puts it in the sidebar. Without Root.tsx, users must type the URL directly. The CBA tests this rookie mistake: plugin builds but invisible = missing sidebar registration.

Q10
You need to build a plugin that shows jobpost metrics from 3 different sources (DB, K8s, Sentry). How would you architect it?
Show Answer
Answer

Build a full-stack plugin: the backend creates 3 API endpoints — /metrics/db (queries jobpost PostgreSQL), /metrics/k8s (calls K8s API for pod stats), /metrics/errors (calls Sentry API). The frontend calls these 3 endpoints via the API proxy and displays the aggregated data in MUI cards and charts. This keeps data access secure and centralized.

Explanation

Multi-source plugin architecture: backend aggregates 3 data sources (DB, K8s, Sentry) into 3 API endpoints. Frontend calls via proxy (security), renders in MUI cards/charts. Pattern: 1 backend endpoint per data source, frontend merges results. CBA: know the full-stack plugin pattern for multi-source data.

Chapter 19: Deploying Backstage on Kubernetes

Production Backstage runs on Kubernetes — the same platform your services run on. This chapter walks through building Docker images, writing K8s manifests, deploying with Helm, and scaling Backstage for enterprise use. You'll deploy a complete Backstage instance running on K8s with PostgreSQL, Secrets, and Ingress.

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why Kubernetes is the right platform for production Backstage
  • ✅ Build a production Docker image with multi-stage builds

🎓 CBA Relevance
Infrastructure 22%
Deploying Backstage = CBA Infrastructure (22%)

The CBA tests your ability to deploy Backstage to production. Know: Docker multi-stage builds, K8s Deployment structure (replicas, env vars from Secrets, ConfigMap volumes), PostgreSQL as the required production database, and Helm as the preferred deployment method.

19.1 Why Deploy Backstage on Kubernetes?

🔄
High Availability

Run multiple replicas. If one pod crashes, K8s auto-restarts it. Traffic is load-balanced across healthy pods.

📈
Auto-Scaling

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) scales Backstage pods based on CPU/memory. Handle traffic spikes automatically.

🏥
Self-Healing

K8s monitors pod health with liveness/readiness probes. Unhealthy pods are restarted or replaced automatically.

📋
GitOps Ready

Everything declared in YAML. Deploy via ArgoCD/Flux. Git is the single source of truth for your Backstage config.

19.3 Docker Image for Backstage

Multi-Stage Dockerfile

  # Stage 1: Build
  FROM node:18-bookworm-slim AS build
  WORKDIR /app
  COPY package.json yarn.lock ./
  RUN yarn install --frozen-lockfile --production=false
  COPY . .
  RUN yarn tsc && yarn build

  # Stage 2: Production (smaller image)
  FROM node:18-bookworm-slim AS runtime
  WORKDIR /app
  COPY --from=build /app/packages/backend/dist ./dist
  COPY --from=build /app/packages/backend/package.json ./
  COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
  ENV NODE_ENV=production
  EXPOSE 7007
  CMD ["node", "packages/backend", "--config", "app-config.yaml"]

Multi-Stage Build

Stage 1 installs ALL dependencies (including devDependencies for TypeScript), compiles, and builds. Stage 2 copies only the compiled output and production dependencies. This keeps the final image small (~300MB vs ~1.5GB).

Image Tagging Strategy

Use semantic versioning: v1.2.3. Tag each build with the Git commit SHA: registry.anihpj.com/backstage:v1.2.3-abc1234. This ensures every deployment is traceable to a specific commit.

19.4 Kubernetes Manifests

Deployment

Complete K8s Deployment YAML for Backstage

  apiVersion: apps/v1
  kind: Deployment
  metadata:
    name: backstage
    namespace: backstage
  spec:
    replicas: 3
    selector:
      matchLabels:
        app: backstage
    template:
      metadata:
        labels:
          app: backstage
      spec:
        containers:
        - name: backstage
          image: registry.anihpj.com/backstage:v1.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 7007
          env:
            - name: POSTGRES_HOST
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: backstage-secrets
                  key: postgres-host
            - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: backstage-secrets
                  key: postgres-password
            - name: GITHUB_TOKEN
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: backstage-secrets
                  key: github-token
          volumeMounts:
            - name: app-config
              mountPath: /app/app-config.yaml
              subPath: app-config.yaml
          resources:
            requests:
              memory: "512Mi"
              cpu: "500m"
            limits:
              memory: "2Gi"
              cpu: "2000m"
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthcheck
              port: 7007
            initialDelaySeconds: 30
            periodSeconds: 10
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthcheck
              port: 7007
            initialDelaySeconds: 10
            periodSeconds: 5
        volumes:
          - name: app-config
            configMap:
              name: backstage-config

Service + Ingress

ClusterIP Service on port 7007. Ingress with TLS termination and host: backstage.anihpj.com. Annotations for cert-manager if using Let's Encrypt.

ConfigMap + Secret

ConfigMap stores app-config.yaml (mounted as file). Secret stores: POSTGRES_HOST, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, GITHUB_TOKEN. Never put secrets in ConfigMap!

PersistentVolumeClaim

Used for TechDocs cache if using local publisher. In production with cloud publisher (GCS/S3/Azure), PVC is not needed for TechDocs — only for PostgreSQL data.

19.5 Helm Chart for Backstage

Deploying with Helm

  # Add Backstage Helm repo
  $ helm repo add backstage https://backstage.github.io/charts
  $ helm repo update

  # Install with custom values
  $ helm install backstage backstage/backstage \
      --namespace backstage --create-namespace \
      --set appConfig.app.title="anihpj Developer Portal" \
      --set database.client=pg \
      --set database.connection.host=postgres.anihpj.com \
      --set ingress.enabled=true \
      --set ingress.host=backstage.anihpj.com

  # Upgrade
  $ helm upgrade backstage backstage/backstage -n backstage

  # Rollback
  $ helm rollback backstage -n backstage
⚡ SPEED TIP — K8s Deployment Must-Haves: For the CBA, know the 6 K8s resources: Deployment (3 replicas), Service (ClusterIP:7007), Ingress (TLS+host), ConfigMap (app-config.yaml), Secret (DB creds+tokens), PVC (PostgreSQL data). Also: PostgreSQL (not SQLite!), cloud storage for TechDocs, and Elasticsearch for search. These are the "production-ready" checklist items.
