📝 Chapter 19 — CBA Practice Questions

Q1
Why should Backstage use PostgreSQL instead of SQLite in production?
Show Answer
Answer

SQLite only supports a single writer — with 3 Backstage replicas on K8s, concurrent writes would cause data corruption. PostgreSQL handles concurrent connections from multiple pods safely and is the only supported production database for Backstage.

Explanation

SQLite = single-writer lock; multiple replicas = data corruption. PostgreSQL supports concurrent connections via MVCC. This is the #1 reason you can't run SQLite in production with multiple pods. The CBA tests this as a key production requirement — always PostgreSQL on K8s.

Q2
What does a multi-stage Dockerfile achieve for Backstage?
Show Answer
Answer

Stage 1 (build): installs ALL deps, compiles TypeScript, builds the app. Stage 2 (runtime): copies only compiled output + production deps. Result: smaller image (~300MB vs ~1.5GB), faster pulls, smaller attack surface.

Explanation

Multi-stage builds solve the "fat image" problem. Build stage has compilers and devDeps (1.5GB), runtime stage has only what's needed (300MB). Benefits: faster deploys (smaller pull), less CVEs (fewer packages), lower storage costs. CBA: know the 2-stage pattern and its benefits.

# Multi-Stage Dockerfile for Backstage
# STAGE 1: BUILD (1.5GB — compilers, devDeps)
FROM node:18 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json yarn.lock ./
RUN yarn install --frozen-lockfile
COPY . .
RUN yarn build

# STAGE 2: RUNTIME (300MB — production only)
FROM node:18-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/packages/backend/dist ./
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
CMD ["node", "main.js"]
Q3
Where should you store app-config.yaml in a K8s deployment?
Show Answer
Answer

In a ConfigMap, mounted as a file in the pod. Create: kubectl create configmap backstage-config --from-file=app-config.yaml. Mount it as a volume. Secrets (DB passwords, tokens) should be in a separate Secret resource, not in the ConfigMap.

Explanation

ConfigMap = non-sensitive config (app-config.yaml). Secret = sensitive data (passwords, tokens). Both can be mounted as files or env vars. CBA: NEVER put passwords in ConfigMap. ConfigMap changes require pod restart to take effect (unless using subPath mount or reloader).

# ConfigMap vs Secret — K8s Resource Comparison
# ConfigMap (for app-config.yaml)
kubectl create configmap backstage-config \
  --from-file=app-config.yaml -n backstage

# Secret (for passwords/tokens — base64 encoded at rest)
kubectl create secret generic backstage-secrets \
  --from-literal=POSTGRES_PASSWORD=xxx \
  --from-literal=GITHUB_TOKEN=xxx -n backstage

# ❌ NEVER do this:
kubectl create configmap backstage-secrets \
  --from-literal=POSTGRES_PASSWORD=xxx  # ← Secrets in ConfigMap!
Q4
What Kubernetes resources are needed to deploy Backstage in production?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Deployment — 3 replicas, resource limits, env vars from Secrets
2. Service — ClusterIP on port 7007
3. Ingress — TLS termination, host routing
4. ConfigMap — app-config.yaml mounted as volume
5. Secret — PostgreSQL creds, GitHub tokens
6. PVC — For PostgreSQL data (or TechDocs cache if using local publisher)

Explanation

Six mandatory resources for production Backstage on K8s. Deployment runs the app, Service exposes it internally, Ingress routes external traffic with TLS, ConfigMap holds app config, Secret holds credentials, PVC persists PostgreSQL data. CBA: memorize these 6 — they're the production K8s checklist.

# K8s Resource Stack for Backstage
# ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
# │  1. Deployment (3 replicas)     │ → Runs Backstage pods
# │  2. Service (ClusterIP:7007)    │ → Internal networking
# │  3. Ingress (TLS + host)        │ → External traffic routing
# │  4. ConfigMap (app-config.yaml) │ → Non-sensitive config
# │  5. Secret (DB creds + tokens)  │ → Sensitive credentials
# │  6. PVC (PostgreSQL data)       │ → Persistent storage
# └─────────────────────────────────┘
Q5
How do you pass environment variables from a K8s Secret to a Backstage pod?
Show Answer
Answer

Use env.valueFrom.secretKeyRef in the Deployment spec. Example:
env:
- name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
valueFrom:
secretKeyRef:
name: backstage-secrets
key: postgres-password

Explanation

secretKeyRef maps a K8s Secret key to an env var inside the container. The Secret exists in K8s (base64-encoded at rest), and is injected as plaintext env var at pod startup. Alternative: mount Secret as a file. CBA: know env.valueFrom.secretKeyRef syntax.

# secretKeyRef — Injecting Secrets into Pods
spec:
  containers:
    - name: backstage
      env:
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:              # ← K8s Secret reference
              name: backstage-secrets   # ← Secret resource name
              key: postgres-password    # ← Key within the Secret
        - name: GITHUB_TOKEN
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: backstage-secrets
              key: github-token
Q6
What image tagging strategy should you use for production Backstage?
Show Answer
Answer

Use semantic versioning + Git SHA: registry.anihpj.com/backstage:v1.2.3-abc1234. This ensures: (1) every deployment is traceable to a specific commit, (2) you can quickly identify which version is running, (3) rollbacks are precise. Never use :latest in production.

Explanation

Immutable tags = traceability. :latest is mutable — you never know which image is running. Semantic version + Git SHA gives you both human-readable version AND exact commit reference. CBA: :latest in production = wrong answer. Always use versioned, immutable tags.

# Image Tagging Strategy
# ✅ GOOD — Immutable, traceable
registry.anihpj.com/backstage:v1.2.3-abc1234
#                                   ^^^^^^^^  ← Git commit SHA (traceable)
#                                   ^^^^^  ← Semantic version (human-readable)

# ❌ BAD — Mutable, untraceable
registry.anihpj.com/backstage:latest   # ← NEVER in production!
Q7
What Helm commands deploy, upgrade, and rollback Backstage?
Show Answer
Answer

Install: helm install backstage backstage/backstage -n backstage --create-namespace
Upgrade: helm upgrade backstage backstage/backstage -n backstage
Rollback: helm rollback backstage -n backstage

Explanation

Helm is the preferred Backstage deployment method. Three commands cover the lifecycle: install (first deploy), upgrade (update config/image), rollback (revert to previous release). Helm manages all 6 K8s resources as a single release. CBA: know these 3 Helm commands and their flags.

Q8
Why do you need liveness and readiness probes for Backstage on K8s?
Show Answer
Answer

Liveness probe: Checks if the pod is still running. If it fails, K8s restarts the pod. Endpoint: /healthcheck.
Readiness probe: Checks if the pod is ready to serve traffic. If it fails, K8s removes the pod from the Service load balancer. Use /healthcheck for both.

Explanation

Liveness = restart if dead. Readiness = stop sending traffic if not ready. Both use /healthcheck endpoint. Without these probes, K8s can't detect hung or broken pods. CBA: know the difference — liveness kills+restarts, readiness removes from Service endpoint list.

Q9
You have 3 Backstage pods but only one shows TechDocs. What's wrong?
Show Answer
Answer

You're using the local TechDocs publisher. Each pod has its own ./techdocs-output/ directory — only the pod that built the docs has them. Fix: switch to cloud storage (GCS/S3/Azure) so all pods access the same docs, or use builder: external to pre-build docs in CI/CD.

Explanation

Local publisher = pod-local filesystem. With 3 replicas, each pod has its own copy — inconsistent results. Production fix: use cloud storage (GCS/S3/Azure) with all pods reading from the same bucket. Alternative: external builder pre-builds in CI, pods just serve. CBA: local publisher only works for single-replica dev.

Q10
Write the kubectl commands to deploy Backstage from scratch.
Show Answer
Answer

kubectl create namespace backstage
kubectl create secret generic backstage-secrets --from-literal=POSTGRES_PASSWORD=xxx --from-literal=GITHUB_TOKEN=xxx -n backstage
kubectl create configmap backstage-config --from-file=app-config.yaml -n backstage
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
kubectl apply -f k8s/service.yaml
kubectl apply -f k8s/ingress.yaml
kubectl scale deploy/backstage --replicas=3 -n backstage

Explanation

7 commands, 6 resources. Order matters: namespace first, then Secrets (needed by Deployment), ConfigMap, then apply manifests, finally scale. CBA: know the correct order — Secrets and ConfigMap must exist before the Deployment references them, or pods will fail to start.

Chapter 20: Kubernetes Plugin Deep Dive

The K8s plugin connects Backstage to your clusters and displays live deployment status on entity pages. This chapter dives into the plugin architecture, multi-cluster setup, custom dashboards, and troubleshooting.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours☸️ Deep Dive🎯 CBA 22%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand the K8s plugin architecture (frontend tab + backend API client)
  • ✅ Configure multi-cluster setups with different auth methods per cluster
  • ✅ Build custom K8s dashboards showing pod health, replicas, and service endpoints
  • ✅ Troubleshoot common K8s plugin connection and annotation issues

🎯 CBA Exam Relevance — Backstage Infrastructure 22%

The CBA tests your ability to connect Backstage to Kubernetes clusters and display deployment information. Key exam topics: the backstage.io/kubernetes-id and backstage.io/kubernetes-namespace annotations, multi-cluster configuration in app-config.yaml, and how the plugin discovers K8s resources by matching entity names to Deployment names.

🎯 CBA Exam Tip — K8s Annotations Are Critical

The CBA frequently asks: "How does Backstage know which K8s resources belong to an entity?" Answer: The backstage.io/kubernetes-id annotation on the entity's catalog-info.yaml MUST match the K8s Deployment name. Without this annotation, the K8s tab shows "No resources found." Also know: backstage.io/kubernetes-namespace overrides the default namespace for that entity.

20.1 K8s Plugin Architecture — How It Connects

K8s Plugin — Frontend + Backend Architecture
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     K8s PLUGIN — DUAL LAYER                                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  🖥️ FRONTEND (Browser)                                                   │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  Entity Page → "KUBERNETES" Tab                                     │  │
  │  │  ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐                │  │
  │  │  │ Deployments  │ │    Pods      │ │  Services    │                │  │
  │  │  │ jobpost: 3/3 │ │ ✅ Running   │ │ :8000 (TCP)  │                │  │
  │  │  └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘                │  │
  │  └──────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                 │ REST: /api/kubernetes/services/:ref    │
  │  ⚙️ BACKEND (Node.js)           │                                        │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  KubernetesServiceApi                                               │  │
  │  │  • Reads entity annotations (kubernetes-id, namespace, selector)    │  │
  │  │  • Calls K8s API Server (get/list/watch resources)                  │  │
  │  │  • Returns merged results to frontend                               │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 How Entity Annotations Drive Discovery

Backstage reads 3 annotations from the entity: backstage.io/kubernetes-id (exact Deployment name match), backstage.io/kubernetes-namespace (scope to specific namespace), backstage.io/kubernetes-label-selector (label-based query). The K8s API is queried with these filters, and results appear as cards on the entity's K8s tab.

20.3 Custom Kubernetes Dashboards — Build Your Own Cards

📊 Pod Metrics Card

Show CPU usage, memory consumption, restart count. Fetch from K8s metrics API. Render as MUI progress bars and charts.

📜 Deployment History

Show last 10 deployments with status, age, and trigger. Use kubectl rollout history equivalent via K8s API.

🏥 Cluster Health

Aggregate view: total pods, nodes, deployments across all namespaces. Color-coded health indicators.

🔧 Custom Actions

Add buttons for: restart deployment, scale replicas, view logs. Use K8s API with proper RBAC (write permissions needed).

🛠️ Building Custom Cards

Use createComponentExtension() to create entity page cards. Access K8s data via the kubernetesApiRef. Render using MUI components (Card, Table, LinearProgress). Register the card on the entity page to appear alongside built-in K8s tabs.

20.4 Troubleshooting K8s Plugin

ErrorCauseFix
"403 Forbidden"RBAC: ServiceAccount lacks permissionsAdd get/list/watch on Deployments, Pods, Services
"Connection refused"Wrong API server URL or network issueVerify cluster URL and network connectivity
"TLS certificate"Self-signed cert not trustedSet skipTLSVerify: true (dev only) or add CA cert
No K8s tabMissing annotation or pluginAdd backstage.io/kubernetes-id annotation
⚡ SPEED TIP — K8s Plugin Config: The CBA tests the kubernetes config block: serviceLocatorMethod: multiTenant (most common), clusterLocatorMethods[].clusters[] (list of clusters with name, URL, auth). Entity annotation backstage.io/kubernetes-id must match the K8s Deployment name EXACTLY. Case-sensitive. Missing or mismatched annotation = no K8s data on entity page.

📝 Chapter 20 — CBA Practice Questions

Q1
What RBAC permissions does Backstage need for the K8s plugin?
Show Answer
Answer

get, list, watch on Deployments, Pods, Services, Ingresses, ReplicaSets. Backstage is read-only — it never creates or modifies K8s resources. Create a ClusterRole with these permissions and bind it to the ServiceAccount.

Explanation

Backstage is read-only to K8s — only get/list/watch verbs needed. No create/update/delete. A ClusterRole (not Role) is needed because it needs cluster-wide access to discover resources across namespaces. CBA: know the 3 read verbs and that ClusterRoleBinding is required.

Q2
How do you connect Backstage to multiple K8s clusters?
Show Answer
Answer

Add multiple entries to kubernetes.clusterLocatorMethods[0].clusters[]. Each has its own name, URL, authProvider, and serviceAccountToken. Backstage queries all clusters and merges results.

Explanation

Multi-cluster = array of cluster configs. Each entry needs: name (label), url (API server), authProvider (serviceAccount/oidc), serviceAccountToken. Backstage queries ALL clusters in parallel and merges results by cluster name. CBA: know the YAML array structure for multiple clusters.

Q3
Your K8s plugin shows "403 Forbidden". What's wrong?
Show Answer
Answer

The ServiceAccount token doesn't have sufficient RBAC permissions. Check the ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding — the SA needs get, list, watch verbs on Deployments, Pods, Services, Ingresses, and ReplicaSets.

Explanation

403 = RBAC denied. Fix: verify ClusterRole has correct resources and verbs, check ClusterRoleBinding links to the right ServiceAccount. Common mistake: using Role (namespace-scoped) instead of ClusterRole (cluster-scoped). CBA: 403 error = RBAC issue, not network.

Q4
What is the difference between singleTenant and multiTenant service locator methods?
Show Answer
Answer

singleTenant: Looks for K8s resources in ONE configured namespace. multiTenant: Looks in ALL namespaces matching the entity's annotations. Multi-tenant is the default and most common — it lets each team's services live in their own namespace while Backstage discovers them all.

Explanation

singleTenant = 1 namespace for all. multiTenant = each entity's namespace from annotation. multiTenant is default because organizations run services in per-team namespaces. CBA: know which is default (multiTenant) and the config key serviceLocatorMethod.type.

Q5
How does the K8s plugin discover which resources belong to an entity?
Show Answer
Answer

Through annotations on the Catalog entity: backstage.io/kubernetes-id (match by name), backstage.io/kubernetes-namespace (scope to namespace), or backstage.io/kubernetes-label-selector (match by labels). The plugin queries the K8s API using these filters.

Explanation

3 annotation methods: kubernetes-id (exact name match — most common), kubernetes-namespace (override namespace), kubernetes-label-selector (label query). The plugin reads these from entity metadata.annotations in catalog-info.yaml. CBA: kubernetes-id must match Deployment name exactly, case-sensitive.

Q6
What cluster locator methods are available besides 'config'?
Show Answer
Answer

Besides config (static list), there are cloud-specific locators: gke (Google Kubernetes Engine), eks (Amazon EKS), aks (Azure AKS). These auto-discover clusters in your cloud account without manual configuration. config is the most commonly used for explicit control.

Explanation

config = manual list (most control). gke/eks/aks = auto-discovery via cloud API. Auto-discovery is convenient but gives less control. Most enterprises use config for production. CBA: know the 4 locator types and that config is the most common.

Q7
How do you add a custom K8s dashboard card to an entity page?
Show Answer
Answer

Create a custom plugin using createComponentExtension() that fetches K8s data via the K8s API and renders it in MUI components. Register it on the entity page. The card can show pod CPU/memory metrics, deployment history, or any custom K8s data.

Explanation

createComponentExtension() lets you add custom cards to entity pages. The card fetches data from the K8s API (via Backstage's proxy) and renders using MUI. Common uses: pod metrics (CPU/Memory), deployment history, error rates. CBA: know createComponentExtension for custom entity page cards.

Q8
Your K8s plugin can't connect because of a self-signed certificate. What do you do?
Show Answer
Answer

Option 1 (dev only): Set skipTLSVerify: true in the cluster config. Option 2 (production): Add the CA certificate to Backstage's trusted certificates and set skipTLSVerify: false. Never use skipTLSVerify in production — it disables TLS verification entirely.

Explanation

TLS errors with self-signed certs: dev fix = skipTLSVerify:true (quick, insecure). Production fix = add CA cert to trust store. skipTLSVerify in production = MITM attack risk. CBA: know both approaches and that skipTLSVerify is dev-only — wrong answer for production scenarios.

Q9
What K8s permissions does the Backstage ServiceAccount need at minimum?
Show Answer
Answer

get, list, watch on: pods, services, deployments, replicasets, ingresses, configmaps (in all relevant namespaces). Backstage is read-only — it never creates, updates, or deletes K8s resources. Create a ClusterRole with these permissions bound to the Backstage ServiceAccount.

Explanation

Minimum RBAC: 3 verbs (get/list/watch) on 6 resources. ClusterRole (not Role) for cluster-wide discovery. Backstage is read-only — no create/update/delete. CBA: this is a frequently tested question — memorize the 3 verbs and 6 resource types.

Q10
You add a second K8s cluster to Backstage. How do you verify both are working?
Show Answer
Answer

Visit an entity page with K8s annotations — both clusters' resources should appear in the K8s tab, labeled by cluster name. Check Backstage backend logs for successful connections to both cluster APIs. Verify with: curl :7007/api/kubernetes/services/:entityRef — the response should include resources from both clusters.

Explanation

Verification: UI check (K8s tab shows both clusters), logs check (backend logs show connections), API check (curl /api/kubernetes/services/). Multi-cluster responses are labeled by cluster name. CBA: know the 3 verification methods and the API endpoint path.

Chapter 21: GitOps with Backstage and ArgoCD

GitOps means Git is the single source of truth — all infrastructure and application config lives in Git, and automated tools reconcile the actual state with the desired state. Backstage + ArgoCD together create a complete GitOps workflow visible from a single pane of glass.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1 hour🔄 GitOps🎯 CBA 22%
📝
Git as Truth

All config in Git. No manual kubectl apply. PR reviews for changes.

📄
Declarative

Everything defined in YAML. Desired state is explicit and versioned.

🔄
Auto-Sync

ArgoCD/Flux continuously reconcile. Actual state → desired state.

⬇️
Pull-Based

Cluster pulls from Git. No external push access needed. More secure.

    │  Developer pushes code ──▶ GitHub Actions builds Docker image    │
    │         │                          │                             │
    │         │                          ▼                             │
    │         │              Updates K8s manifest with new image tag    │
    │         │                          │                             │
    │         │                          ▼                             │
    │         │              ArgoCD detects Git change                 │
    │         │                          │                             │
    │         │                          ▼                             │

    │  │  • GitHub Actions: ✅ Build passed                        │    │
    │  │  • ArgoCD: ✅ Synced & Healthy                            │    │
    │  │  • K8s: 3/3 pods running                                  │    │

    │                                                                  │
    │  🔙 ROLLBACK: git revert manifest → ArgoCD auto-syncs back      │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

21.1 What is GitOps?

GitOps — Push vs Pull Deployment Models
  ❌ PUSH (Old Way):                           ✅ PULL / GitOps (Modern Way):
  ┌──────────┐    kubectl apply               ┌──────────┐    polls every 3min
  │ CI/CD    │──────────────▶ K8s Cluster      │ Git Repo │◀──────────────┐
  │ Pipeline │                                 │ (truth)  │               │
  └──────────┘                                 └────┬─────┘         ┌─────┴─────┐
  CI/CD needs cluster credentials               │               │ ArgoCD    │
  (SECURITY RISK!)                              ▼               │ Flux      │
                                            ┌──────────┐         └───────────┘
                                            │ K8s      │         Runs INSIDE
                                            │ Cluster  │         the cluster
                                            └──────────┘         (more secure!)
📋 GitOps 4 Principles

1. Git as source of truth — all config in Git
2. Declarative — everything YAML
3. Automated reconciliation — ArgoCD/Flux syncs
4. Pull-based — cluster pulls from Git

🔒 Why Pull-Based?

CI/CD never touches the cluster directly. No external cluster credentials needed. The reconciliation agent runs inside the cluster and pulls from Git. This eliminates a major attack vector.

21.2 Backstage + ArgoCD Integration

ArgoCD Plugin — What It Shows on Entity Pages

  │                    ARGOCD PLUGIN ON ENTITY PAGE                        │
  │                                                                      │
  │  catalog-info.yaml annotation:       Entity Page — ArgoCD Tab:       │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────┐      ┌────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ argocd/app-name: jobpost   │──▶  │ 🟢 SYNCED                  │  │

  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

21.3 GitOps Workflow for anihpj

The complete flow: Developer pushes code → GitHub Actions builds Docker image → Updates K8s manifest with new image tag in Git → ArgoCD detects change → Auto-syncs to K8s cluster → Backstage shows deployment status. Rollback: git revert the manifest change → ArgoCD auto-syncs back. Entire pipeline visible in Backstage.

# k8s/overlays/production/kustomization.yaml — GitOps Image Update
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
  - ../../base          # Base manifests (Deployment, Service, etc.)

namespace: backstage

images:
  - name: jobpost
    newName: ghcr.io/anihpj/jobpost
    newTag: v2.4.2      # ← ArgoCD watches this. CI/CD updates this tag.

# ArgoCD Application that watches this kustomization
---
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: jobpost
  namespace: argocd
  annotations:
    # Links this ArgoCD app to the Backstage entity
    argocd/app-name: jobpost
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/anihpj/k8s-manifests
    path: overlays/production
    targetRevision: main
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: backstage
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true        # Remove resources not in Git
      selfHeal: true     # Auto-fix drift
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true
📝
Git = Source of Truth

Every change flows through Git. No kubectl apply directly. The Kustomization file IS the desired state. ArgoCD enforces it.

🔄
Auto-Sync

ArgoCD polls Git every 3 minutes. Detects drift and auto-heals. If someone manually edits a pod, ArgoCD reverts it back to Git state.

🔙
Instant Rollback

git revert the image tag change → ArgoCD syncs back to old version. Rollback = git history. No manual kubectl commands.

💡 CBA GitOps Insight

The CBA tests the GitOps flow: developer pushes → CI builds image → updates manifest in Git → CD tool (ArgoCD/Flux) syncs → Backstage displays status. Know that ArgoCD uses pull-based deployment (cluster pulls from Git), not push-based. The annotation argocd/app-name links the ArgoCD application to the Backstage entity.

Part 7 Quick Wins for CBA: Backstage production = PostgreSQL + K8s + Helm. NEVER use SQLite on K8s. Docker multi-stage builds keep images small (~300MB). K8s manifests: Deployment (3 replicas, probes) + Service (ClusterIP) + Ingress (TLS) + ConfigMap + Secret. The K8s plugin needs get/list/watch RBAC. GitOps = Git is truth + ArgoCD reconciles. Rollback = git revert, not kubectl.

📝 Chapter 21 — CBA Practice Questions

Q1
What are the 4 principles of GitOps?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Git as single source of truth
2. Declarative configuration (YAML)
3. Automated reconciliation (ArgoCD/Flux)
4. Pull-based deployment (cluster pulls from Git)

Explanation

GitOps 4 principles: (1) Git is the single source of truth for desired state, (2) everything declared in YAML, (3) a reconciliation agent (ArgoCD/Flux) enforces desired state, (4) the cluster pulls changes (more secure than pushing). CBA: know all 4, especially pull-based.

# GitOps Flow — 4 Principles Visualized
#   Git Repo                  ArgoCD/Flux              K8s Cluster
#  ┌──────────┐             ┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────┐
#  │ k8s/     │───pull────▶│ Reconciliation│──sync──▶│ Live State   │
#  │ deploy.yaml│   (every  │   Agent       │         │ (pods, svc)  │
#  │ svc.yaml  │   3 min)  │               │         │              │
#  └──────────┘             └──────────────┘         └──────────────┘
#   DESIRED STATE                                     ACTUAL STATE
#   (Single Source of Truth)                          (Continuously reconciled)
Q2
How does the ArgoCD plugin integrate with Backstage?
Show Answer
Answer

It shows ArgoCD application sync status, health, and deployment history on entity pages. Configure the ArgoCD API URL in app-config.yaml and add argocd/app-name annotation to entity YAML.

Explanation

ArgoCD plugin = entity page integration. Shows sync status, health, and history. Two config pieces: ArgoCD API URL in app-config.yaml + entity annotation. Without the annotation, the ArgoCD tab on entity pages shows nothing. CBA: know the annotation and config structure.

Q3
How do you rollback a deployment in a GitOps workflow?
Show Answer
Answer

git revert the commit that changed the image tag. ArgoCD detects the Git change and auto-syncs the cluster back to the previous version. No manual kubectl commands needed — everything through Git.

Explanation

GitOps rollback = git revert, not kubectl. Git revert creates an auditable undo commit. ArgoCD detects and auto-syncs. Advantage: rollbacks are reviewed via PR, fully auditable, and no direct cluster access needed. CBA: rollback through Git, never kubectl.

Q4
What annotation links an entity to its ArgoCD application?
Show Answer
Answer

argocd/app-name: my-app or argocd/app-selector: app=my-app. This tells the ArgoCD plugin which application to display status for on the entity page. Add it to the entity's metadata.annotations.

Explanation

Two annotation formats: argocd/app-name (exact) or argocd/app-selector (label query). app-name is simpler and more common. Add to metadata.annotations in catalog-info.yaml. CBA: know both formats and where to add them.

# ArgoCD Annotation — Linking Entity to Deployment
# catalog-info.yaml
metadata:
  annotations:
    argocd/app-name: jobpost          # ← Exact ArgoCD app name
    # OR
    argocd/app-selector: app=jobpost  # ← Label-based selection
Q5
What's the difference between push-based and pull-based deployment?
Show Answer
Answer

Push-based: CI/CD pushes changes to the cluster (kubectl apply). The cluster is passive.
Pull-based (GitOps): An agent (ArgoCD) inside the cluster pulls changes from Git and applies them. The cluster is active. GitOps is pull-based — the cluster continuously reconciles with Git.

Explanation

Push = CI/CD has cluster creds (security risk, external access). Pull = agent inside cluster polls Git (more secure, no external access). GitOps uses pull-based. CBA: know the security advantage of pull — no external cluster credentials needed.

Q6
How does Backstage show ArgoCD deployment status on entity pages?
Show Answer
Answer

The ArgoCD plugin calls the ArgoCD API server and displays: application sync status (synced/out-of-sync), health status (healthy/degraded), deployment history, and sync duration. Configure the ArgoCD API URL in app-config.yaml and annotate entities with argocd/app-name.

Explanation

ArgoCD plugin displays 4 metrics: sync status, health, history, duration. All fetched from ArgoCD API and rendered on entity page. Config: API URL + entity annotation. CBA: know the 4 displayed data points.

Q7
What are Flux and how does it compare to ArgoCD?
Show Answer
Answer

Both are GitOps tools. ArgoCD has a web UI, is application-focused, and has a native Backstage plugin. Flux is CLI-focused, uses K8s custom resources for configuration, and integrates natively with Helm. Both achieve the same goal: Git as source of truth → auto-sync to cluster.

Explanation

ArgoCD = UI + Backstage plugin (preferred for Backstage). Flux = CLI + K8s CRDs. Both CNCF graduated. For Backstage, ArgoCD has the native plugin advantage. CBA: ArgoCD has a Backstage plugin, Flux does not directly.

Q8
Describe the complete GitOps flow for anihpj from code push to Backstage visibility.
Show Answer
Answer

1. Dev pushes code → 2. CI builds Docker image → 3. CI updates image tag in Git (k8s/deployment.yaml) → 4. ArgoCD detects Git change → 5. ArgoCD syncs new image to K8s cluster → 6. Backstage K8s plugin fetches new pod status → 7. ArgoCD plugin shows sync status → Full visibility in Backstage.

Explanation

7-step flow: code → CI build → Git update → ArgoCD detect → ArgoCD sync → K8s plugin → ArgoCD plugin. Key: CI updates Git, ArgoCD deploys, Backstage observes. CBA: know that CI never touches the cluster directly in GitOps.

Q9
Your ArgoCD app shows "Out of Sync" in Backstage. What does this mean?
Show Answer
Answer

It means the live state in the K8s cluster doesn't match the desired state in Git. Someone may have manually changed a resource (kubectl edit), or a new commit changed the manifests but ArgoCD hasn't synced yet. ArgoCD will auto-sync (if configured) or wait for manual sync.

Explanation

Out of Sync = live ≠ desired. Causes: drift (manual kubectl), pending sync (new commit), or auto-sync disabled. ArgoCD continuously compares live vs desired. CBA: Out of Sync means Git and cluster don't match — either drift or pending sync.

Q10
How would you set up a complete GitOps pipeline for anihpj using Backstage + GitHub Actions + ArgoCD?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Backstage Template creates the repo with Dockerfile, CI workflow, and K8s manifests
2. GitHub Actions on push: runs tests → builds Docker image → pushes to registry → updates image tag in k8s/deployment.yaml → commits back to repo
3. ArgoCD monitors the repo → detects the manifest change → auto-syncs to K8s
4. Backstage shows: CI/CD status (GitHub Actions card), deployment status (ArgoCD card), pod health (K8s tab). All from one entity page.

Explanation

Full pipeline: Template (scaffold) → CI (build+update Git) → ArgoCD (deploy) → Backstage (observe). Backstage is both the starting point (template) and endpoint (visibility). CBA: know each tool's role in the complete pipeline.

🔐 Part 8: Authentication & RBAC 🔴 Advanced

Chapter 22: Authentication Providers

Authentication is how Backstage knows who you are. This chapter covers the sign-in flow, all major auth providers (GitHub, Okta, Azure AD, Google, Auth0, Keycloak), how to configure them, and how to handle guest access. The CBA exam tests your ability to configure authentication correctly.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~2 hours🔐 Auth🎯 CBA 22%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand the Backstage authentication flow
  • ✅ Compare all major auth providers and choose the right one
  • ✅ Configure GitHub OAuth step-by-step
  • ✅ Set up enterprise SSO with Okta/Azure AD
  • ✅ Configure multiple auth providers simultaneously
🎓 CBA Relevance
Infrastructure 22%
Auth = Infrastructure Domain (22% of CBA)

The CBA tests auth configuration: which provider to use, how to configure OAuth/OIDC, sign-in resolvers, and the auth flow. Key concepts: providers (GitHub, Okta, Azure AD), JWT session tokens, group mapping, and NEVER using guest access in production.

22.1 Authentication in Backstage — The Sign-In Flow

Authentication Flow
  👤 User clicks "Sign In"
       │
       ▼
  🔀 Redirect to Auth Provider (GitHub/Okta/Google)
       │
       ▼
  ✅ User authenticates with provider
       │
       ▼
  🎫 Provider returns token to Backstage callback URL
       │
       ▼
  🔑 Backstage creates session (JWT)
       │  • Identity from provider (name, email, avatar)
       │  • Mapped to Backstage User entity
       │  • Group memberships synced
       ▼
  🖥️ User is logged in! Session stored in browser cookie.

22.2 Auth Provider Comparison

ProviderTypeBest ForSetup Effort
GitHubOAuth2Dev teams on GitHub. Auto-maps teams→Groups🟢 Easy
Okta / Azure ADOIDC/SAMLEnterprise SSO. Group sync via claims🟡 Medium
GoogleOAuth2GSuite/Google Workspace orgs🟢 Easy
Auth0 / KeycloakOIDCFlexible identity hub / Self-hosted🟡-🔴 Medium-Complex
Guest (No Auth)None⚠️ Development ONLY — NEVER in production🟢 None

22.3 GitHub Authentication — Step by Step

Setting Up GitHub OAuth

  # 1. Create GitHub OAuth App
  #    GitHub → Settings → Developer settings → OAuth Apps → New
  #    Callback URL: http://localhost:7007/api/auth/github/handler/frame

  # 2. Configure app-config.yaml
  auth:
    environment: development
    providers:
      github:
        development:
          clientId: ${GITHUB_CLIENT_ID}
          clientSecret: ${GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET}

  # 3. Set env vars and start
  $ export GITHUB_CLIENT_ID=abc123
  $ export GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET=xyz789
  $ yarn dev

  # 4. Test: Click Sign In → GitHub → Authorize → Logged in!

22.4 Enterprise SSO (Okta / Azure AD)

For enterprise organizations, Okta and Azure AD (now Microsoft Entra ID) are the most common SSO providers. They use OpenID Connect (OIDC) — a modern, simpler protocol built on OAuth 2.0 — rather than the older SAML protocol.

🔑 OIDC vs SAML — What You Need to Know

OIDC (OpenID Connect): Modern, JSON-based, mobile-friendly. Uses ID tokens (JWTs). Backstage's preferred protocol. SAML: Older, XML-based, enterprise-focused. More complex to configure. Backstage supports OIDC natively for Okta/Azure AD — SAML requires additional middleware.

StepOkta ConfigurationAzure AD (Entra ID) Configuration
1. Create AppOkta Admin → Applications → Create App Integration → OIDC → Web AppAzure Portal → Entra ID → App Registrations → New Registration
2. Redirect URIhttps://backstage.anihpj.com/api/auth/okta/handler/framehttps://backstage.anihpj.com/api/auth/microsoft/handler/frame
3. Client ID/SecretCopy from Okta App → General tabCopy from Azure App → Certificates & Secrets
4. Group ClaimsOkta → API → Authorization Servers → Add "groups" claimAzure → Token Configuration → Add "groups" claim (set to "All groups")
5. Assign UsersAssign users/groups to the Okta ApplicationEnterprise Applications → Users and Groups → Add

Okta Configuration Example:

# app-config.yaml — Okta OIDC Provider
auth:
  environment: production
  providers:
    okta:
      production:
        clientId: ${OKTA_CLIENT_ID}
        clientSecret: ${OKTA_CLIENT_SECRET}
        audience: "api://default"          # Okta API audience
        callbackUrl: "https://backstage.anihpj.com/api/auth/okta/handler/frame"

# Sign-in resolver maps Okta profile → Backstage User
signInPage: okta
auth:
  signInResolvers:
    okta:
      resolver: emailMatchingUserEntityProfileEmail

Azure AD Configuration Example:

# app-config.yaml — Azure AD / Entra ID Provider
auth:
  environment: production
  providers:
    microsoft:
      production:
        clientId: ${AZURE_CLIENT_ID}
        clientSecret: ${AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET}
        tenantId: ${AZURE_TENANT_ID}      # Your Azure tenant ID
        callbackUrl: "https://backstage.anihpj.com/api/auth/microsoft/handler/frame"

# Custom resolver for Azure AD groups
signInResolvers:
  microsoft:
    resolver: emailMatchingUserEntityProfileEmail

💡 Group Mapping — Automatic Team Syncing

Both Okta and Azure AD support group claims — when a user logs in, their Okta/Azure group memberships are included in the OIDC token. Backstage's sign-in resolver automatically maps these to Backstage Group entities. This means zero manual group management — when someone joins the "platform-team" group in Okta, they automatically get access to platform-team resources in Backstage.

🏢
Okta

Best for: companies using Okta as their primary identity provider. Strong group management. OIDC-native. Widely adopted among tech companies.

☁️
Azure AD / Entra ID

Best for: Microsoft 365 shops. Deep integration with Office, Teams, and Azure. Combined app registration + enterprise app model. Free with most M365 plans.

22.5 Multiple Auth Providers — One Backstage, Many Identities

Backstage supports running multiple auth providers simultaneously. This is critical for organizations where some teams use GitHub, others use Okta, and contractors use a separate identity provider.

    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │              MULTI-PROVIDER AUTH ARCHITECTURE                      │
    │                                                                  │
    │                     ┌─────────────────┐                          │
    │                     │  SIGN-IN PAGE    │                          │
    │                     │                 │                          │
    │                     │  [GitHub]  [Okta]│  ← Multiple buttons     │
    │                     │  [Azure] [Google]│                          │
    │                     └───┬───┬───┬───┬─┘                          │
    │                         │   │   │   │                            │
    │              ┌──────────┘   │   │   └──────────┐                │
    │              ▼              ▼   ▼              ▼                │
    │         ┌─────────┐  ┌─────────┐  ┌─────────┐  ┌─────────┐    │
    │         │ GitHub   │  │ Okta    │  │ Azure   │  │ Google  │    │
    │         │ Provider │  │ Provider│  │ Provider│  │ Provider│    │
    │         └────┬─────┘  └────┬────┘  └────┬────┘  └────┬────┘    │
    │              │             │            │            │          │
    │              └─────────────┼────────────┼────────────┘          │
    │                            │            │                       │
    │                            ▼            ▼                       │
    │                    ┌─────────────────────────┐                  │
    │                    │   SIGN-IN RESOLVERS     │                  │
    │                    │   (One per provider)    │                  │
    │                    │                         │                  │
    │                    │  GitHub → email match   │                  │
    │                    │  Okta   → email match   │                  │
    │                    │  Azure  → email match   │                  │
    │                    └───────────┬─────────────┘                  │
    │                                │                                │
    │                                ▼                                │
    │                    ┌─────────────────────────┐                  │
    │                    │   BACKSTAGE USER ENTITY  │                  │
    │                    │   (Single unified user)  │                  │
    │                    │   Same user, regardless  │                  │
    │                    │   of which provider used │                  │
    │                    └─────────────────────────┘                  │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
# app-config.yaml — Multiple Auth Providers
auth:
  environment: production
  providers:
    github:
      production:
        clientId: ${GITHUB_CLIENT_ID}
        clientSecret: ${GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET}
    okta:
      production:
        clientId: ${OKTA_CLIENT_ID}
        clientSecret: ${OKTA_CLIENT_SECRET}
        audience: "api://default"
    microsoft:
      production:
        clientId: ${AZURE_CLIENT_ID}
        clientSecret: ${AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET}
        tenantId: ${AZURE_TENANT_ID}
    google:
      production:
        clientId: ${GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID}
        clientSecret: ${GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET}

# All 4 providers appear on the sign-in page.
# User picks whichever one they prefer.
# Sign-in resolvers map each identity to the same Backstage User.

🔑 The Critical Role of Sign-In Resolvers

When the same person logs in via GitHub (using alice@anihpj.com) AND via Okta (also alice@anihpj.com), Backstage needs to know they're the SAME user. This is the sign-in resolver's job — it matches by email and creates/links to a single Backstage User entity. Without proper resolvers, the same person gets TWO separate Backstage accounts — one per provider — causing duplicate ownership and permission issues.

🔗
GitHub

Developers, contractors with GitHub accounts. Auto-maps GitHub teams.

🏢
Okta

Full-time employees. Enterprise SSO with group claims for team mapping.

☁️
Azure AD

Microsoft 365 orgs. Integrated with Office, Teams, Azure RBAC.

🌐
Google

G Suite orgs. Simple OAuth setup. Good for Google-first companies.

22.6 Guest Access — Development Only!

Guest access allows anyone to browse Backstage without logging in. It's designed for local development convenience, NOT for production.

⚠️ The Security Risk of Guest Access in Production
  • 🔴 No authentication: Anyone on the internet can access your Backstage instance
  • 🔴 Full catalog exposure: All services, APIs, systems, and their metadata are visible
  • 🔴 Documentation leaks: TechDocs may contain internal architecture, API keys in examples, and sensitive design decisions
  • 🔴 Plugin data exposure: CI/CD status, K8s pod info, Sentry errors — all publicly visible
  • 🔴 No audit trail: Can't track who viewed what. Zero accountability
  • 🔴 Template abuse: Anyone can execute software templates — creating repos, consuming resources

🚫 THE GOLDEN RULE

NEVER enable guest access in production. The CBA exam WILL test this. Guest access is configured via auth.environment: development with NO providers listed. If you see this in a production config, it's an immediate security failure. Production MUST have at least one auth provider configured.

SettingDevelopment (Guest OK)Production (Guest NEVER)
auth.environmentdevelopmentproduction
auth.providersEmpty or minimalAt least 1 (GitHub/Okta/Azure)
Who can access?Anyone on localhostOnly authenticated users
PermissionsNone (everything is open)RBAC enforced
Audit loggingOptionalRequired for compliance
# ❌ WRONG — Never do this in production!
auth:
  environment: development    # ← Guest access enabled!
  # providers:               # ← No providers = NO AUTH!
  #   (empty)

# ✅ CORRECT — Production configuration
auth:
  environment: production     # ← Guest access DISABLED
  providers:
    github:
      production:
        clientId: ${GITHUB_CLIENT_ID}
        clientSecret: ${GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET}
    # Always have at least ONE provider in production
🎯 CBA Exam Alert

The CBA exam will almost certainly include a question about guest access. The correct answer pattern: "Guest access (auth.environment: development with no providers) is for local development ONLY. Production MUST use auth.environment: production with at least one configured auth provider." If the exam shows a production config without auth providers, the correct answer is "This is a security vulnerability."

⚡ SPEED TIP — Auth Flow: Memorize the auth flow: User clicks Sign In → Redirect to provider (OAuth/OIDC) → Authenticate → Callback to /api/auth/{provider}/handler/frame → Backstage creates JWT session cookie. Guest access (development only!) = auth.environment: development with no providers. Production MUST = auth.environment: production with at least 1 provider. This is a guaranteed CBA question.

📊 Chapter 22 — Visual Summary

🔀OAuth FlowRedirect → Authenticate → Token → JWT Session → Logged In.
🐙GitHubEasiest setup. Auto-maps teams. Best for GitHub-native teams.
🏢EnterpriseOkta/Azure AD for SSO. Group sync via claims. Medium setup.
⚠️GuestDev only. NEVER in production. CBA explicitly tests this.

📝 Chapter 22 — CBA Practice Questions

Q1
What is the Backstage auth flow from sign-in to logged-in?
Show Answer
Answer

User clicks Sign In → Redirect to provider (OAuth/OIDC) → User authenticates → Provider returns token to Backstage callback URL → Backstage creates JWT session → User is logged in with identity and group memberships.

Explanation

6-step auth flow: click → redirect → authenticate → token → JWT → session. Key: the callback URL is /api/auth/{provider}/handler/frame. Backstage issues its own JWT after validating the provider token. CBA: memorize the 6 steps in order.

Q2
Which auth provider is best for a team already using GitHub?
Show Answer
Answer

GitHub OAuth — it auto-maps GitHub teams to Backstage Groups, uses existing GitHub accounts, and is the easiest to set up (just create an OAuth App). Perfect for dev teams already on GitHub.

Explanation

GitHub OAuth = easiest provider. Auto-maps teams to Groups (no manual config). Uses existing accounts (no new passwords). Create a GitHub OAuth App, set client ID/secret in app-config.yaml. CBA: GitHub is the simplest auth provider to configure.

Q3
Can you use guest access in production?
Show Answer
Answer

NO — never. Guest access exposes your entire Backstage instance without authentication. Anyone can see all your services, APIs, docs, and potentially sensitive information. Production MUST have auth configured. Guest access is for local development only.

Explanation

Guest access = no login required, anyone can see everything. Dev only (auth.environment: development). Production must have auth.environment: production with at least one provider. CBA: guest in production = guaranteed wrong answer. This is a frequently tested concept.

Q4
What is the callback URL for GitHub OAuth in Backstage?
Show Answer
Answer

http://localhost:7007/api/auth/github/handler/frame for development. For production, replace localhost with your Backstage domain: https://backstage.anihpj.com/api/auth/github/handler/frame. This URL must be registered in the GitHub OAuth App settings.

Explanation

Callback URL = /api/auth/{provider}/handler/frame. Must match exactly between GitHub OAuth App settings and Backstage's app.baseUrl. Mismatch = redirect_uri error. CBA: know the callback URL pattern and that it must match the baseUrl.

# Auth Callback URL Pattern
# GitHub OAuth App Settings → Callback URL:
https://backstage.anihpj.com/api/auth/github/handler/frame

# app-config.yaml must match:
app:
  baseUrl: https://backstage.anihpj.com   # ← Must match the domain
auth:
  providers:
    github:
      development:
        clientId: ${GITHUB_CLIENT_ID}
        clientSecret: ${GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET}
Q5
How does Backstage store user sessions after authentication?
Show Answer
Answer

As a JWT (JSON Web Token) stored in a browser cookie. The JWT contains the user's identity, group memberships, and expiration time. This token is sent with every request to the Backstage backend for authorization. Sessions expire after a configurable duration.

Explanation

JWT cookie = session storage. Contains: user identity, groups, expiry. Sent with every request for authorization checks. CBA: sessions use JWT cookies, not server-side sessions. Know what the JWT contains (identity + groups + expiration).

Q6
What is sign-in resolver and what does it do?
Show Answer
Answer

A sign-in resolver maps the identity from an auth provider to a Backstage User entity. It takes the provider's profile (email, username, display name) and creates or matches a Backstage User. Custom resolvers handle cases where the default mapping doesn't fit your organization's identity model.

Explanation

Sign-in resolver = identity mapping (provider → Backstage User). Takes provider profile fields (email, name) and creates/matches a User entity. Custom resolvers needed when default mapping doesn't fit your org's identity model. CBA: know what a sign-in resolver does.

Q7
How do GitHub teams map to Backstage Groups?
Show Answer
Answer

Backstage automatically reads the user's GitHub team memberships from the OAuth token and creates/matches Backstage Group entities. The sign-in resolver handles this mapping. Team names become Group names, and the hierarchy (parent/child teams) is preserved.

Explanation

GitHub teams → Backstage Groups: automatic via sign-in resolver. Team name = Group name. Hierarchy preserved (parent/child). OAuth token contains team memberships. CBA: GitHub teams auto-map to Groups — no manual group creation needed.

Q8
Can you use multiple auth providers simultaneously in Backstage?
Show Answer
Answer

Yes. Configure each provider in auth.providers in app-config.yaml. Users see all configured providers on the sign-in page and can choose which one to use. Each provider needs its own sign-in resolver to map identities correctly.

Explanation

Multiple providers = multiple sign-in options. Each needs its own config block in auth.providers + its own sign-in resolver. Users pick on the sign-in page. CBA: Backstage supports multiple simultaneous auth providers.

Q9
Where do you configure auth providers in Backstage?
Show Answer
Answer

In app-config.yaml under auth.providers. Each provider has its own configuration block with clientId, clientSecret, and provider-specific settings. Secrets MUST use ${ENV_VAR} syntax — never hardcode client secrets.

Explanation

Auth config = auth.providers in app-config.yaml. Each provider needs clientId + clientSecret. Secrets use ${ENV_VAR} syntax (environment variable substitution). NEVER hardcode secrets in YAML. CBA: know the config path and ${ENV_VAR} pattern.

# Multi-Provider Auth Config (app-config.yaml)
auth:
  environment: production       # ← MUST be 'production' (no guest!)
  providers:
    github:
      development:
        clientId: ${GITHUB_CLIENT_ID}
        clientSecret: ${GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET}
    okta:
      development:
        clientId: ${OKTA_CLIENT_ID}
        clientSecret: ${OKTA_CLIENT_SECRET}
        audience: ${OKTA_AUDIENCE}
# Users see BOTH GitHub AND Okta on the sign-in page
Q10
You configured GitHub auth but sign-in fails with "redirect_uri mismatch". What's wrong?
Show Answer
Answer

The callback URL registered in your GitHub OAuth App doesn't match the one Backstage is using. Check: (1) The OAuth App's callback URL matches YOUR_DOMAIN/api/auth/github/handler/frame, (2) The app.baseUrl in app-config.yaml matches the domain in the callback URL, (3) No trailing slashes in either URL.

Explanation

redirect_uri mismatch = callback URL in GitHub OAuth App doesn't match Backstage's baseUrl + /api/auth/github/handler/frame. Fix: ensure app.baseUrl matches the domain in the callback, no trailing slashes. CBA: this is the most common auth misconfiguration.

Chapter 23: Permissions & RBAC

Permissions control what users can do in Backstage. The permission framework uses Allow/Deny rules with conditions to create fine-grained access control. This chapter covers the framework, policy configuration, RBAC roles, and testing.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1.5 hours🛡️ RBAC🎯 CBA 22%

23.1 The Backstage Permission Framework

Permission System
  ┌─────────────────────┐
  │   Permission Policy │ ← Define what actions exist & who can do them
  └────────┬────────────┘
           │
           ▼
  ┌─────────────┐   ┌─────────────┐
  │ Allow Rules │   │ Deny Rules  │
  │ "If owner,  │   │ "If not in  │
  │  allow del" │   │  group, deny"│
  └──────┬──────┘   └──────┬──────┘
         └────────┬────────┘
                  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │    Permission Evaluator      │
  │ Checks each request against  │
  │ the policy rules             │
  └──────────────────────────────┘

23.2 Configuring Permission Policies

Permission Policy Example

  // packages/backend/src/plugins/permission.ts
  export default createPermissionPolicy({
    allow: [
      { // Anyone can READ entities
        permission: catalogEntityReadPermission,
        resourceType: 'catalog-entity',
        action: 'read',
      },
      { // Only OWNERS can DELETE their entities
        permission: catalogEntityDeletePermission,
        resourceType: 'catalog-entity',
        action: 'delete',
        conditions: {
          rule: 'IS_ENTITY_OWNER',
          resourceType: 'catalog-entity',
        },
      },
    ],
  });

23.3 RBAC Configuration — Mapping Groups to Roles

In Backstage, RBAC is implemented by mapping Backstage Groups (teams) to permission policies. There are no built-in "roles" like admin/developer/viewer — instead, you create permission rules that check group membership.

RBAC — How Groups Map to Permissions
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    BACKSTAGE RBAC MODEL                       │
  │                                                              │
  │  Group: team-platform (admins)                               │
  │    │                                                         │
  │    └──▶ Allow: ALL permissions (create, read, update, delete)│
  │                                                              │
  │  Group: team-fe (developers)                                 │
  │    │                                                         │
  │    ├──▶ Allow: catalog.entity.read (all entities)            │
  │    ├──▶ Allow: catalog.entity.create (with IS_ENTITY_OWNER)  │
  │    └──▶ Deny:  catalog.entity.delete (can't delete anything) │
  │                                                              │
  │  Group: interns (viewers)                                    │
  │    │                                                         │
  │    └──▶ Allow: catalog.entity.read (all entities)            │
  │         (Everything else is implicitly DENIED)               │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  RULE OF THUMB:
  • Admin team → Allow ALL
  • Dev team → Allow read/create/update (with ownership checks)
  • Viewer team → Allow read only
  • Unauthenticated → Deny ALL (unless guest access enabled)

Common RBAC Patterns

PatternAllow RuleConditionWho Gets It
Admin AccessALL permissionsHAS_MEMBER: team-platformPlatform team
Owner-Only Deletecatalog.entity.deleteIS_ENTITY_OWNEREntity owners
Team-Scoped Accesscatalog.entity.readHAS_ANNOTATION: team=XYZSpecific team members
Read-Onlycatalog.entity.readNone (everyone)All authenticated users

23.4 Conditional Permissions — Fine-Grained Access Control

Conditions are the power behind Backstage's permission system. Without conditions, permissions are all-or-nothing. With conditions, you can say "allow delete IF you're the owner" or "allow read IF the entity has a specific annotation."

IS_ENTITY_OWNER

The most common condition. Checks if the current user matches the entity's spec.owner. Used for: "Owners can delete their own services."

hasAnnotation

Checks if an entity has a specific annotation and value. Used for: "Only show entities with visibility: public to external users."

hasLabel

Checks if an entity has a specific label. Used for: "Developers can only see entities labeled with their team name."

hasSpec

Checks fields within the entity's spec. Used for: "Only production services can be deployed; experimental services are blocked."

💡 Combining Conditions with AND/OR

You can combine multiple conditions: "Allow delete IF (owner AND lifecycle is experimental)" or "Allow read IF (hasAnnotation visibility=public OR hasLabel team=platform)". AND requires ALL conditions to match; OR requires ANY condition to match. This enables complex access policies without custom code.

23.5 Testing Permissions

Test permissions thoroughly before deploying to production. A misconfigured permission can either block legitimate users (false positive) or allow unauthorized access (false negative).

Test ApproachToolHow It WorksCBA Note
Permission EvaluatorPermissionEvaluator APIProgrammatically test if a user/group can perform an action. Returns ALLOW or DENY.Most reliable test method
Role-Based TestingDifferent test usersCreate test users in different groups (admin, dev, viewer). Test each one's access to protected resources.Simulates real-world scenarios
Backend Log Analysisenv.loggerCheck backend logs for permission denial reasons. Set log level to debug to see full permission evaluation trace.Debugging production issues
Negative TestingManual / AutomatedDeliberately try to access resources without permission. Verify the request is denied with proper error messaging.Always test deny rules!
// __tests__/permissions.test.ts — Permission Testing Example
import { PermissionEvaluator } from '@backstage/plugin-permission-common';
import { catalogEntityReadPermission } from '@backstage/plugin-catalog-common/alpha';

describe('Catalog Permissions', () => {
  let permissionEvaluator: PermissionEvaluator;

  beforeEach(() => {
    permissionEvaluator = createMockPermissionEvaluator();
  });

  it('allows admin user to read any entity', async () => {
    const result = await permissionEvaluator.authorize(
      [{ permission: catalogEntityReadPermission }],
      { credentials: { 'user:default/admin': [] } }
    );
    expect(result[0].result).toBe('ALLOW');
  });

  it('denies viewer from deleting entities', async () => {
    const result = await permissionEvaluator.authorize(
      [{ permission: catalogEntityDeletePermission }],
      { credentials: { 'user:default/viewer': [] } }
    );
    expect(result[0].result).toBe('DENY');
  });

  it('allows owner to update their own component', async () => {
    const result = await permissionEvaluator.authorize(
      [{ permission: catalogEntityUpdatePermission }],
      { credentials: { 'user:default/anihpj-owner': [] } }
    );
    expect(result[0].result).toBe('ALLOW');
  });
});
✅
Permission Evaluator

Backstage's built-in API for testing permissions programmatically. Returns ALLOW/DENY for any permission + user combination.

👥
User Simulation

Test as different users with different roles. Simulate: admin, developer, viewer, team-lead. Verify each role gets correct access.

📋
Deny-First Testing

Start with ALL denied, then add allows. This prevents accidental over-permission. Default-deny is the secure default.

⚠️ CBA Permission Testing Pattern

The CBA tests permission scenarios: "Admin Alice can delete entities, but Developer Bob cannot — how do you verify this?" Answer: Use PermissionEvaluator.authorize() with Alice's credentials (expect ALLOW) and Bob's credentials (expect DENY). Always test BOTH positive AND negative cases before deploying. A permission that's too restrictive breaks workflows; too permissive creates security holes.

📝 Chapter 23 — CBA Practice Questions

Q1
What's the difference between Allow and Deny rules in the permission framework?
Show Answer
Answer

Allow rules: Grant access when conditions are met. "If owner, allow delete."
Deny rules: Block access when conditions are met. "If not in group X, deny." Deny rules take precedence over Allow rules — if a Deny matches, access is blocked regardless of any Allow rules.

Explanation

Allow = grant, Deny = block. Deny ALWAYS wins over Allow. This follows security best practice: default deny, explicit allow. CBA: know that Deny > Allow and this precedence is by design for security.

Q2
What does the IS_ENTITY_OWNER condition do?
Show Answer
Answer

IS_ENTITY_OWNER checks if the current user is the owner of the entity being accessed. Used to restrict actions like delete, update, or unregister to only the entity's owner. Combined with Allow rules to grant owner-only permissions.

Explanation

IS_ENTITY_OWNER = most common permission condition. Checks if user matches entity's owner field. Used with Allow for owner-only access. CBA: know this condition name and its purpose.

Q3
Where is the permission policy file located?
Show Answer
Answer

packages/backend/src/plugins/permission.ts. This file defines Allow and Deny rules using createPermissionPolicy(). Any changes require restarting the Backstage backend to take effect.

Explanation

Permission policy file = packages/backend/src/plugins/permission.ts. Uses createPermissionPolicy(). Changes need backend restart. CBA: know the exact file path.

Q4
Do Deny rules or Allow rules take precedence?
Show Answer
Answer

Deny rules take precedence. If any Deny rule matches a request, access is blocked — even if an Allow rule also matches. This follows the security principle of "deny by default, allow explicitly." Always test Deny rules carefully — they can accidentally block legitimate access.

Explanation

Deny > Allow always. Single Deny match = access blocked. Security principle: deny by default, explicit allow. CBA: Deny always wins — frequently tested.

Q5
What built-in permission conditions are available?
Show Answer
Answer

IS_ENTITY_OWNER — user is the entity's owner
hasAnnotation — entity has a specific annotation
hasLabel — entity has a specific label
hasSpec — check entity spec fields
Conditions can be combined with AND/OR for complex access rules.

Explanation

4 built-in conditions: IS_ENTITY_OWNER, hasAnnotation, hasLabel, hasSpec. Composable with AND/OR. CBA: know all 4 and that they combine for complex rules.

Q6
How do you map Backstage Groups to RBAC roles?
Show Answer
Answer

Define roles in the permission policy with group-based conditions. Example: allow catalogEntityDeletePermission only for members of team-platform (admins). Use hasMember or group-based conditions to check the user's group membership against allowed groups.

Explanation

RBAC via group conditions. hasMember checks group membership. Allow delete for team-platform admins only. CBA: know how to map groups to permissions in the policy.

Q7
What's the difference between catalogEntityReadPermission and catalogEntityDeletePermission?
Show Answer
Answer

catalogEntityReadPermission controls who can VIEW entities. Usually granted to everyone.
catalogEntityDeletePermission controls who can DELETE entities. Usually restricted to owners or admins.
There are also create and update permissions for fine-grained control over entity lifecycle.

Explanation

CRUD permissions: Read (view, public), Create, Update, Delete (restricted). Read is usually open; Delete is restricted. CBA: know the 4 CRUD permission types.

Q8
How do you test that permissions are working correctly?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Log in as different users with different group memberships
2. Try actions that should be allowed and denied
3. Check backend logs for permission evaluation results
4. Use the permission evaluator API: POST /api/permission/authorize to test rules programmatically
Always test BOTH allow and deny paths.

Explanation

4 testing methods: multi-user login, manual action tests, backend logs, permission API. Test BOTH allow and deny. CBA: know POST /api/permission/authorize endpoint.

Q9
A user reports they can't delete their own entity despite being the owner. What's likely wrong?
Show Answer
Answer

The permission policy likely doesn't have an Allow rule for catalogEntityDeletePermission with IS_ENTITY_OWNER condition. Check: (1) Is the delete permission configured in the policy? (2) Is the IS_ENTITY_OWNER condition applied? (3) Is the user correctly identified as the entity's owner in the catalog?

Explanation

Common RBAC bug: missing Allow+IS_ENTITY_OWNER for Delete. 3 checks: permission exists, condition applied, user is owner. CBA: typical troubleshooting scenario for RBAC issues.

Q10
How would you restrict the Scaffolder (template creation) to only the platform-team group?
Show Answer
Answer

Add an Allow rule for scaffolderTemplateCreatePermission with a condition checking group membership: conditions: { rule: 'HAS_MEMBER', params: { group: 'team-platform' } }. This grants template creation access only to members of team-platform. All other users are implicitly denied.

Explanation

Scaffolder restriction = Allow + HAS_MEMBER + group. Only platform-team creates templates. Everyone else implicitly denied. CBA: know the HAS_MEMBER condition syntax and Scaffolder permission name.

# RBAC Permission Policy — Scaffolder Restriction
# packages/backend/src/plugins/permission.ts
import { createPermissionPolicy } from '@backstage/plugin-permission-backend';

export default createPermissionPolicy({
  allow: [
    {
      permission: 'scaffolder.template.create',
      conditions: {
        rule: 'HAS_MEMBER',
        params: { group: 'team-platform' }
      }
    }
  ]
  // All other users are IMPLICITLY DENIED
});

Chapter 24: Integrating External Identity Providers

Beyond authentication, you can sync users and groups from external identity sources like LDAP, Active Directory, Okta, and Azure AD. This keeps your Backstage org chart automatically in sync with your actual organization.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1 hour🆔 Identity🎯 CBA 22%

📋 Identity Sync Methods Comparison (CBA Key)

MethodSync TypeUpdate SpeedBest For
LDAP ModuleScheduled pull30-60 minBulk import from AD/LDAP directories
Okta/Azure Group ClaimsReal-time (on sign-in)Instant (next login)Real-time group membership sync
GitHub TeamsReal-time (on sign-in)Instant (next login)Dev teams using GitHub orgs
Custom ResolverOn sign-in (custom logic)Instant (next login)Non-standard identity mapping
📂
LDAP/AD Sync

Scheduled bulk import. Good for initial migration and periodic sync of existing directory users. Module: @backstage/plugin-catalog-backend-module-ldap.

🔑
Group Claims (OIDC)

Real-time group membership via auth token. User's groups update on every sign-in. No scheduled sync needed — always current.

24.1 LDAP / Active Directory Integration

LDAP Sync Architecture
  ┌─────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────┐
  │  LDAP / AD      │──pull──▶│  Backstage       │──store─▶│  PostgreSQL     │
  │  Directory      │ (30min) │  LDAP Module     │         │  (Users/Groups) │
  │                 │         │                  │         │                 │
  │  Users: 5000    │         │  @backstage/     │         │  kind: User     │
  │  Groups: 200    │         │  plugin-catalog- │         │  kind: Group    │
  │  OUs: 50        │         │  backend-module- │         │                 │
  │                 │         │  ldap            │         │                 │
  └─────────────────┘         └─────────────────┘         └─────────────────┘

  Config: app-config.yaml → catalog.providers.ldap
  Schedule: Configurable (default every 30-60 min)
  Filter: users.options.filter: "(objectClass=person)"
🔑 LDAP Sync Is Scheduled (Not Real-Time)

Changes in LDAP appear in Backstage after the next sync cycle. For real-time updates, use Okta/Azure AD group claims instead. LDAP is best for initial bulk import and periodic sync of existing directory users.

24.2 Okta / Azure AD Group Sync

Real-Time Group Sync via OIDC Claims
  ┌─────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────┐
  │  Okta / Azure AD│──login─▶│  Backstage      │
  │                 │         │                 │
  │  User signs in  │         │  Reads group    │
  │  → ID Token     │         │  claims from    │
  │  contains:      │         │  auth token     │
  │  groups: [      │         │  → Auto-updates │
  │   "platform",   │         │  Group entities │
  │   "engineering" │         │  → Instant sync │
  │  ]              │         │                 │
  └─────────────────┘         └─────────────────┘

  ADVANTAGE: Real-time! Changes reflect on next sign-in.
  No scheduled sync needed unlike LDAP.
🔑 Okta

Group claims included in OIDC token. Configure in app-config.yaml under auth.providers.okta. Backstage auto-creates Group entities from claims.

🔑 Azure AD

Group membership via Microsoft Graph API or OIDC claims. Supports nested groups. Configure under auth.providers.microsoft.

24.3 Custom Sign-In Resolvers

Sign-In Resolver — Mapping External Identity to Backstage User
  ┌─────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────┐
  │  Auth Provider  │──token─▶│  Sign-In        │──maps──▶│  Backstage      │
  │  (GitHub/Okta)  │         │  Resolver       │         │  User Entity    │
  │                 │         │                 │         │                 │
  │  Profile:       │         │  Input:         │         │  name: jane     │
  │  email, name,   │         │  provider       │         │  email: ...     │
  │  avatar, groups │         │  profile data   │         │  memberOf: [...]│
  └─────────────────┘         └─────────────────┘         └─────────────────┘

  Use Custom Resolver When:
  • Non-standard claims from identity provider
  • Need to transform usernames/emails
  • Multiple identity sources need merging
  • External API call needed during sign-in
💡 Built-in vs Custom

Built-in resolvers handle GitHub, Okta, Google, Azure AD out of the box. Build custom only when your identity mapping doesn't fit the standard patterns. Custom resolvers receive the full provider profile and return a Backstage User reference.

Part 8 Quick Wins for CBA: Auth = who you are (OAuth/OIDC). Permissions = what you can do (Allow/Deny rules). NEVER use guest access in production. GitHub is easiest for dev teams — auto-maps teams to Groups. Okta/Azure AD for enterprise SSO. Sign-in resolvers map provider identities to Backstage Users. Deny rules ALWAYS take precedence over Allow rules. IS_ENTITY_OWNER is the most common permission condition. LDAP syncs on schedule; Okta claims update on sign-in.

🔄Group SyncOkta/Azure AD group claims auto-sync on every sign-in.
