📝 Chapter 24 — CBA Practice Questions

Q1
How does Backstage sync users from LDAP?
Show Answer
Answer

Using the @backstage/plugin-catalog-backend-module-ldap module. Configure LDAP server URL, bind DN, and search filters in app-config.yaml. Users and Groups are ingested as Catalog entities on a configurable schedule.

Explanation

LDAP sync uses the ldap catalog module. Config: server URL, bind DN, search filters, schedule. Users/Groups become Catalog entities. CBA: know the module name and that LDAP is scheduled (not real-time).

Q2
What is a sign-in resolver?
Show Answer
Answer

A sign-in resolver maps the identity from an auth provider (GitHub, Okta, etc.) to a Backstage User entity. It takes the provider's profile data and determines which Backstage user this corresponds to. Custom resolvers are used when the built-in mapping doesn't fit your needs.

Explanation

Sign-in resolver = identity mapper (provider → Backstage User). Takes profile data, returns User entity. Custom when built-in doesn't fit. CBA: know the resolver's role in the auth flow.

Q3
How do group memberships stay in sync with Okta/Azure AD?
Show Answer
Answer

Group claims are included in the auth token from the provider. Backstage reads these claims on every sign-in and updates the user's Group memberships automatically. Changes in Okta/Azure AD are reflected the next time the user signs in.

Explanation

Okta/Azure sync via OIDC group claims in auth token. Updated on every sign-in (real-time). No scheduled sync needed. CBA: group claims = real-time; LDAP = scheduled. Know the difference.

Q4
What module is needed for LDAP integration?
Show Answer
Answer

@backstage/plugin-catalog-backend-module-ldap. Install it and configure the LDAP server URL, bind DN, bind credentials, and search filters in app-config.yaml. The module runs on a schedule to sync Users and Groups from LDAP into the Backstage Catalog.

Explanation

LDAP module = @backstage/plugin-catalog-backend-module-ldap. Config in app-config.yaml. Runs on schedule. CBA: know the exact npm package name for LDAP integration.

Q5
How often does Backstage sync users from LDAP?
Show Answer
Answer

The sync schedule is configurable in app-config.yaml. Default is typically every 30-60 minutes. You can configure the frequency, timeout, and initial delay. Changes in LDAP appear in Backstage after the next sync cycle — not instantly.

Explanation

LDAP sync schedule = configurable (default 30-60 min). Not real-time — changes appear after next sync. CBA: LDAP is scheduled pull, not real-time. This contrasts with Okta group claims.

Q6
What's the difference between LDAP sync and Okta group claims?
Show Answer
Answer

LDAP sync: Scheduled bulk import. Backstage pulls users/groups from LDAP on a timer. Changes take effect after the next sync cycle.
Okta group claims: Real-time. Group info is in the auth token received at sign-in. Changes take effect on the user's next sign-in (immediate for new sessions).

Explanation

LDAP = scheduled (30-60 min delay). Okta = real-time (next sign-in). LDAP pulls on timer; Okta pushes via token claims. CBA: know the fundamental timing difference between these two sync methods.

Q7
When would you build a custom sign-in resolver?
Show Answer
Answer

When built-in resolvers don't fit your needs: (1) Your identity provider uses non-standard claims, (2) You need to transform usernames/emails before mapping, (3) You have multiple identity sources that need custom merging logic, (4) You need to call external APIs to determine user attributes during sign-in.

Explanation

4 scenarios for custom resolver: non-standard claims, username transform, multi-source merging, external API enrichment. CBA: know when to build custom vs use built-in resolvers.

Q8
How do you configure the LDAP search filter for users?
Show Answer
Answer

In app-config.yaml under the LDAP provider config: users.options.filter: "(objectClass=person)". Customize to filter by department, group membership, or any LDAP attribute. Example: "(&(objectClass=person)(department=Engineering))" for only engineering users.

Explanation

LDAP filter in app-config.yaml. Default: (objectClass=person). Can filter by department, group, attributes. Uses LDAP filter syntax with & (AND), | (OR). CBA: know the config path and basic LDAP filter syntax.

Q9
What happens when a user is removed from LDAP but still exists in Backstage?
Show Answer
Answer

The user entity remains in the Backstage Catalog but is marked as orphaned. On the next LDAP sync, Backstage can be configured to either: (1) Remove the user (clean sync), or (2) Keep the user but flag them (preserve history). Choose based on your compliance requirements.

Explanation

Orphaned users = removed from LDAP, still in Backstage. Options: clean sync (remove) or preserve (flag). Choose based on compliance. CBA: know both options and that this is a config decision.

Q10
You need to sync users from both LDAP and Okta into backstage. How would you architect this?
Show Answer
Answer

Configure BOTH: (1) LDAP catalog module for bulk sync of existing users/groups, (2) Okta as an auth provider for sign-in with group claims. LDAP handles initial import and periodic sync; Okta handles real-time auth and group updates. Use custom sign-in resolvers to merge identities from both sources into the same Backstage User entity.

Explanation

Dual identity: LDAP for bulk import + Okta for real-time auth. Custom resolver merges both sources. LDAP = initial + periodic; Okta = real-time sign-in. CBA: know how to architect multi-source identity integration.

🏭 Part 9: Production & CI/CD 🔴 Advanced

Chapter 25: CI/CD Integration with Backstage

Backstage brings CI/CD visibility into one place — build status, deploy history, and pipeline results appear directly on entity pages. This chapter covers integrating GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI, and ArgoCD so developers see CI/CD status without leaving Backstage.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1.5 hours🔄 CI/CD🎯 CBA 22%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Integrate GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI, and ArgoCD with Backstage
  • ✅ Understand the proxy pattern for secure CI/CD API access
  • ✅ Configure CI/CD annotations to link entities to pipelines
  • ✅ Build a unified CI/CD dashboard combining multiple tools on one entity page

🎯 CBA Exam Relevance — Backstage Infrastructure 22%

CI/CD integration demonstrates Backstage's plugin flexibility. The CBA tests which plugins and annotations connect to which CI/CD tools. Key mappings: GitHub Actions → github.com/project-slug, Jenkins → jenkins.io/job-full-name, ArgoCD → argocd/app-name. The proxy configuration pattern (proxy.endpoints in app-config.yaml) is also tested.

🎯 CBA Exam Tip — Proxy Pattern

The Backstage proxy is a CRITICAL exam topic. It routes frontend API calls through the Backstage backend, keeping auth tokens server-side (never exposed to browsers). Configuration format: proxy.endpoints['/jenkins']: { target: 'https://jenkins.example.com', headers: { Authorization: 'Bearer ${JENKINS_TOKEN}' } }. The frontend calls /api/proxy/jenkins/... and Backstage forwards to Jenkins with the token.

    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │              BACKSTAGE PROXY — Secure CI/CD Access                │
    │                                                                  │
    │  Browser (Frontend)          Backstage Backend        CI/CD Tool │
    │  ┌──────────────┐           ┌──────────────┐       ┌──────────┐ │
    │  │ Plugin calls  │──HTTP──▶  │ Proxy routes  │──API─▶│ Jenkins  │ │
    │  │ /api/proxy/   │           │ with token    │       │ GitHub   │ │
    │  │ jenkins/...   │◀─JSON──   │ (server-side) │◀─data─│ ArgoCD   │ │
    │  └──────────────┘           └──────────────┘       └──────────┘ │
    │                                                                  │
    │  🔒 Token NEVER reaches browser — Proxy injects it server-side   │
    │  🔒 Browser only sees Backstage domain — no CORS issues          │
    │  🔒 Centralized auth — one proxy config for all CI/CD tools      │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🐙
GitHub Actions

Annotation: github.com/project-slug. Workflow runs, logs, status.

🔧
Jenkins

Annotation: jenkins.io/job-full-name. Build history, trigger jobs.

🦊

🚀

Entity pages show CI/CD status cards with: build status (passing/failing/running), recent builds, success rate, duration, and deep links to the CI/CD tool. Plugins fetch this data from your CI/CD system's API and render it on the entity page.

💡 Why CI/CD in Backstage?

Developers spend 30% less time context-switching when CI/CD status is embedded in the service catalog. Instead of opening Jenkins → GitHub → ArgoCD in 3 tabs, they see everything on one entity page. This is Backstage's "single pane of glass" value proposition.

25.2 GitHub Actions Integration

25.2a Workflow Configuration

Install @backstage/plugin-github-actions in both packages/app and packages/backend. Add the github.com/project-slug annotation to entity YAML. Backstage auto-discovers workflow runs and displays status, logs, and duration on the entity's CI/CD card.

spec:
  type: service

  owner: anihpj-team
  system: recruitment-platform

25.2b Viewing Runs in Backstage

The GitHub Actions tab on the entity page shows: recent workflow runs, status (✅ pass / ❌ fail / 🔄 running), trigger type (push / PR / schedule), duration, and links to detailed logs on GitHub. Developers see build status at a glance without opening GitHub.

GitHub Actions — Data Flow

  │  project-slug:   │  │  │ ✅ main  (3m) │  │

  └──────────────────┘  │  │ 🔄 dev   (1m) │  │

🔑
Token Scopes Required

GitHub personal access token needs repo scope (private repos) or public_repo (public). For workflow runs specifically: actions:read. Set as GITHUB_TOKEN env var referenced in app-config.yaml.

⚠️
Common Pitfall

Plugin installed but no runs showing? Check: (1) github.com/project-slug format is owner/repo (NOT full URL), (2) GITHUB_TOKEN has correct scopes, (3) plugin registered in BOTH frontend and backend.

25.3 Jenkins Integration

Install @backstage/plugin-jenkins and @backstage/plugin-jenkins-backend. Configure the Jenkins proxy endpoint in app-config.yaml. Add jenkins.io/job-full-name annotation to entity YAML. The plugin shows build history, allows triggering jobs, and displays test results — all on the entity page.

# app-config.yaml — Jenkins proxy configuration
proxy:
  endpoints:
    '/jenkins':
      target: 'https://jenkins.anihpj.com'
      headers:
        # 🔒 Token injected server-side — NEVER reaches the browser
        Authorization: 'Bearer ${JENKINS_TOKEN}'
      # Optional: change origin header for CORS compatibility
      changeOrigin: true

# catalog-info.yaml — Entity linked to Jenkins job
# metadata:
#   annotations:
#     jenkins.io/job-full-name: anihpj/jobpost-build  # ← Job path in Jenkins
Jenkins Integration — How It Works
  Entity Page (Frontend)           Backstage Backend            Jenkins Server
  ┌─────────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐
  │ CI/CD Tab            │    │ Proxy Layer             │    │              │
  │ ┌─────────────────┐  │    │ /jenkins ──────────────▶│    │ 🔧 Jenkins   │
  │ │ 🟢 Build #42   │  │    │   target: jenkins URL   │    │   /job/      │
  │ │ 🟢 Build #41   │  │    │   + JENKINS_TOKEN      │    │   anihpj/    │
  │ │ 🔴 Build #40   │  │    │                         │    │   jobpost-   │
  │ │ [Trigger Build]│──┼───▶│ POST /jenkins/job/.../  │───▶│   build/     │
  │ └─────────────────┘  │    │   build                 │    │              │
  └─────────────────────┘    └─────────────────────────┘    └──────────────┘
     ▲ No token in browser      ▲ Token injected here         ▲ Jenkins API
📋
Build History

Displays last N builds with status, duration, timestamp. Each row links to the full Jenkins build page.

▶️
Trigger Jobs

"Run Build" button on the entity page triggers a Jenkins job via the proxy. No need to open Jenkins.

🧪
Test Results

Shows pass/fail counts, test duration trend, and links to individual test reports from Jenkins.

⚠️ Jenkins Proxy Security

The JENKINS_TOKEN must be a Jenkins API token (NOT your password). Create it at Jenkins → User → Configure → API Token. The token is stored as an environment variable and injected into headers by Backstage. It never leaves the server — the frontend only sees /api/proxy/jenkins/....

25.4 GitLab CI Integration

Install @backstage/plugin-gitlab. This plugin displays pipeline status, job logs, and merge request overview from GitLab CI/CD on the entity page. Add the gitlab.com/project-id annotation to link entities to their GitLab projects.

# catalog-info.yaml — Entity with GitLab CI annotation
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: jobpost
  annotations:
    # 🔑 GitLab project ID (numeric or namespace/project path)
    gitlab.com/project-id: '12345678'
    # Alternative: gitlab.com/project-slug: anihpj/jobpost
    gitlab.com/merge-request: 'true'  # Enable MR overview
spec:
  type: service
  lifecycle: production
  owner: anihpj-team
FeatureWhat It ShowsCBA Relevance
Pipeline Status✅ passed / ❌ failed / 🔄 running / ⏸️ pending for the latest pipeline on each branchKnow the annotation gitlab.com/project-id
Job LogsIndividual job output within a pipeline. Helps debug which step failed.Understand that logs are fetched via proxy
Merge Request OverviewOpen MRs with pipeline status per MR. Shows whether an MR is ready to merge.Know that gitlab.com/merge-request enables this
Kubernetes IntegrationIf using GitLab K8s agent, shows deployment status alongside pipeline status.Bonus: combines CI + CD in one view
📖 GitLab CI vs GitHub Actions in Backstage

Both show CI/CD status, but GitLab's plugin also shows merge request pipelines — a unique feature for GitLab Flow users. GitHub Actions focuses on workflow runs per branch. Both use the same proxy pattern (/api/proxy/gitlab/... or /api/proxy/github-actions/...) with server-side tokens.

25.5 ArgoCD / Flux (GitOps CD)

The ArgoCD plugin shows application sync status, deployment history, and health directly on the entity page. Flux integration provides similar GitOps visibility. Both answer the critical question: "Does the live state match the desired state in Git?"

GitOps CD Visibility — ArgoCD + Flux Flow

# catalog-info.yaml — Entity linked to ArgoCD application
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: jobpost
  annotations:
    # 🔑 Links entity to ArgoCD application by name
    argocd/app-name: jobpost
    # The ArgoCD plugin searches for an Application named "jobpost"
spec:
  type: service
  lifecycle: production
  owner: anihpj-team

---
# app-config.yaml — ArgoCD plugin configuration
argocd:
  # ArgoCD API server URL
  baseUrl: https://argocd.anihpj.com
  # Auth token for API access (server-side)
  token: ${ARGOCD_AUTH_TOKEN}
  # Optional: refresh interval for sync status polling
  refreshInterval: 60s
🔄
ArgoCD Plugin

Annotation: argocd/app-name. Shows sync status (🟢 Synced / 🟡 OutOfSync), health (🏥 Healthy / 🟡 Degraded), deployment history timeline, and revision info. Also provides a "Sync" button to trigger sync from Backstage.

⚡
Flux Plugin

Annotation: fluxcd.io/namespace + fluxcd.io/name. Shows Kustomization/HelmRelease status, reconciliation state, and dependents. Flux-native GitOps visibility in Backstage.

💡 ArgoCD vs Flux — Which to Use?

Both are excellent GitOps tools. ArgoCD has a rich UI and is more popular in the Backstage ecosystem (better plugin support). Flux is lighter-weight and integrates deeply with Helm. The CBA exam focuses on ArgoCD integration, but knowing Flux exists at a high level is sufficient. Both follow the same pattern: annotation → plugin → entity page card.

Build Visibility

Deploy Visibility

☸️
Runtime Visibility

📖 The "Single Pane of Glass" Pattern

This is Backstage's killer feature. Instead of:
🔗 github.com/anihpj/jobpost/actions → argocd.anihpj.com/applications/jobpost → grafana.anihpj.com/d/jobpost → k9s → jobpost pods
Developers open ONE page (backstage.anihpj.com/catalog/default/component/jobpost) and see everything. The CBA exam emphasizes this "single pane of glass" value proposition repeatedly.

⚡ SPEED TIP — CI/CD Annotations: Memorize the plugin-to-annotation mappings: GitHub Actions → github.com/project-slug, Jenkins → jenkins.io/job-full-name, ArgoCD → argocd/app-name, GitLab CI → gitlab.com/project-id. All CI/CD plugins use the proxy pattern — frontend calls /api/proxy/..., backend forwards with auth token. The token NEVER reaches the browser.

📝 Chapter 25 — CBA Practice Questions

Q1
What annotation links an entity to GitHub Actions?
Show Answer
Answer

github.com/project-slug: owner/repo. The GitHub Actions plugin uses this to find workflow runs for the entity's repository.

Explanation

GH Actions annotation = github.com/project-slug with owner/repo format. Without this, the plugin can't find workflow runs. CBA: know the annotation name and format (owner/repo).

Q2
How does Backstage display Jenkins build status?
Show Answer
Answer

Via the Jenkins plugin using jenkins.io/job-full-name annotation. The plugin calls the Jenkins API through the Backstage proxy and displays build history, status, and allows triggering builds.

Explanation

Jenkins annotation = jenkins.io/job-full-name. Uses Backstage proxy pattern (token never in browser). Shows build history, status, trigger button. CBA: know annotation and proxy pattern.

Q3
What CI/CD tools can Backstage integrate with?
Show Answer
Answer

GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI, ArgoCD, CircleCI, and more. Each has its own plugin and annotation. All display build/deploy status on entity pages.

Explanation

Backstage integrates with all major CI/CD tools: GH Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI, ArgoCD, CircleCI. Each has its own plugin + annotation. CBA: know the plugin-annotation mapping for each tool.

Q4
How do you configure the Jenkins proxy endpoint in Backstage?
Show Answer
Answer

In app-config.yaml under proxy.endpoints: '/jenkins': { target: 'https://jenkins.anihpj.com', headers: { Authorization: 'Bearer ${JENKINS_TOKEN}' } }. This routes frontend requests through Backstage to Jenkins securely.

Explanation

Jenkins proxy config = proxy.endpoints in app-config.yaml. target URL + Authorization header with token. Frontend calls /api/proxy/jenkins/..., backend forwards with auth. CBA: know proxy config structure and ${ENV_VAR} token pattern.

# Backstage Proxy — Secure CI/CD Access
# app-config.yaml
proxy:
  endpoints:
    '/jenkins':
      target: https://jenkins.anihpj.com
      headers:
        Authorization: Bearer ${JENKINS_TOKEN}  # ← Token stays server-side
    '/github-actions':
      target: https://api.github.com
      headers:
        Authorization: Bearer ${GITHUB_TOKEN}
# Frontend call: /api/proxy/jenkins/job/anihpj/build
# Backend forwards: https://jenkins.anihpj.com/job/anihpj/build
Q5
What does the ArgoCD plugin show on entity pages?
Show Answer
Answer

Application sync status (synced/out-of-sync), health status (healthy/degraded), deployment history, and sync duration. Configure with argocd/app-name annotation and ArgoCD API URL in app-config.yaml.

Explanation

ArgoCD plugin shows 4 metrics: sync status, health, history, duration. Config: API URL + annotation. CBA: know all 4 displayed data points and the config requirements.

Q6
How would you set up CI/CD visibility for the anihpj/jobpost service?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Add github.com/project-slug: anihpj/jobpost for GitHub Actions status
2. Add argocd/app-name: jobpost for deployment status
3. Install both plugins (frontend + backend)
4. Configure ArgoCD API URL in app-config.yaml
Result: Build status AND deploy status visible on jobpost entity page.

Explanation

Multi-tool CI/CD: GH Actions for build + ArgoCD for deploy. Two annotations, two plugins, one entity page. CBA: know how to combine multiple CI/CD tools on one entity.

Q7
What's the difference between the GitHub integration plugin and the GitHub Actions plugin?
Show Answer
Answer

GitHub integration: Shows repo metadata — README, contributors, languages. Configured in integrations.github.
GitHub Actions: Shows CI/CD workflow runs — build status, logs, duration. Part of the same plugin family but focuses on CI/CD specifically.

Explanation

GitHub integration = repo info (README, contributors). GitHub Actions = CI/CD (builds, logs). Different purposes, same plugin family. CBA: know the distinction between integration and CI/CD plugins.

Q8
How does Backstage proxy CI/CD API calls securely?
Show Answer
Answer

Through the Backstage proxy — the frontend calls /api/proxy/jenkins/..., and the Backstage backend forwards the request to Jenkins with the configured auth token. The token never reaches the browser. Configured in app-config.yaml under proxy.endpoints.

Explanation

Proxy pattern: frontend → /api/proxy/... → backend → CI/CD tool. Token server-side only — never in browser. Configured in proxy.endpoints. CBA: this is a critical security pattern for all CI/CD integrations.

Q9
Your GitHub Actions plugin shows no workflow runs. What 3 things do you check?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Annotation: Is github.com/project-slug correct? (must be owner/repo format)
2. Token: Is ${GITHUB_TOKEN} set with repo and workflow scopes?
3. Plugin installed: Is @backstage/plugin-github-actions in both packages/app and packages/backend?

Explanation

3 checks: annotation (correct format), token (correct scopes), plugin (installed in both app and backend). CBA: typical troubleshooting scenario — check annotation first, then token, then plugin.

Q10
How would you add a custom CI/CD card showing data from a tool that has no Backstage plugin?
Show Answer
Answer

Build a custom plugin: (1) Create a frontend plugin with createPlugin() and createComponentExtension(), (2) Create a backend plugin that calls your tool's API, (3) Register both in App.tsx/Root.tsx and backend/index.ts, (4) Use the proxy to route API calls securely. The custom card renders on entity pages alongside built-in CI/CD cards.

Explanation

Custom CI/CD plugin: frontend + backend + proxy. createPlugin() + createComponentExtension() for the UI. Backend plugin for API access. Proxy for secure routing. CBA: know the full pattern for custom CI/CD integration.

Chapter 26: Production Operations

Running Backstage in production requires proper planning — PostgreSQL, TechDocs storage, search engine, upgrades, and monitoring. This chapter covers the essential production checklist and operational procedures.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1.5 hours🏭 Ops🎯 CBA 22%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Complete the 10-point production readiness checklist
  • ✅ Set up PostgreSQL with backups, pooling, and monitoring
  • ✅ Configure cloud storage for TechDocs and external doc building
  • ✅ Deploy Elasticsearch for production-grade search
  • ✅ Execute safe Backstage version upgrades with rollback plans

🎯 CBA Exam Relevance — Backstage Infrastructure 22%

Production operations is tested at a practical level. The CBA expects you to know the production checklist, why PostgreSQL is required (not SQLite), why TechDocs needs cloud storage in multi-pod setups, and the upgrade process. Scenario: "You're deploying Backstage with 3 replicas — what database, storage, and search engine do you choose?"

🎯 CBA Exam Tip — Production "Must-Haves"

The CBA frequently tests production readiness: (1) PostgreSQL — SQLite corrupts data with multiple writers, (2) Cloud storage for TechDocs — local storage means each pod has different docs, (3) Elasticsearch — SQLite-based search doesn't scale, (4) Auth configured — no guest access in production, (5) 3+ replicas — for high availability. These 5 items appear in some form on nearly every exam.

🗄️
PostgreSQL

Required for production. Never SQLite. Managed (RDS) or StatefulSet.

☁️
Cloud Storage

S3/GCS/Azure for TechDocs. All pods share same docs. External builder.

🔍
Elasticsearch

Production search engine. Clustered, fast full-text. Not SQLite search.

📊
Monitoring

Prometheus /metrics endpoint + Grafana dashboards. P95 latency alerts.

📋 Production Upgrade Checklist (CBA Pattern)

StepActionRisk Level
1Read changelog & migration guide🟢 Low
2Backup PostgreSQL database🔴 Critical
3Update package.json versions🟡 Medium
4Run yarn backstage-cli migrate🔴 Critical
5Test in staging environment🟡 Medium
6Deploy with Helm upgrade🟡 Medium
7Monitor logs and metrics for 24hrs🟢 Low

26.1 Production Checklist — The Complete 10-Point Readiness Assessment

Before deploying Backstage to production, EVERY item on this checklist must be verified. The CBA exam tests this checklist heavily — expect scenario questions like "A team deployed Backstage with SQLite and 3 replicas. What will happen?"

☑ 1. PostgreSQL (not SQLite)

SQLite corrupts with concurrent writes. PostgreSQL via managed service (RDS/Cloud SQL) or K8s StatefulSet.

☑ 2. HTTPS/TLS Enabled

All traffic encrypted. Use cert-manager + Let's Encrypt or enterprise CA. No plain HTTP in production.

☑ 3. Auth Configured

At least one provider (GitHub/Okta/Azure AD). Guest access disabled. auth.environment: production.

☑ 4. Cloud Storage for TechDocs

GCS, S3, or Azure Blob. NOT local publisher. All pods share same docs. External builder in CI/CD.

☑ 5. Elasticsearch

Not SQLite search. Elasticsearch cluster for fast full-text search across all entities and TechDocs.

☑ 6. Monitoring (Prometheus + Grafana)

Scrape /metrics. Dashboards for request rate, errors, latency. Alerts for downtime and error spikes.

☑ 7. Centralized Logging

Ship logs to Loki/ELK/Splunk. Include request IDs for tracing. Log level: info (not debug).

☑ 8. Automated Backups

PostgreSQL daily backups with point-in-time recovery. Test restore procedure monthly.

☑ 9. 3+ Replicas (HA)

Minimum 3 replicas across multiple AZs/nodes. Pod anti-affinity for resilience.

☑ 10. CI/CD for Backstage Itself

GitOps deployment via ArgoCD/Flux. Automated testing before deploy. Rollback capability.

⚠️ CBA Exam Trap — The "SQLite in Production" Question

This is the MOST tested production concept. SQLite supports only ONE concurrent writer. With 3 Backstage replicas, concurrent writes WILL corrupt data. The CBA WILL ask: "Can you use SQLite with 3 replicas?" Answer: NO. Always PostgreSQL.

26.2 PostgreSQL Setup — Production Database Configuration

PostgreSQL is the only supported production database for Backstage. SQLite works for local development but fails catastrophically with multiple concurrent writers. Here's the complete production setup:

PostgreSQL Deployment Options — Decision Flow
                        ┌─────────────────────────────┐
                        │  "I need PostgreSQL for     │
                        │   Backstage production"     │
                        └─────────────┬───────────────┘
                                      │
                    ┌─────────────────┴─────────────────┐
                    ▼                                   ▼
        ┌───────────────────────┐         ┌───────────────────────┐
        │  OPTION A: MANAGED    │         │  OPTION B: STATEFULSET│
        │  (⭐⭐⭐ Recommended)  │         │  (⭐⭐ Self-Managed)   │
        │                       │         │                       │
        │  AWS RDS PostgreSQL   │         │  K8s StatefulSet      │
        │  Google Cloud SQL     │         │  + PersistentVolume    │
        │  Azure PostgreSQL     │         │  + PgBouncer sidecar   │
        │                       │         │                       │
        │  ✅ Auto backups      │         │  ✅ Full control       │
        │  ✅ Point-in-time     │         │  ✅ No vendor lock-in  │
        │     recovery          │         │  ❌ Ops overhead       │
        │  ✅ Built-in pooling  │         │  ❌ You manage backups │
        │  ✅ Monitoring        │         │  ❌ You handle failover│
        │  ✅ Minimal ops       │         │                       │
        └───────────────────────┘         └───────────────────────┘

Option A: Managed Service (Recommended)

Use AWS RDS, Google Cloud SQL, or Azure Database for PostgreSQL. Benefits: automated backups, point-in-time recovery, connection pooling, monitoring, and zero maintenance.

ProviderService NameConnection PoolingCBA Note
AWSRDS for PostgreSQL / AuroraRDS Proxy (built-in option)Most commonly referenced on exam
Google CloudCloud SQL for PostgreSQLCloud SQL Auth ProxyAlternative; know it exists
AzureAzure Database for PostgreSQLPgBouncer (built-in)Flexible Server includes pooling

Option B: Kubernetes StatefulSet

Run PostgreSQL in-cluster with a StatefulSet and PersistentVolumeClaim. More ops overhead but full control over version, extensions, and configuration.

# postgres-statefulset.yaml — In-cluster PostgreSQL for Backstage
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: backstage-postgres-secret
  namespace: backstage
stringData:
  POSTGRES_USER: backstage
  POSTGRES_PASSWORD: changeme123!  # Use Sealed Secrets or Vault!
  POSTGRES_DB: backstage
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: postgres-data
  namespace: backstage
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 20Gi  # Size based on catalog size + template history
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: postgres
  namespace: backstage
spec:
  serviceName: postgres
  replicas: 1  # Single master (use Patroni/Stolon for HA)
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: postgres
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: postgres:16-alpine
          ports:
            - containerPort: 5432
          envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: backstage-postgres-secret
          volumeMounts:
            - name: postgres-data
              mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 500m
              memory: 512Mi
            limits:
              cpu: "2"
              memory: 2Gi
      volumes:
        - name: postgres-data
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: postgres-data
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: postgres
  namespace: backstage
spec:
  selector:
    app: postgres
  ports:
    - port: 5432
  clusterIP: None  # Headless service for StatefulSet
# app-config.yaml — Backstage database configuration
backend:
  database:
    client: pg
    connection:
      host: ${POSTGRES_HOST}           # postgres.backstage.svc.cluster.local
      port: ${POSTGRES_PORT}           # 5432
      user: ${POSTGRES_USER}           # backstage
      password: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}   # From K8s Secret
      database: ${POSTGRES_DB}         # backstage
      # 🔑 Connection pool size — tune based on replicas + plugins
      # Too high = exhaust DB connections. Too low = slow response.
      pool:
        min: 2       # Minimum idle connections
        max: 10      # Maximum connections per Backstage instance
      ssl:
        rejectUnauthorized: true  # Always use SSL in production

🔑 Connection Pooling — Critical for Production

Backstage opens many database connections — one per plugin that accesses the database. Without connection pooling (PgBouncer or built-in), you can easily exhaust PostgreSQL's connection limit (default: 100). Managed services include pooling; for self-hosted PostgreSQL, deploy PgBouncer as a sidecar.

Connection Pooling — PgBouncer Sidecar Pattern
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │                 Backstage Pod (1 of 3)                      │
    │                                                            │
    │  ┌──────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────────────┐   │
    │  │  Backstage       │      │  PgBouncer (Sidecar)     │   │
    │  │  Backend         │      │                          │   │
    │  │                  │      │  20 Backstage ──────┐    │   │
    │  │  Catalog Plugin  │──DB──▶  connections         │    │   │
    │  │  Scaffolder      │──DB──▶  multiplexed into    │    │   │
    │  │  Search Plugin   │──DB──▶  5 PostgreSQL ───────┼────┼──▶ PostgreSQL
    │  │  Auth Plugin     │──DB──▶  connections         │    │   │   (max 100
    │  │  User Settings   │──DB──▶                      │    │   │    connections)
    │  │                  │      │  localhost:5432      │    │   │
    │  └──────────────────┘      └──────────────────────┘   │   │
    │                                                            │
    │  WITHOUT PgBouncer: 3 pods × 20 conns each = 60 conns    │
    │  WITH PgBouncer:    3 pods × 5 conns each  = 15 conns    │
    │  💡 75% reduction in database connections!                 │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔌
Why Pooling Matters

Each Backstage plugin opens its own DB connection. 10 plugins × 3 replicas = 30+ connections. PostgreSQL defaults to 100 max — you'll hit the limit fast without pooling.

📦
PgBouncer

Lightweight connection pooler. Deploy as a sidecar in the Backstage pod. Configure Backstage to connect to localhost:5432 (PgBouncer) instead of the PostgreSQL Service.

☁️
Managed Pooling

AWS RDS Proxy, Cloud SQL Auth Proxy, Azure PgBouncer — all handle pooling automatically. No sidecar needed. Recommended for production simplicity.

📋 Automated Backups — Non-Negotiable

💾
Managed Backups

RDS/Cloud SQL/Azure: enable automated daily backups with 7-35 day retention. Enable point-in-time recovery (PITR). Test restore monthly — a backup you haven't tested isn't a backup.

🛠️
Self-Managed Backups

Use pg_dump as a CronJob, ship to S3/GCS. For PITR, configure WAL archiving. Kubernetes CronJob example:

# K8s CronJob: daily PostgreSQL backup to S3
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: postgres-backup
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"  # 2 AM daily
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
            - name: backup
              image: postgres:16-alpine
              command: ["pg_dump", "-h", "postgres",
                        "-U", "backstage", "-Fc",
                        "backstage"]
              env:
                - name: PGPASSWORD
                  valueFrom:
                    secretKeyRef:
                      name: backstage-postgres-secret
                      key: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
🚨 CBA Exam Trap — "SQLite in Production"

This is the MOST tested production concept on the CBA. SQLite supports only ONE concurrent writer. With 3 Backstage replicas, concurrent writes WILL corrupt data. The exam WILL ask: "Can you use SQLite with multiple replicas?" Answer: NO. Always PostgreSQL in production.

26.3 TechDocs in Production — Cloud Storage Architecture

In production with multiple replicas, TechDocs MUST use cloud storage. Here's why and how:

TechDocs Production Architecture
  CI/CD PIPELINE                     CLOUD STORAGE              BACKSTAGE PODS
  ┌──────────────┐                 ┌──────────────┐           ┌──────────────┐
  │ GitHub Push  │                 │  GCS / S3 /  │◀──────────│  Pod 1       │
  │ (docs/*.md)  │──build──▶      │  Azure Blob  │◀──────────│  Pod 2       │
  │              │                 │              │◀──────────│  Pod 3       │
  │ mkdocs build │                 │ techdocs/    │           │              │
  │ → HTML       │──upload──▶     │  anihpj/     │           │ All pods read│
  │              │                 │  jobpost/    │           │ same bucket  │
  └──────────────┘                 └──────────────┘           └──────────────┘

  KEY CONFIG: builder: external | publisher: googleGcs/awsS3/azureBlobStorage

Why not local publisher? Each pod has its own filesystem. Pod A builds docs → only Pod A has them. Requests to Pod B or Pod C = no docs. Cloud storage = single shared source, all pods serve the same content.

26.4 Search in Production — Elasticsearch Deep Dive

Backstage's default search uses SQLite, which works for single-pod dev but FAILS at scale. For production, you have two options:

OptionSetup ComplexityPerformanceBest For
ElasticsearchMedium (separate cluster)Excellent — clustered, full-textLarge catalogs (1000+ entities), high traffic
PostgreSQL SearchLow (same DB)Good — single node, basic textSmall-medium catalogs (<500 entities)

Configure in app-config.yaml under search.elasticsearch with node URLs, auth credentials, and index settings. Elasticsearch requires a separate cluster deployment.

26.5 Backstage Upgrades — Safe Upgrade Process

Upgrading Backstage versions is a multi-step process that MUST be followed in order. Skipping steps can corrupt your database or break plugins.

1
Read Changelog

Review the changelog and migration guide for breaking changes, deprecated APIs, and new required config.

2
Backup PostgreSQL

pg_dump backstage > backup_$(date +%Y%m%d).sql — ALWAYS backup before any upgrade.

3
Update Versions

Update package.json with new Backstage versions. Run yarn install.

4
Run Migrations

yarn backstage-cli migrate — applies DB schema changes. NEVER skip this step.

5
Test in Staging

Deploy to staging. Test all plugins, templates, and auth flows. Fix issues BEFORE production.

6
Deploy & Monitor

helm upgrade backstage backstage/backstage -n backstage. Monitor logs/metrics for 24 hours.

🔴 If Upgrade Fails — Rollback Procedure

1. helm rollback backstage (revert K8s deployment). 2. Restore PostgreSQL from backup (if migrations corrupted data). 3. Check logs for the specific error. 4. Fix the issue in staging. 5. Retry. NEVER upgrade production without a tested rollback plan.

⚡ SPEED TIP — Production Non-Negotiables: The CBA's 5 production "must-haves": (1) PostgreSQL (SQLite corrupts with multiple writers), (2) Cloud storage for TechDocs (local storage = inconsistent across pods), (3) Elasticsearch (SQLite search doesn't scale), (4) Auth configured (no guest access!), (5) 3+ replicas (HA). These 5 items separate dev from production — expect them on the exam.

📝 Chapter 26 — CBA Practice Questions

Q1
Why must you use PostgreSQL (not SQLite) in production?
Show Answer
Answer

SQLite can't handle concurrent writes — with 3+ Backstage replicas, you'd get data corruption. PostgreSQL supports concurrent connections and is the only supported production database for Backstage.

Explanation

SQLite = single writer lock. 3 replicas = concurrent writes = corruption. PostgreSQL = MVCC concurrent access. This is the #1 production requirement. CBA: never SQLite in production — guaranteed exam question.

# Production Database Config (app-config.yaml)
backend:
  database:
    client: pg                          # ← PostgreSQL (NOT sqlite3!)
    connection:
      host: ${POSTGRES_HOST}            # ← RDS/Cloud SQL endpoint
      port: 5432
      user: ${POSTGRES_USER}
      password: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}    # ← NEVER hardcode!
Q2
What should the TechDocs builder be set to in production?
Show Answer
Answer

builder: external — docs are pre-built by CI/CD and published to cloud storage. Backstage only serves them. This keeps pods stateless and fast.

Explanation

External builder = CI/CD builds docs, Backstage serves. Keeps pods stateless. Alternative: local builder (dev only, pod-local filesystem). CBA: builder: external is the production setting.

Q3
What's the upgrade process for Backstage?
Show Answer
Answer

Read changelog → Update versions → Run yarn backstage-cli migrate → Test in staging → Deploy with Helm upgrade → Backup PostgreSQL before major upgrades.

Explanation

5-step upgrade: changelog → migrate → test → deploy → backup. migrate handles DB schema changes. Always backup before major upgrades. CBA: know the upgrade steps in order.

# Backstage Upgrade Flow (with commands)
# Step 1: Backup PostgreSQL
pg_dump backstage > backstage_backup_$(date +%Y%m%d).sql

# Step 2: Update versions in package.json
# Step 3: Run database migrations
yarn backstage-cli migrate

# Step 4: Test in staging (same commands)
# Step 5: Deploy to production
helm upgrade backstage backstage/backstage -n backstage

# If rollback needed:
helm rollback backstage -n backstage
Q4
What 5 items are on the production checklist for Backstage?
Show Answer
Answer

1. PostgreSQL (not SQLite)
2. HTTPS/TLS enabled
3. Auth configured (no guest access)
4. Cloud storage for TechDocs
5. Monitoring (Prometheus + Grafana)
Plus: search engine, logging, backups, 3+ replicas, CI/CD pipeline.

Explanation

5 production must-haves: PostgreSQL, HTTPS, Auth, Cloud storage, Monitoring. Plus 5 extras: search, logging, backups, replicas, CI/CD. CBA: these 10 items are the production checklist.

Q5
Why should you use Elasticsearch for production search?
Show Answer
Answer

SQLite-based search (default) doesn't scale and only works on a single pod. Elasticsearch provides: distributed full-text search, high availability with multiple nodes, fast queries across millions of entities/docs, and shared access for all Backstage replicas.

Explanation

SQLite search = single pod only, doesn't scale. Elasticsearch = distributed, HA, fast full-text. Production requirement for multi-replica setups. CBA: know that SQLite search is dev-only; Elasticsearch is production.

Q6
What does yarn backstage-cli migrate do?
Show Answer
Answer

It applies database schema migrations that come with new Backstage versions. When you upgrade Backstage, the database schema may change — migrate updates your PostgreSQL tables to match. Always backup before running this command.

Explanation

yarn backstage-cli migrate = applies DB schema changes for new versions. Updates PostgreSQL tables. Always backup first — migrations can fail. CBA: know this command and that backup is mandatory before running it.

Q7
How do you configure a managed PostgreSQL service for Backstage?
Show Answer
Answer

In app-config.yaml: backend.database.client: pg, connection.host: ${POSTGRES_HOST} (RDS/Cloud SQL endpoint), connection.port: 5432, connection.user/password via env vars. Use SSL connection. Configure the managed service with automated backups and monitoring.

Explanation

Managed PostgreSQL config: client: pg, host (RDS/Cloud SQL), port 5432, user/password via env vars, SSL enabled. Automated backups + monitoring on the managed side. CBA: know the config keys and env var pattern.

Q8
Your Backstage upgrade failed and the app won't start. How do you recover?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Rollback the deployment: helm rollback backstage to previous version
2. Restore PostgreSQL from backup if migrations corrupted data
3. Check logs for the specific error
4. Fix the issue in staging before retrying
5. Never upgrade production without testing in staging first.

Explanation

Failed upgrade recovery: helm rollback + DB restore + logs + fix in staging + retry. Key: always test in staging first. CBA: know the recovery sequence and that staging testing is mandatory.

Q9
What cloud storage options exist for TechDocs in production?
Show Answer
Answer

Google Cloud Storage (GCS), AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, or OpenStack Swift. Configure the publisher in app-config.yaml: techdocs.publisher.type: 'googleGcs' with bucket name and credentials. Cloud storage = shared access for all K8s replicas.

Explanation

4 cloud storage options: GCS, S3, Azure Blob, Swift. Config: techdocs.publisher.type. All K8s replicas share the same bucket. CBA: know the 4 options and that cloud storage = multi-pod consistency.

Q10
You need to migrate Backstage from SQLite to PostgreSQL. What are the steps?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Set up PostgreSQL (managed service or K8s StatefulSet)
2. Export SQLite data (if needed)
3. Update app-config.yaml: client: pg with connection details
4. Set PostgreSQL env vars (POSTGRES_HOST, POSTGRES_PASSWORD)
5. Run yarn backstage-cli migrate to create schema
6. Test in staging
7. Deploy to production
Note: SQLite → PostgreSQL migration may require a fresh start if schema differs.

Explanation

SQLite → PostgreSQL migration: setup PG, export if needed, update config to pg, set env vars, migrate, test, deploy. May need fresh start if schema incompatible. CBA: know the migration steps and that it may not be lossless.

27.2 Logging — Winston Structured Logging

📝 Winston Logger

Backstage uses Winston — a structured JSON logging library for Node.js. All logs are output as JSON, making them easy to parse, ship, and query.

⚙️ Configuration

Set log level via LOG_LEVEL env var. debug for dev (verbose), info for production (important events only). NEVER use debug in production — excessive volume + sensitive data risk.

AspectDevelopmentProduction
Log Leveldebug (detailed)info (important events)
OutputConsole (pretty-printed)JSON → Loki/ELK/Splunk
Request IDsOptionalRequired (for tracing)
VolumeHigh (all requests)Controlled (errors + key events)

27.3 Alerting — What to Monitor & Where to Route

AlertThresholdRoute ToPriority
Backstage is down>1 minute🔴 PagerDutyCritical
Error rate spike>5% of requests🔴 PagerDutyCritical
DB connection failureAny occurrence🔴 PagerDutyCritical
Certificate expiring<30 days🟡 SlackWarning
Disk space high>80%🟡 SlackWarning
High latencyp95 > 2 seconds🟡 SlackWarning
⚠️ CBA Exam Note — Alert Routing

Critical = PagerDuty (wakes someone up). Warning = Slack (can wait until morning). The CBA may ask: "An alert fires for 85% disk usage — where should it go?" Answer: Slack (warning threshold, not critical).

27.4 Backstage Analytics — Measuring Developer Productivity

📊 Catalog Analytics

Most viewed entities, most searched terms. Shows what services developers care about most.

🚀 Template Analytics

Most used templates, average time-to-create. Measures self-service adoption.

👥 User Analytics

Daily active users, new vs returning, session duration. Tracks portal engagement.

💡 ROI Justification

Use Backstage's built-in analytics API or integrate Google Analytics/Matomo. Track: "How many services were created via templates this month?" (self-service adoption) and "How many daily active users?" (portal engagement). These numbers justify Backstage investment to leadership.

Catalog/api/catalogCRUD on entities/entities, /locations, /entity-facets
Scaffolder/api/scaffolder/v2Execute templates/tasks, /tasks/:id, /tasks/:id/eventstream
Search/api/searchQuery search index/query — accepts ?term= and filter params
TechDocs/api/techdocsAccess documentation/metadata/:kind/:ns/:name, /docs/:kind/:ns/:name/*
Auth/api/authToken management/:provider/refresh, /:provider/logout

Authentication: All API calls require Authorization: Bearer <token>. Tokens come from the auth provider (e.g., GitHub OAuth). For service-to-service automation, use a Backstage-generated service token configured in app-config.yaml under backend.auth.keys.

📖 List & Get

GET /entities with ?filter=kind=Component,spec.lifecycle=production. Get single: /entities/by-name/:kind/:namespace/:name.

✏️ Create & Update

POST /entities (push JSON), POST /locations (register URL — GitOps style), PUT /entities/by-uid/:uid (update).

🗑️ Delete & Refresh

DELETE /entities/by-uid/:uid (needs delete permission). POST /refresh (force re-read all). POST /locations/:id (refresh one).

28.3 Scaffolder REST API — Templates as Code

The Scaffolder API lets you trigger software templates from any system — CI/CD pipelines, Slack bots, internal CLIs, or even scheduled jobs.

Scaffolder API — Execute & Track Templates
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                      SCAFFOLDER v2 API FLOW                                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  1. SUBMIT TASK                                                           │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ POST /api/scaffolder/v2/tasks                                       │  │
  │  │ Body: { templateRef: "template:default/django-service",             │  │
  │  │         values: { name: "my-svc", owner: "team-plat" } }            │  │
  │  │ Response: { "id": "abc-123", "status": "open" }                     │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                   │                                      │
  │  2. TRACK PROGRESS                ▼                                      │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ GET /api/scaffolder/v2/tasks/abc-123                                │  │
  │  │ Response: { "status": "processing" | "completed" | "failed" }       │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                   │                                      │
  │  3. STREAM LOGS (SSE)             ▼                                      │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ GET /api/scaffolder/v2/tasks/abc-123/eventstream                    │  │
  │  │ → Server-Sent Events — real-time step-by-step log output            │  │
  │  │ → event: log | data: "Fetching template skeleton..."                │  │
  │  │ → event: complete | data: "Template execution finished"             │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🚀 Execute a Template

POST /api/scaffolder/v2/tasks. Body: templateRef + values. Returns taskId. Async — template runs in background.

📊 Track Task Status

GET /tasks/:taskId → status (open/processing/completed/failed). GET /tasks/:taskId/eventstream → SSE real-time logs.

🔑 CBA Key Concept — Scaffolder v2 (Not v1!)

The CBA exam tests on v2 (/api/scaffolder/v2/). v1 is deprecated. v2 introduced async task-based execution: submit a task → get taskId → poll/stream for results. This is a critical architectural improvement because templates can take minutes to run. Always reference v2 endpoints in exam answers.

28.4 Automation Examples — CI/CD & Beyond

Here are real-world examples you can use in your pipelines:

Auto-Register a Service in CI/CD

# Register a new entity via CI/CD pipeline
curl -X POST \
  https://backstage.anihpj.com/api/catalog/entities \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BACKSTAGE_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "apiVersion": "backstage.io/v1alpha1",
    "kind": "Component",
    "metadata": {
      "name": "new-service",
      "description": "Auto-registered from CI/CD"
    },
    "spec": {
      "type": "service",
      "lifecycle": "production",
      "owner": "team-platform"
    }
  }'

Trigger a Template from CI/CD

# Trigger a Django service template from CI/CD
curl -X POST \
  https://backstage.anihpj.com/api/scaffolder/v2/tasks \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BACKSTAGE_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "templateRef": "template:default/django-service",
    "values": {
      "name": "new-service",
      "owner": "team-platform",
      "description": "Created via CI pipeline"
    }
  }'

Sync External Data into Catalog

Use the API to push data from external sources (CMDB, asset management, spreadsheets) into Backstage's catalog. This is how large orgs migrate from legacy systems: write a script that transforms external data → entity JSON → POST to catalog API. Run as a cron job for ongoing sync.

⚡ SPEED TIP: The Catalog API is the most-tested API on the CBA. Know: (1) POST /entities creates, (2) POST /locations registers, (3) POST /refresh refreshes all. The Scaffolder API uses /scaffolder/v2/tasks (not v1!). For automation, always use Bearer tokens from env vars — never hardcode.

📝 Chapter 28 — CBA Practice Questions (10 Questions)

Q1
How do you list all entities via the Catalog API?
Show Answer
Answer

GET /api/catalog/entities. Returns JSON array of all entities. Supports filtering: ?filter=kind=Component,spec.lifecycle=production.

Explanation

The Catalog API is Read-only by default for GET requests. The filter query parameter uses Backstage's entity filter syntax: kind=X,spec.lifecycle=Y. This is the most common API call for building automation scripts — always check /entities first before creating duplicates.

# List All Entities (with filters)
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "http://localhost:7007/api/catalog/entities"

# Filter: only Components in production
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "http://localhost:7007/api/catalog/entities?filter=kind=Component,spec.lifecycle=production"
Q2
How do you create an entity via the API? Which two approaches exist?
Show Answer
Answer

Approach 1: POST /api/catalog/entities with a JSON body containing the full entity definition. Approach 2: POST /api/catalog/locations to register a URL/file path pointing to a catalog-info.yaml — Backstage then ingests and processes it.

Explanation

Approach 1 (POST /entities) is "push-based" — you push the entity directly. Approach 2 (POST /locations) is "pull-based" — you register a source and Backstage pulls from it. The CBA favors Approach 2 because it follows GitOps: the catalog-info.yaml lives in Git, and Backstage auto-discovers it. Approach 1 is useful for programmatic/automated entity creation where no Git repo exists.

# Approach 1: Push entity directly (POST /entities)
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"apiVersion":"backstage.io/v1alpha1","kind":"Component",...}' \
  http://localhost:7007/api/catalog/entities

# Approach 2: Register location (POST /locations) — GitOps style
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"type":"url","target":"https://github.com/org/repo/blob/main/catalog-info.yaml"}' \
  http://localhost:7007/api/catalog/locations
Q3
What's the difference between POST /entities and POST /locations?
Show Answer
Answer

POST /entities directly creates the entity in the catalog. POST /locations registers a source (URL or file) that Backstage will read and process — entities are created as a result of ingestion. Locations are the preferred approach for GitOps workflows.

Explanation

Think of it like this: POST /entities is like handing a book directly to a librarian. POST /locations is like telling the librarian "new books arrive at this URL every day — go check it." The location approach scales better because one location URL can produce many entities (e.g., a GitHub org with 100 repos, each with catalog-info.yaml).

Q4
What endpoint refreshes the entire catalog? When should you use it?
Show Answer
Answer

POST /api/catalog/refresh. Use after adding/updating catalog locations or after changes to catalog-info.yaml files in Git. Forces immediate re-processing. In production, Backstage auto-refreshes periodically (configurable via catalog.processingInterval), but you can trigger this for urgent updates.

Explanation

By default, Backstage refreshes the catalog every few minutes. But when you push a new catalog-info.yaml to GitHub and need it visible NOW (e.g., during a demo or incident), POST /refresh forces immediate ingestion. Note: this refreshes ALL locations, which can be expensive on large catalogs. For a single location, use POST /api/catalog/locations/:id instead.

Q5
How do you execute a software template via the Scaffolder API?
Show Answer
Answer

POST /api/scaffolder/v2/tasks with a JSON body containing templateRef (e.g., "template:default/django-service") and values (the template input parameters). Returns a taskId. Track progress with GET /api/scaffolder/v2/tasks/:taskId.

Explanation

The templateRef format is template:<namespace>/<template-name>. The values object must match the template's defined parameters in its template.yaml. The Scaffolder API is asynchronous — it returns immediately with a taskId, and the template runs in the background. Always check the task status before assuming success: completed = success, failed = check the event stream for errors.

# Execute a Template via Scaffolder API
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "templateRef": "template:default/django-service",
    "values": { "name": "my-service", "owner": "team-platform" }
  }' \
  http://localhost:7007/api/scaffolder/v2/tasks
# Response: { "id": "abc-123", "status": "open" }

# Track progress
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  http://localhost:7007/api/scaffolder/v2/tasks/abc-123
Q6
How do you authenticate Backstage API calls?
Show Answer
Answer

All API calls require Authorization: Bearer <token> header. Tokens come from the auth provider (user tokens via OAuth). For service-to-service automation, configure backend.auth.keys in app-config.yaml to generate service tokens.

Explanation

There are two token types: User tokens (obtained via OAuth login — used for user-driven API calls) and Service tokens (static tokens configured in app-config.yaml under backend.auth.keys — used for CI/CD automation). Service tokens bypass the OAuth flow and are ideal for pipelines. Never share user tokens in scripts — always use service tokens for automation.

Q7
What are the 5 main API categories in Backstage?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Catalog API (/api/catalog) — CRUD on entities. 2. Scaffolder API (/api/scaffolder/v2) — execute templates. 3. Search API (/api/search) — query search index. 4. TechDocs API (/api/techdocs) — access documentation. 5. Auth API (/api/auth) — token management.

Explanation

Memorize these 5 for the CBA exam. The most-tested are Catalog and Scaffolder. Remember: the Scaffolder API uses /v2/ (not v1!), and the Search API is /query (not /search — that's the UI route). Each API category is backed by a separate backend plugin that you can extend or replace.

Q8
How do you get entity counts grouped by kind (facets)?
Show Answer
Answer

GET /api/catalog/entity-facets. Returns JSON with aggregate counts: "kind":[{"value":"Component","count":42},{"value":"API","count":15},...]. Also supports faceting by spec.lifecycle, spec.owner, and metadata.namespace.

Explanation

Facets are pre-computed aggregate counts — they're fast even on catalogs with 10,000+ entities. Use them for building dashboards (e.g., "42 Components, 15 APIs, 8 Systems"). The facet endpoint doesn't return entity details, just counts. This is a CBA favorite because it tests whether you understand the difference between listing entities (heavy) and faceting (lightweight).

Q9
How do you track the status of a Scaffolder task?
Show Answer
Answer

GET /api/scaffolder/v2/tasks/:taskId returns the current status: open → processing → completed or failed. For real-time streaming, use GET /api/scaffolder/v2/tasks/:taskId/eventstream (SSE — Server-Sent Events).

Explanation

The task lifecycle is: open (queued) → processing (running template actions) → completed (success) or failed (error). The /eventstream endpoint uses SSE (Server-Sent Events) — a one-way stream from server to client — which is ideal for CI/CD pipelines that want real-time log output. Poll /tasks/:taskId every 2-3 seconds for a simple status check; use /eventstream for live debugging.

Q10
What's the difference between Scaffolder API v1 and v2?
Show Answer
Answer

v2 (/api/scaffolder/v2/) is the current version with task-based execution and event streaming. v1 is deprecated. The CBA exam tests on v2. Always use /api/scaffolder/v2/tasks, never /api/scaffolder/v1/.

Explanation

v1 used a synchronous "job" model — you submitted a template and waited for the full response. v2 introduced task-based async execution: submit a task, get a taskId immediately, and poll/stream for results. This was a critical architectural improvement because templates can take minutes to run (cloning repos, running CI, etc.). The CBA exam explicitly tests on v2 — any answer mentioning v1 is a distractor.

Chapter 29: Performance, Scaling & High Availability

As your Backstage adoption grows from 10 to 10,000 developers, you need to scale. This chapter covers performance optimization at every layer, horizontal scaling on Kubernetes, high availability architectures, and caching strategies for enterprise deployments.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1.5 hours📈 Scale🎯 CBA 32%

🎯 Learning Objectives

  • ✅ Identify performance bottlenecks across frontend, backend, catalog, and search layers
  • ✅ Configure horizontal scaling with HPA on Kubernetes
  • ✅ Design a highly available Backstage architecture (multi-AZ, DB failover)
  • ✅ Implement caching at multiple levels (Redis, CDN, DB query cache)
  • ✅ Monitor performance using Backstage's built-in /metrics endpoint

🎯 CBA Exam Relevance — Customizing Backstage 32%

The CBA tests your understanding of Backstage's stateless architecture and scaling principles. Expect questions about why multiple replicas work (stateless design), what external dependencies are needed (PostgreSQL, cloud storage), and how caching fits into the architecture.

💡 CBA TIP: The key exam concept is that Backstage pods are stateless — any pod can handle any request. State lives in PostgreSQL (user data, catalog) and cloud storage (TechDocs). This is WHY horizontal scaling works.

29.1 Performance Optimization

Backstage performance must be tuned at every layer. Here's a systematic breakdown:

📈 Performance Optimization — Layer by Layer

LayerBottleneckSolutionImpact
FrontendLarge JS bundle, slow page loadsCode splitting, lazy loading, tree shaking🔽 40-60% load time
Backend APISlow database queriesQuery optimization, connection pooling, indexing🔽 50-80% query time
Catalog IngestionProcessing 1000s of entitiesBatch processing, incremental ingestion, parallel workers🔽 60% processing time
SearchSlow full-text queriesElasticsearch tuning, index optimization, sharding🔽 70% search latency
TechDocsRebuilding all docs on every changeExternal build storage, CDN, incremental builds🔽 50% build time

Monitoring: Backstage exposes a /metrics endpoint (Prometheus format) with request latency, error rates, and resource usage. Use Grafana dashboards to track trends and identify bottlenecks before they impact users.

DR Plan: Git contains all config (GitOps) — redeploy in new region in <30 min. Backup PostgreSQL daily, retain 30 days.

29.4 Caching Strategies — Speed at Every Layer

⚡ Multi-Layer Caching Architecture

Cache LayerTechnologyWhat It CachesTTL
CDNCloudFront / Cloud CDNStatic assets, TechDocs HTML1 hour — 1 day
Service WorkerBrowser SWJS bundles, CSS, iconsUntil new deploy
Backend CacheRedisSessions, auth tokens, API responses5–15 minutes
DatabasePostgreSQL shared_buffersFrequently queried entitiesAutomatic (LRU)
Catalog ReadsIn-memory (plugin)Entity definitionsConfigurable

Configuration example in app-config.yaml:

# app-config.yaml — Cache configuration
backend:
  cache:
    store: redis
    connection: redis://redis-service:6379
    defaultTtl: 300  # 5 minutes in seconds
  reading:
    allow:
      - host: "backstage.anihpj.com"

catalog:
  processingInterval: { minutes: 5 }  # How often to check for changes
  readCache:
    enabled: true
    maxAge: { minutes: 60 }  # Cache entity reads for 60 minutes

Pro tip: Redis is the most impactful cache — it reduces database load by 60-80% for repeated queries. For TechDocs, a CDN in front of your cloud storage bucket provides near-instant page loads globally.

⚡ SPEED TIP: Remember: Backstage is stateless → horizontal scaling works. The 3 external dependencies for HA are: PostgreSQL (data), Cloud Storage (TechDocs), Elasticsearch (search). If any of these is a single point of failure, Backstage isn't truly HA.

📝 Chapter 29 — CBA Practice Questions (10 Questions)

Q1
Why can Backstage be horizontally scaled across multiple replicas?
Show Answer
Answer

Backstage pods are stateless. All state lives in external services: PostgreSQL (catalog, users, sessions) and cloud storage (TechDocs). Any pod can handle any request since they all connect to the same database and storage.

Explanation

This is the single most important architectural concept for the CBA. Unlike monolithic apps that store session data in memory (requiring sticky sessions), Backstage was designed cloud-native from day one. Every pod is interchangeable — if Pod A handles your login and Pod B handles your catalog search, it doesn't matter. This is why Kubernetes HPA works seamlessly with Backstage.

Q2
What Kubernetes resource enables automatic scaling of Backstage pods?
Show Answer
Answer

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA). Configure with: kubectl autoscale deployment backstage --cpu-percent=70 --min=3 --max=10. HPA monitors CPU/memory metrics and automatically adds/removes pods based on load.

Explanation

HPA works specifically because Backstage is stateless. If Backstage required sticky sessions, HPA would cause problems — a new pod wouldn't have the user's session data. The minimum 3 replicas ensures high availability (survive 1 pod failure). The max (10+) depends on your PostgreSQL connection pool size — too many pods can overwhelm the database.

Q3
What are the 3 external dependencies needed for a highly available Backstage?
Show Answer
Answer

1. PostgreSQL (with replication/failover) — stores catalog, users, sessions. 2. Cloud Storage (S3/GCS/Azure Blob, multi-region) — stores TechDocs. 3. Elasticsearch (cluster) — powers search. All must be HA for Backstage to be HA.

Explanation

If any of these 3 is a single point of failure, Backstage is NOT truly HA. PostgreSQL failing means no catalog access. Cloud storage failing means no TechDocs. Elasticsearch failing means search is broken. This is a common CBA "trick question" — they'll describe a setup with multiple Backstage pods but a single PostgreSQL instance and ask "Is this HA?" Answer: No.

Q4
What caching options are available for Backstage? Which is most impactful?
Show Answer
Answer

Redis (backend cache — most impactful, 60-80% DB load reduction), CDN (static assets + TechDocs), Service Worker (frontend JS/CSS), PostgreSQL shared_buffers (database level), Catalog in-memory cache (entity reads). Redis is the most impactful for API performance.

Explanation

Redis sits between the Backstage backend and PostgreSQL. When a user requests an entity, Backstage checks Redis first — if found (cache hit), it returns immediately without touching the database. This is critical because database connections are expensive. A well-configured Redis cache can reduce PostgreSQL load by 60-80%, enabling fewer database resources to serve more users.

Q5
How do you configure Redis caching in Backstage?
Show Answer
Answer

In app-config.yaml, set backend.cache.store: redis and backend.cache.connection: redis://redis-service:6379. Optional: backend.cache.defaultTtl: 300 (seconds = 5 minutes). Requires the Redis plugin to be installed.

Explanation

The store field accepts memory (default, per-pod, not shared) or redis (shared across all pods). Always use redis in multi-pod deployments — memory caching means each pod has its own cache, leading to inconsistency and wasted memory. The defaultTtl (Time To Live) controls how long cached data lives before being refreshed from the database.

Q6
What makes Backstage highly available? List the key components.
Show Answer
Answer

Multi-AZ K8s cluster (≥3 zones), multiple Backstage replicas, PostgreSQL with streaming replication + auto-failover (Patroni/PgBouncer), cloud storage with cross-region replication, Elasticsearch cluster (≥3 nodes), load balancer with health checks, GitOps config for DR.

Explanation

The key insight: HA is NOT just about multiple Backstage pods. It's about ensuring EVERY dependency is HA. The "weakest link" principle applies — if PostgreSQL is a single instance, your entire Backstage is a single point of failure regardless of how many pods you run. The CBA will test this concept by presenting scenarios with 5 Backstage pods but a single DB — the correct answer is "NOT highly available."

Q7
What are the 5 performance optimization layers in Backstage?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Frontend: Code splitting, lazy loading. 2. Backend API: Query optimization, connection pooling. 3. Catalog Ingestion: Batch processing, parallel workers. 4. Search: Elasticsearch tuning, index optimization. 5. TechDocs: External build storage, CDN, incremental builds.

Explanation

Performance optimization is never one-size-fits-all. The frontend bottleneck (slow page loads) requires different solutions than the catalog bottleneck (slow entity processing). The CBA expects you to match the problem to the solution: "Users complain about slow page loads" → Frontend optimization. "New entities take 10 minutes to appear" → Catalog ingestion optimization. "Search returns results slowly" → Elasticsearch tuning.

Q8
Where does Backstage store its state? Why does this matter for scaling?
Show Answer
Answer

Backstage pods are stateless — state lives in external services: PostgreSQL (catalog data, user sessions) and cloud storage (TechDocs files). This matters because it means ANY pod can serve ANY request, enabling true horizontal scaling without sticky sessions.

Explanation

This is the architectural foundation that everything else builds on. Compare with a stateful app like Jenkins (where each agent has local state): you can't just add more Jenkins masters. Backstage's stateless design means scaling is as simple as kubectl scale deployment backstage --replicas=5. The load balancer can use round-robin — no session affinity needed.

Q9
What's the disaster recovery plan for Backstage?
Show Answer
Answer

Since all config is in Git (GitOps), you can redeploy Backstage to a new region in <30 minutes. Backup PostgreSQL daily (retain 30 days). Cloud storage (TechDocs) should use cross-region replication. Elasticsearch snapshots for search index recovery.

Explanation

The beauty of GitOps: your app-config.yaml, catalog-info.yaml files, and template definitions are all in Git. If your K8s cluster burns down, you: (1) create a new K8s cluster, (2) restore PostgreSQL from backup, (3) run kubectl apply on your Backstage manifests, (4) Backstage is back. Cloud storage cross-region replication means TechDocs data is already in the backup region — no restore needed.

Q10
How do you monitor Backstage performance in production?
Show Answer
Answer

Backstage exposes a /metrics endpoint in Prometheus format. Use Prometheus + Grafana dashboards to track request latency, error rates, CPU/memory, and catalog processing times. Set up alerts for high latency (>2s p95) and error rate spikes.

Explanation

The Prometheus /metrics endpoint is built into Backstage's backend — no extra plugin needed. Key metrics to watch: http_request_duration_seconds (p95 latency), http_requests_total (request rate), catalog_processing_duration_seconds (catalog ingestion time). Alert when p95 latency exceeds 2 seconds or error rate exceeds 1%. This is an often-overlooked CBA topic — they want to know you understand observability.

Chapter 30: Security Best Practices

Security is non-negotiable for production Backstage. This chapter covers the complete security checklist, secret management strategies, network security layers, vulnerability scanning, and audit logging — everything you need to run Backstage securely in production.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1.5 hours🔒 Security🎯 CBA 32%

🎯 Learning Objectives

  • ✅ Complete a production security checklist for Backstage
  • ✅ Manage secrets securely using K8s Secrets, Vault, or cloud secret managers
  • ✅ Configure network security: TLS, NetworkPolicies, WAF, CORS, rate limiting
  • ✅ Run vulnerability scans on dependencies and container images
  • ✅ Enable audit logging and set up security monitoring

🎯 CBA Exam Relevance — Customizing Backstage 32%

The CBA exam tests security fundamentals: where to store secrets (NOT in Git!), how to configure CORS, which auth providers to use, and the principle of least privilege. Expect at least 2-3 security-specific questions.

💡 CBA TIP: The #1 security question on the exam: "Where should secrets be stored?" Answer: Never in app-config.yaml or Git. Use ${ENV_VAR} references, K8s Secrets, or external vaults. This is almost guaranteed to appear.

30.1 Production Security Checklist

🔒 Backstage Production Security Checklist

#CheckRequirementPriority
1HTTPS EverywhereTLS 1.2+ on all endpoints. Redirect HTTP→HTTPS.🔴 Critical
2Auth EnforcedSSO required. No guest access in production.🔴 Critical
3Secrets ExternalNo secrets in app-config.yaml or Git. Use K8s Secrets/Vault.🔴 Critical
4RBAC — Least PrivilegeUsers get minimum permissions needed. Default deny.🟡 High
5Image UpdatesRegularly update Backstage images. Scan for CVEs.🟡 High
6WAF + Rate LimitingWeb Application Firewall on Ingress. Rate limit API calls.🟡 High
7Audit LoggingEnable and ship audit logs to SIEM (Splunk/Datadog).🟢 Medium
8Network PoliciesRestrict pod-to-pod traffic. Backstage pods → DB only.🟢 Medium
9CORS ConfiguredRestrict API origins. Never use * in production.🟢 Medium
10Dependency ScanningAutomated yarn audit / Snyk / Dependabot in CI.🟢 Medium

30.2 Secret Management — Never in Git

⚠️ The Golden Rule

NEVER put secrets (tokens, passwords, keys) in app-config.yaml or any file committed to Git. Always use environment variable substitution: ${GITHUB_TOKEN}. The CBA exam WILL ask about this.

Environment Variables (K8s)

# Kubernetes Secret — store sensitive values
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: backstage-secrets
type: Opaque
stringData:
  GITHUB_TOKEN: "ghp_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"
  POSTGRES_PASSWORD: "supersecretpassword"
  BACKSTAGE_SECRET: "random-generated-secret"
---
# Deployment — reference secrets as env vars
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: backstage
        env:
        - name: GITHUB_TOKEN
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: backstage-secrets
              key: GITHUB_TOKEN

External Vaults (Advanced)

For enterprise: HashiCorp Vault (dynamic secrets, auto-rotation), AWS Secrets Manager (auto-rotation, IAM integration), or Azure Key Vault. Use External Secrets Operator (ESO) to sync vault secrets into K8s Secrets automatically. Token rotation: Use fine-grained GitHub PATs (scoped to specific repos) and rotate every 90 days. Automate rotation via CI pipeline.

30.3 Network Security — Defense in Depth

TLS & Ingress

# Ingress with TLS + WAF annotations (NGINX example)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: backstage-ingress
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: "letsencrypt-prod"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rate-limit: "100r/s"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/whitelist-source-range: "10.0.0.0/8"
spec:
  tls:
  - hosts: [backstage.anihpj.com]
    secretName: backstage-tls
  rules:
  - host: backstage.anihpj.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: backstage
            port:
              number: 7007

NetworkPolicies & CORS

NetworkPolicies: Restrict Backstage pods to only talk to PostgreSQL, Redis, and Elasticsearch. Block all other egress. Deny all ingress except from the load balancer.

CORS Configuration in app-config.yaml:

# app-config.yaml — CORS + CSP
backend:
  cors:
    origin: "https://backstage.anihpj.com"  # NEVER use "*" in prod!
    methods: [GET, POST, PUT, DELETE]
    credentials: true
  csp:
    connect-src: ["'self'", "https://api.anihpj.com"]
    img-src: ["'self'", "data:", "https://avatars.githubusercontent.com"]

30.4 Vulnerability Management — Scan Everything

🛡️ Security Scanning Tools

ToolWhat It ScansIntegrationFrequency
yarn auditNode.js dependenciesCI pipeline (GitHub Actions)Every commit
SnykDependencies + base imageCI + GitHub integrationEvery PR
Dependabotnpm/yarn packagesGitHub native (auto-PRs)Daily
TrivyContainer imagesCI pipeline (image build)Every build
GrypeContainer images + SBOMCI pipelineEvery build
Backstage UpdatesPlatform itselfManual upgrade cycleMonthly

Workflow: 1) CI builds Backstage image → 2) Trivy/Grype scans it → 3) If critical CVEs found, fail the build → 4) Dependabot auto-opens PRs for vulnerable npm packages → 5) Monthly Backstage version upgrades for platform-level fixes. Subscribe to GitHub Security Advisories for Backstage.

⚡ SPEED TIP: The 3 things the CBA will ask about secrets: (1) Use ${ENV_VAR} in config, never hardcode. (2) K8s Secrets + External Vaults for production. (3) Rotate tokens regularly. Also remember: CORS origin must be specific — "*" is a security fail in production.
